Ferra.rs — User Guide

Introduction

Ferra is a Rust framework for building HTTP APIs from a single source of truth: a Sea-ORM entity with one derive, #[derive(FerraModel)]. From it Ferra derives the routes, the SQL queries, the OpenAPI document, the documentation page, the hypermedia links and the authorization checks, at compile time. If the struct changes, everything downstream changes with it. If the generated code would be inconsistent, the build fails.

The priorities, in order, are security, developer experience, and the experience of the AI agents that write code against Ferra. Where they pull apart, security wins: a model declares who may do what, and a route that has no rule is refused, not served.

The problem Ferra solves

Building a conventional REST API means describing the same data structure multiple times:

  • once in a migration file (the database schema),
  • once as a Rust struct (the model),
  • once in each handler (request body, response type, SQL query),
  • once in OpenAPI annotations (#[utoipa::path(...)], response schemas),
  • once in validation rules.

Every copy can drift from the others, and none of these mismatches are caught at compile time. A field renamed in the struct but not in the OpenAPI annotation is a silent documentation lie. A validation rule missing from one handler is a silent security gap.

Ferra collapses the copies into one struct:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")] // every operation requires a valid token
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(min_length = 1, max_length = 255, filterable, sortable)]
    pub title: String,
    #[field(min = 1888, max = 2100)]
    pub year: i32,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

(The hidden lines are the imports and the Relation enum that every Sea-ORM entity carries; Getting started shows a complete file.)

What you get

Mount the model on a Foundry, give it a JWT configuration, and serve it:

use ferra::{ClaimCheck, FerraIdentity, FerraModel, Foundry, HmacAlgorithm, JwtConfig};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct MyClaims { sub: String }
impl FerraIdentity for MyClaims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str { &self.sub }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool { false }
}
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?).await?;
    let jwt = JwtConfig::single_secret(
        "key-1",
        std::env::var("JWT_SECRET")?,
        HmacAlgorithm::Hs256,
        ClaimCheck::expect("https://auth.example.com/"),
        ClaimCheck::expect("films-api"),
    )?;
    let app = Foundry::new(conn)
        .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
        .with_auth::<MyClaims>(jwt)
        .mount::<film::Model>()
        // Public in development: /docs needs no token (see `with_docs_protected` in ferra-openapi.md).
        .with_docs()
        .build();
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
    axum::serve(
        listener,
        app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>(),
    )
    .await?;
    Ok(())
}

Running it gives you all of the following, with no further code.

CRUD routes

MethodPathDescription
GET/filmsPaginated collection, ?page=1&per_page=20 (filter[...], sort and cursor for the fields that opt in)
GET/films/{id}One resource by key
POST/filmsCreate: 201 and a Location header; the server chooses the key
PUT/films/{id}Update the row the path names: 200, or 404
PATCH/films/{id}Change the fields the body names (application/merge-patch+json) and leave the others: 200, or 404
DELETE/films/{id}Delete: 204, or 404

Pagination is first-class. The collection endpoint answers a page envelope with items, total, page, per_page and, in the HAL representation, the _links for self, next, prev, first and last; Pagination has the cursor mode.

Authorization that refuses by default

Every route passes one checkpoint before the path, the query or the body is read. A model with no declared posture does not compile (FRG-100), a model that needs an identity does not mount on a chain without .with_auth() (FRG-151), and #[authorize(...)] states a rule per operation (IsOwner, HasRole(...), Authenticated, Anyone), with the owner of a row read from the token. Authentication and Authorization is the page.

Hypermedia _links in the HAL representation

By default, and with Accept: application/hal+json, every item response includes a _links block following the HAL standard, so that clients and AI agents can navigate the API without prior knowledge of its URL structure. Accept: application/json gets the same body without it (Response representations):

{
  "id":    1,
  "title": "Amélie",
  "year":  2001,
  "_links": {
    "self":       { "href": "/films/1" },
    "collection": { "href": "/films" }
  }
}

The links, like the Location header, are relative by default: resolve them against the URL you called. The request’s Host and X-Forwarded-* headers are never read, so that a client cannot make the API emit links to another origin. Configure the public origin once with .with_base_url("https://api.example.com")? for absolute links (Ferra HTTP).

An OpenAPI document that cannot drift

The OpenAPI 3.2 document is served at /docs/openapi.json and the interactive Scalar page at /docs (when the chain says .with_docs()). Both are derived from the same struct the routes are derived from, so they cannot disagree with the running code. There are no annotations to forget.

Add a field to Film and it appears in the document, the Scalar page, the request validation and the SQL insert, at the next cargo build.

Typed SQL, bound by construction

Every query a generated route runs is parameterized: a filter value is bound, a sort key is taken only from the fields the model declares sortable, a cursor is decoded before any query is built. The generated routes have no mechanism to put request data in SQL text. Your own code keeps Sea-ORM’s full SQL access on the connection it owns (sea_orm::Statement, execute_unprepared): there, the query is yours. The framework has #![forbid(unsafe_code)] on every crate.

RFC 7807 errors, typed and machine-readable

Every error response follows RFC 7807 problem details. The type field is a URI from a closed set the framework maintains as a constant, not a free-form string. SDK generators and AI agents can produce a typed branch for every possible error.

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found",
  "title":  "Resource Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "films/42 not found"
}

The complete error URI table is in Error Handling.

Validation on the field

#[field(min_length, max_length, min, max, pattern, email, url, required)] become garde validators, applied on POST and PUT before the query runs, and on the values a PATCH sets (a field it leaves out is not judged). A violation answers 422 with an errors array of {field, code, message}, every failing field in one response (Ferra Forge).

Behaviors

#[behavior(timestampable, soft_delete)] uses the created_at, updated_at and deleted_at columns of your table (under other names with timestampable(created = "..", updated = "..") and soft_delete(column = "..")) and adds the matching logic: both stamps are in every read response, an update refreshes updated_at in its own statement, a delete sets deleted_at (which no response carries), and a soft-deleted row is a 404, never a deleted record (Behaviors).

Security defaults, not security options

  • Rate limiting on mutation routes (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), out of the box, keyed on the peer address (serve with into_make_service_with_connect_info).
  • Body size cap: requests over 1 MiB are rejected before the body is read.
  • CORS: restrictive by default. You opt in to origins, not out of open access.
  • #![forbid(unsafe_code)] on every crate in the workspace.

Extending beyond the generated surface

The generated CRUD surface is a floor, not a ceiling. Foundry::build() returns a standard axum Router: hand-written routes merge in beside the generated ones, and answer with a body of their own:

use axum::{Json, Router, routing::get};
use ferra::{FerraError, Foundry};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, ferra::FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
async fn film_count(
    axum::extract::State(conn): axum::extract::State<DatabaseConnection>,
) -> Result<Json<u64>, FerraError> {
    let count = film::Entity::find()
        .count(&conn)
        .await
        .map_err(|err| FerraError::Internal(ferra::InternalError::new(err)))?;
    Ok(Json(count))
}

fn demo(conn: DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app: Router = Foundry::new(conn.clone())
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .mount::<film::Model>()
    .build()
    .merge(Router::new().route("/films/count", get(film_count)).with_state(conn));
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

A route of your own is not covered by Ferra’s authorization: protect it yourself, as Custom Handlers shows. It can reuse the FerraError enum and so emit the same RFC 7807 bodies: clients handle one error shape across the whole API.

What Ferra is not

Not an ORM. Database schema management (migrations, table creation) is Sea-ORM’s: sea-orm-migration or the Sea-ORM CLI, outside the framework. Ferra generates the routes and the queries; you manage the schema.

Not a general-purpose web framework. No template engines, no session handling, no WebSockets. Ferra is narrowly focused on REST, hypermedia and typed errors. When you need to go further, axum handlers compose directly alongside Ferra routes.

Not an identity provider. Ferra validates a JWT signed with a shared HMAC secret; it does not issue tokens, and in 0.9 it has no RS256/JWKS verifier or pluggable authenticator (Authentication and Authorization).

Not on crates.io. An application depends on a tag of the Git repository. The public contract of the 0.9 line is frozen, and a change of it needs a new minor version; Stability policy says what is in the contract, and Migrating from 0.8 to 0.9 what changed.

  • Authentication and Authorization: tokens, postures, #[authorize] rules, owned rows.
  • Ferra Core, Ferra DB, Ferra HTTP, Ferra OpenAPI: what each library crate does, and which part of it is the contract.

  • Compile-time diagnostics: every FRG-NNN code, with a bad and a good example, both compiled.

Getting started with Ferra

Ferra is a Rust framework for building HTTP APIs from a single Sea-ORM entity and one derive, #[derive(FerraModel)]. The entity gives you a CRUD router, an OpenAPI 3.2 document, a Scalar documentation page, hypermedia responses and typed RFC 7807 errors, all derived at compile time, with every route behind an authorization check that refuses by default.

This page takes you from cargo new to a running, protected, documented API. Every step below is run, as written, against a real database, by the cold_start check of the Ferra repository: if a step on this page is wrong, that check fails. Five minutes is the target, most of it spent compiling.

Create the project

cargo new my-api
cd my-api

Ferra is not published on crates.io: an application depends on a tag of the Ferra Git repository. Replace the Cargo.toml that cargo new wrote with:

[package]
name    = "my-api"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

[dev-dependencies]
ferra = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0", features = ["test-support"] }

ferra is the only Ferra crate you declare: ferra-core, ferra-db, ferra-forge, ferra-http and ferra-openapi are reached through it, and the repository’s own examples are held to that by the dep_gate check. The repository is private until the first release: your Git credentials must give Cargo access to it, for example with net.git-fetch-with-cli = true in .cargo/config.toml.

sea-orm is the one dependency you also declare yourself, with the same major version as Ferra (each release of Ferra names the major in its CHANGELOG.md). A different major is a second copy of the crate, and #[derive(FerraModel)] refuses it with FRG-400. cargo tree -d -i sea-orm prints nothing when there is a single copy. The facade also re-exports Sea-ORM whole, so an application may declare none and write ferra::sea_orm::…; Architecture shows that form.

The test-support feature, in [dev-dependencies] only, gives the example below the helper that signs a token; it is not in your application.

The model, and the server

A Ferra model is a Sea-ORM entity with the FerraModel derive next to DeriveEntityModel, and a posture: #[ferra(auth = "bearer")] says every operation requires a valid bearer token. A model with no posture does not compile (FRG-100): Ferra never decides for you between a public and a protected API.

Put this in src/main.rs:

use ferra::{ClaimCheck, FerraIdentity, FerraModel, Foundry, HmacAlgorithm, JwtConfig};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use sea_orm::{ConnectionTrait, Schema};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

mod film {
    use super::*;

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        #[sea_orm(unique)]
        #[field(filterable, sortable)]
        pub title: String,
        pub director: String,
        pub year: Option<i32>,
    }

    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

// What the token says about its bearer. Ferra needs two things of it:
// a stable id and a role test.
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Claims {
    sub: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    roles: Vec<String>,
}

impl FerraIdentity for Claims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str {
        &self.sub
    }
    fn has_role(&self, role: &str) -> bool {
        self.roles.iter().any(|r| r == role)
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // A bare URL leaves `acquire_timeout` at sqlx's 30 s, past the 10 s request
    // budget below. Under the budget, a full pool answers 503
    // `service_unavailable` (see ferra-db.md) instead of the budget's 503 `timeout`.
    let mut options = sea_orm::ConnectOptions::new(std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?);
    options.acquire_timeout(std::time::Duration::from_secs(3));
    let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(options).await?;

    // Development only: create the table when it is missing. A real
    // application owns its schema with `sea-orm-migration`.
    let table = Schema::new(conn.get_database_backend())
        .create_table_from_entity(film::Entity)
        .if_not_exists()
        .to_owned();
    conn.execute(&table).await?;

    // The secret comes from the environment, never from the source: at least
    // 32 bytes for HS256. A token must name this issuer and this audience.
    let jwt = JwtConfig::single_secret(
        "key-1",
        std::env::var("JWT_SECRET")?,
        HmacAlgorithm::Hs256,
        ClaimCheck::expect("https://auth.example.com/"),
        ClaimCheck::expect("my-api"),
    )?;

    // The key that signs the entity tags: at least 32 bytes, the same on every
    // replica, and never the JWT secret. The request budget is off unless you
    // set it: choose a value under your infrastructure's timeout (a gateway,
    // a proxy, a platform limit). 10 s plus the 1 s Ferra may spend after a
    // commit stays under the lowest common default, Envoy's 15 s route
    // timeout (API Gateway allows 29 s, Heroku 30 s, ALB and nginx 60 s). It is
    // a margin, not a maximum: a slow `COMMIT` is not cut, and with a
    // `BelongsTo` the read of the written row's parents after the commit is
    // under no deadline either (`acquire_timeout` bounds the wait for the
    // connection, `statement_timeout` the query).
    let app = Foundry::new(conn)
        .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
        .with_auth::<Claims>(jwt)
        .request_budget(std::time::Duration::from_secs(10))
        .mount::<film::Model>()
        // Public in development: /docs needs no token (see `with_docs_protected` in ferra-openapi.md).
        .with_docs()
        .build();

    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
    eprintln!("listening on 0.0.0.0:3000");
    // Serve with the peer address: the rate limiter keys on it, and the bare
    // router would answer every write with a 500.
    axum::serve(
        listener,
        app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>(),
    )
    .await?;
    Ok(())
}

What you get:

URLBehaviour
GET /filmsPaginated list (HAL _links, or flat JSON on Accept: application/json).
GET /films/{id}One film and its self-link.
POST /filmsCreate: validates, answers 201 Created. The server chooses id.
PUT /films/{id}Update the row named by the path.
PATCH /films/{id}Change the fields the body names (JSON merge patch); the others stay.
DELETE /films/{id}Delete.
GET /docs/openapi.jsonThe generated OpenAPI 3.2 document.
GET /docsThe Scalar page rendered from it.

The URL segment (films) is the model’s table name. To serve a table under another name, say so: #[ferra(resource = "movies")] on the model.

Errors come back as RFC 7807 application/problem+json, with a type from the closed namespace https://ferra.rs/errors/<name>.

A token to call it with

Ferra validates tokens; it does not issue them (your identity provider does). For development, sign one yourself with the helper of the test-support feature. Put this in examples/token.rs:

use ferra::HmacAlgorithm;
use ferra::testing::bearer;
use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Claims {
    sub: String,
    iss: &'static str,
    aud: &'static str,
    exp: u64,
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let now = std::time::SystemTime::now().duration_since(std::time::UNIX_EPOCH)?;
    let claims = Claims {
        sub: "alice".to_owned(),
        iss: "https://auth.example.com/",
        aud: "my-api",
        exp: now.as_secs() + 3600,
    };
    let secret = std::env::var("JWT_SECRET")?;
    // Prints `Bearer eyJ…`, valid for an hour.
    println!("{}", bearer("key-1", &secret, HmacAlgorithm::Hs256, &claims)?);
    Ok(())
}

Run it

You need PostgreSQL reachable at DATABASE_URL. The fastest local setup uses Podman or Docker:

podman run --rm -d --name pg \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=ferra -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=ferra \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=my_api \
  -p 5432:5432 \
  postgres:17

export DATABASE_URL=postgres://ferra:ferra@127.0.0.1:5432/my_api
export JWT_SECRET=a-development-secret-of-at-least-32-bytes
export ETAG_KEY=another-development-key-of-at-least-32-bytes

Start the server (the first build is the long part of the five minutes):

cargo run

You should see listening on 0.0.0.0:3000; open http://localhost:3000/docs in a browser. In another terminal, from the same directory, ask for a token and call the API. A request with no token is refused, before anything about it is read:

curl -s -i http://localhost:3000/films                                        # expect: 401

export TOKEN=$(cargo run -q --example token)

curl -s -i -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/films             # expect: 200
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Alien","director":"Ridley Scott","year":1979}' http://localhost:3000/films   # expect: 201 contains "Alien"
curl -s -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/films/1              # expect: 200 contains "Ridley Scott"
curl -s -X PUT -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Alien","director":"Ridley Scott","year":1980}' http://localhost:3000/films/1   # expect: 200 contains "1980"
curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/films/1    # expect: 204
curl -s -i -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/films/1           # expect: 404
curl -s http://localhost:3000/docs/openapi.json                               # expect: 200 contains "openapi"

The # expect: … comments say the status each line answers; the check that runs this page reads them.

MSRV and toolchain

Ferra’s MSRV is Rust 1.94 (edition 2024, resolver v3), set by the sea-orm dependency, which declares rust-version = "1.94.0" itself. Any stable Rust at or above 1.94 works in your project; the pinned toolchain of the Ferra repository (rust-toolchain.toml) does not propagate to you. Building on an older one fails inside sea-orm, not in Ferra.

Ferra and the Rust ecosystem

Ferra is a thin layer over a small set of upstream Rust crates that already solve specific concerns well. This page explains what is Ferra-defined and what is re-exported, so that you know where to look for documentation and which surface to import when you build an application.

If you are looking for “five-minute zero-to-API,” see Getting started. This page is about the long-term shape of the dependency graph you inherit when you depend on ferra.

The principle: cohabitation, not encapsulation

Ferra does not wrap the upstream crates it integrates. Instead, it does one of two things:

  1. Direct re-export — when an upstream crate already offers a stable, namespaced surface, Ferra simply re-exports it under ferra::*. You import ferra::sea_orm::DatabaseConnection, ferra::garde::Validate, and you call them with the API the upstream crate documents. There is no Ferra-renamed equivalent.
  2. Default-locking + opt-in feature — when an upstream crate is correct for some applications but not all, Ferra locks the upstream-default configuration explicitly behind a Cargo feature, so the dependency weight only lands when you opt in.

Ferra introduces a wrapper or a Ferra-defined trait only when one of three things is true:

  • There is concrete behaviour to inject at the call site (authorization, validation, links, error mapping).
  • A typed Ferra newtype prevents misuse that the upstream type does not catch (Id, DateTime, Date, Time).
  • A Ferra trait is the seam an application plugs into (FerraIdentity, which turns your token claims into an identity).

If none of those apply, the upstream surface is exposed verbatim and the upstream documentation is the canonical reference.

What lives under ferra::*

Ferra-defined surface

The ferra:: namespace defines a small, stable user-facing API:

NamespaceWhat it is
ferra::FoundryThe router builder — Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(key)?.mount::<M>().build().
ferra::IdThe framework’s identifier type (a UUID v7), usable as a key.
ferra::FerraErrorThe framework-wide error enum surfaced in HTTP responses.
ferra::FerraLayerThe Tower layer composition entry point.
ferra::JwtConfigThe JWT configuration handed to .with_auth.
ferra::FerraIdentityThe trait your token claims implement: an id and a role test.
ferra::ResourceA model’s rows from a route of your own, under its rules.
#[derive(FerraModel)]The proc-macro that turns a struct into a Ferra resource.
#[ferra(...)]The attribute namespace for Ferra-specific concerns.
#[field(...)]Field-level attributes: validation, filter, sort, owner.
#[behavior(...)]Struct-level behaviors: soft_delete, timestampable.
#[authorize(...)]Operation-level authorization rules.

The names of the implementation crates (ferra-core, ferra-forge, ferra-db, ferra-http, ferra-openapi) belong to the framework’s own sources. You will not see them in your application code.

Re-exported upstream surface

The rest of ferra::* is re-exports. The biggest namespaces:

NamespaceRe-exportsDocumentation
ferra::sea_ormAll of sea_ormsea_orm docs.rs
ferra::gardeAll of gardegarde docs.rs

When you write:

use ferra::sea_orm::Database;

async fn demo() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let conn = Database::connect("postgres://localhost/films").await?;
let _ = conn;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

…you are calling sea_orm::Database::connect. The upstream documentation applies verbatim. There is no Ferra-side wrapping.

The documented way is a direct dependency. An application declares sea-orm next to ferra, at the same major version, and writes sea_orm::… (Getting started); the re-export is offered, supported and tested, for an application that would rather declare none. Both write the same derive: Sea-ORM’s derives expand to sea_orm::… with no leading ::, so the name sea_orm has to be in scope of every file that uses one, which is why use ferra::sea_orm; (or use ferra::prelude::*;) opens a file written the re-export way. A project with a direct sea-orm of another major is refused by FRG-400.

Crate graph: an explicit list at the root

The ferra facade exports a fixed list of names, each one chosen: no pub use ferra_<crate>::* glob, so an item added to an implementation crate does not reach your code by accident. The list is the public contract (api/ferra.txt, stability.md); everything else in the implementation crates is #[doc(hidden)] or not public at all, and may change without notice. ferra::sea_orm and ferra::garde are the exceptions in the other direction: those two are the upstream crates, whole.

ferra::prelude is the module meant to be opened with a glob: the derive, the time types, Foundry, the typed extractors and Sea-ORM’s entity prelude.

Cargo feature surface

An application enables features on ferra, never on an implementation crate. Both are off by default.

FeatureWhat it enablesWhen you want it
(default)The whole framework, with tracing eventsAlways.
observabilityTwo metrics histograms, http.server.request.duration for every response and ferra.db.transaction.duration for each attempt of a write that owns its transaction, and three metrics counters: ferra.db.retries (a write run again), ferra.after_commit.failures (an after_commit that failed) and ferra.sunset.post_sunset_hits (the requests that reach a deprecated API version after its sunset date)You run a metrics recorder.
test-supportMountedRoute and FoundryBuilder::route_table, to enumerate the mounted routes in a test[dev-dependencies] only.
 
[dependencies]
ferra = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0", features = ["observability"] }

The implementation crates have features of their own that you do not set:

  • ferra-core/sea-orm — implements Sea-ORM’s value traits for Id, DateTime, Date and Time, so that they are columns. ferra-db enables it: it is on in every application that uses ferra. It is tied to Sea-ORM 2.x, adds no I/O dependency to ferra-core, and goes away the day Sea-ORM reads jiff itself.
  • ferra-core/openapi — the OpenAPI schemas of the date types; ferra-openapi enables it.

There is no OpenTelemetry feature in 0.9.0.

Where to look for documentation

QuestionSource
How do I declare a model?This user guide → ferra-forge.md
What does Foundry::new(...) do?This user guide → foundry.md
How do I run a database query?Upstream — sea_orm docs.rs (Ferra re-exports verbatim)
What are valid rules in #[authorize]?ferra-auth.md
How do I configure tracing subscribers?Upstream — tracing-subscriber docs.rs (Ferra emits tracing events)

When you ask an AI coding assistant about a Ferra application, the assistant should reach for upstream documentation for re-exported surfaces and for this user guide for Ferra-defined surface. The distinction matters because upstream training corpora are large and Ferra-specific corpora are small — the cohabitation pattern is what makes a Ferra application legible to AI agents trained on the broader Rust ecosystem.

A worked example

A complete Ferra application written the re-export way, with no sea-orm of its own, demonstrating both halves of the principle:

// Cargo.toml: ferra = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }
// (plus tokio, axum and serde, as in Getting started)

// Direct re-export (half A): upstream `sea_orm` reached without renaming.
use ferra::sea_orm::{self, Database};
use ferra::sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;

// Ferra-defined surface: the model derive, the router builder.
use ferra::{FerraModel, Foundry};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

mod film {
    use super::*;

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")] // deliberately public: this example has no JWT
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }

    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Upstream API (sea_orm): no Ferra-side wrapper.
    let conn = Database::connect("postgres://localhost/films").await?;

    // Ferra-defined: the router composition surface.
    let app = Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?.mount::<film::Model>().build();

    // Upstream API (axum): Ferra returns a standard axum Router.
    axum::serve(
        tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?,
        app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>(),
    )
    .await?;
    Ok(())
}

The observability feature (the metrics histograms of the request duration and of each write attempt, and the counters of retries, failed after_commit hooks and post-sunset requests) is off by default: without it, the metrics crate is not in the dependency graph.

When you need a Ferra wrapper that does not yet exist

If you find yourself wanting a Ferra-side wrapper around an upstream type — a Ferra newtype, a Ferra trait abstracting multiple backends, or a Ferra macro that does something the upstream macro does not — the wrapper is a feature request worth filing. The maintainers will ask which of the three justifications applies (concrete behaviour to inject, type-narrowing, swap-out insurance) and ship the wrapper at that point. Until then, the upstream surface is the documented path.

Foundry

Foundry is Ferra’s router-assembly facade. One chain — beginning with a Sea-ORM DatabaseConnection and ending with .build() — declares every resource on your API, mounts the OpenAPI 3.2 docs surface, applies version prefixes, and produces the final axum::Router.

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
mod actor {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "actors")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use actor::Model as Actor;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(&std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?).await?;
    let app = Foundry::new(conn)
        .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
        .mount::<Film>()
        .mount::<Actor>()
        .with_docs()
        .build();
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>()).await?;
    Ok(())
}

The chain is the only way to mount a model: it applies each model’s authorization rules and the JWT layer. The type system enforces one ordering rule at compile time: the chain-wide settings (.with_auth(), .api_version(), .layer()) come before the first .mount(), which also rules out mixing un-versioned with versioned mounts on a single chain. Mounting the same model twice is refused when the chain is assembled, before the server starts (see below).

Foundry::build() -> axum::Router is the sole method whose return type names an axum::* type. Every intermediate value is a Foundry-defined builder. Consumer-added .layer() calls on the returned router land outside the framework’s Tower stack.

Dependencies. The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

The chain at a glance

MethodDefaultOverride
Foundry::new(conn)begins the chain—
.with_auth::<Claims>(jwt)configures JWT bearer validation; required to mount a model whose rules need an identity (without it, .mount::<M>() is a compile error, FRG-151 — see ferra-auth.md § Compile-time auth defense)—
.with_api_keys(keys)accepts API keys next to the JWT (after .with_auth(); see ferra-auth.md)—
.etag_key(secret)?the key that signs the entity tags: at least 32 bytes, the same on every replica, never the JWT secret (see Entity-tag key)—
.api_version("v1")?nests every route under /v1/—
.default_representation(Representation::Flat)the shape of a 2xx for a client that states no Accept preference (Hal unless set); see ferra-http.md—
.layer(layer)per-application transport settings.mount_with_layer::<M>(layer)
.mount::<M>()mounts the model’s routes on /{resource}.mount_and_handle::<M>() (also returns a ResourceHandle<M>)
.deprecated(since, sunset)?versioned chains only: Deprecation: and Sunset: headers + deprecated: true + x-sunset in the spec—
.with_base_url(origin)absolute _links and Location on origin (https://…); relative links otherwise—
.with_docs()publishes /docs/openapi.json + /docs (Scalar UI); /docs/v1/… on a versioned chain.with_docs_at(path)
.with_docs_info(title, version)info.title / info.version of the served document and the Scalar page title (default "API", "1")—
.with_docs_protected(verifier)gates docs behind the verifier (RFC 7807 401 on rejection).with_docs_protected_at(path, verifier)
.build()finalizes the chain into axum::Router—

.with_auth(), .with_api_keys() (after .with_auth()), .api_version(), .etag_key(), .default_representation() and .layer() come before the first .mount(), in any order among themselves; the JWT configuration survives .api_version(). .with_auth() is called at most once per chain. Call .with_docs() after .api_version(): it picks its default path (/docs or /docs/v1) when it is called.

api_version returns Result<FoundryBuilder<…>, ApiVersionError> — prefixes that are empty, contain /, contain whitespace, or contain characters unsafe in a URL path segment are rejected at construction time.

The no-duplicate-mount rule

Mounting the same model twice panics when the chain is assembled, at the second .mount::<M>() call — before the server starts:

the model `Film` is already mounted on this Foundry chain — remove the duplicate
`.mount::<Film>()` or rename the model. See https://ferra.rs/docs/foundry.html#the-no-duplicate-mount-rule.

Stable Rust cannot express “M is not already mounted on this chain” as a trait bound, so the check runs at assembly time rather than at cargo build. If you need two shapes of the same underlying type, define two Rust types.

.mount_with_layer::<M>(layer) and .mount_and_handle::<M>() follow the same rule.

mount_and_handle — mount, and get a handle for routes of your own

.mount_and_handle::<M>() mounts M exactly as .mount::<M>() does — same routes, same JWT layer, same compile-time gates (FRG-150, FRG-151), same duplicate-mount panic — and returns, next to the builder, a ResourceHandle<M>. Keep the handle in the state of the routes you write yourself, and extract Resource<M> in their handlers: it reaches M’s rows under the rules of the generated routes (Custom handlers, Resource<M>).

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
use ferra::Foundry;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let (foundry, films) = Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?.mount_and_handle::<Film>();
let app = foundry.build(); // the generated routes; merge your own router with `.with_state(films)`
let _ = (app, films);
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

The handle holds the connection of the mounted routes and, after .with_auth(), what verifies a bearer token. A model that is not mounted has no handle: a handler that extracts Resource<M> from a state without one does not compile (FRG-152).

The no-mixed-mode rule

.api_version(...) is callable only on an empty chain. Mounting an un-versioned model first and then calling .api_version("v1") is a compile error (FR-014a, ADR-0025). The same error, with the same text, covers .with_auth(...), .etag_key(...) and .layer(...) called after a mount:

error[E0277]: `.api_version(...)`, `.with_auth(...)`, `.etag_key(...)` and `.layer(...)` must come before the first `.mount(...)`
 --> src/main.rs:6:10
  |
6 |         .api_version("v1")?
  |          ^^^^^^^^^^^ this builder already has mounted models
  |
  = help: the trait `IsEmpty` is not implemented for `Mounted`
  = note: these are chain-wide settings: move the call before the first `.mount(...)` of the chain
  = note: to ship mixed-mode (legacy + versioned) routes, build two assemblies and merge them via `axum::Router::merge`. See https://ferra.rs/docs/foundry.html#mixed-mode-pattern-two-assemblies-merged for a worked example.

Mixed-mode pattern: two assemblies merged

If you want a top-level /films and a /v1/films, build two Foundry chains and merge them with axum::Router::merge:

use ferra::{Foundry, date};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let legacy = Foundry::new(conn.clone())
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .mount::<Film>()
    .with_docs() // serves /docs/openapi.json
    .build();

let v1 = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .api_version("v1")?
    .mount::<Film>()
    .deprecated(date!(2026-07-01), date!(2027-01-05))?
    .with_docs() // serves /docs/v1/openapi.json
    .build();

let app: axum::Router = legacy.merge(v1);
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Each Foundry::build() produces its own axum::Router; merging them is the supported way to expose multiple-version surfaces from a single binary. The OpenAPI documents stay separate — one per build.

Versioning + deprecation

.api_version("v1")? nests every mounted resource under /v1/, prefixes every operationId with v1., and serves the spec at /docs/v1/openapi.json.

A versioned chain is authenticated like any other: every model mounted on it gets the same JWT layer and the same authorization rules as on an un-versioned chain.

use ferra::{Foundry, JwtConfig};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct MyClaims { sub: String }
impl ferra::FerraIdentity for MyClaims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str { &self.sub }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool { false }
}
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection, jwt: JwtConfig) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let v1 = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .with_auth::<MyClaims>(jwt)   // before or after `.api_version(...)`
    .api_version("v1")?
    .mount::<Film>()
    .build();
let _ = v1;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

.deprecated(since, sunset) takes two dates: the day the version was deprecated, and the last day it is served as documented. It returns Result<_, DeprecationError>: a sunset earlier than since is refused (DeprecationError::SunsetBeforeDeprecation). It activates these signals:

  • a Deprecation: @<seconds> header on every response under the version (RFC 9745): the start of since, 00:00:00 UTC, in Unix seconds — @1782864000 for 2026-07-01;
  • a Sunset: <HTTP-date> header on every response under the version (RFC 8594): the last second of sunset, in the IMF-fixdate form — Tue, 05 Jan 2027 23:59:59 GMT for 2027-01-05;
  • deprecated: true + x-sunset: YYYY-MM-DD on every operation in the emitted spec, plus an info.x-sunset mirror at the document root.
use ferra::{Foundry, date};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let v1 = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .api_version("v1")?
    .mount::<Film>()
    .deprecated(date!(2026-07-01), date!(2027-01-05))?
    .with_docs()
    .build();
let _ = v1;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

The date! macro validates the calendar date at compile time; an invalid month or day fails cargo build rather than panicking at startup. See ferra-core.md §“Time vocabulary”.

Post-sunset warn-event

When today_utc > sunset (strict greater-than — equality does not trigger; the sunset day is the last day of the grace window), every request under the deprecated version causes the framework to emit a structured warning at tracing::Level::WARN. The event is layered into the same middleware that emits the Sunset: response header, so the two signals always travel together.

Verbatim target string (filterable via tracing-subscriber’s EnvFilter):

ferra_http::sunset

Field set on the event:

Field nameTypeSource
versionstringthe version prefix ("v1")
sunsetstringthe declared sunset date in YYYY-MM-DD form
days_overduei64whole days from sunset to today_utc
http.methodstringthe inbound request method, upper-cased
http.targetstringthe inbound path, without the query string (includes the version prefix; ADR-0076)

Message body (verbatim):

deprecated API version reached after declared sunset date

Once-per-process de-duplication: the framework fires the warning exactly once per (version, sunset) pair within a single running process. Two sequential requests on the same pair produce one warning; two distinct pairs (e.g., v1/2026-01-01 and v2/2026-06-01) each fire once independently. The dedup state is process-local — a process restart re-creates the registry and the first post-restart hit fires the warning again. This is the right default for operational paging: a single human-readable signal per incident, repeated only when a release rolls the world.

Operator filtering. An operator who wants only the post-sunset warnings (and nothing else from the framework) sets:

RUST_LOG=ferra_http::sunset=warn

An operator who wants every framework-emitted event at warn level:

RUST_LOG=ferra_http=warn

The convention follows the <snake-cased crate name>::<event segment> pattern; the rate-limit event lives at ferra_http::rate_limit and is configured the same way.

Metrics counter (gated by the observability Cargo feature). When the observability feature is enabled:

[dependencies]
ferra = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0", features = ["observability"] }

the framework also advances a metrics::counter! named ferra.sunset.post_sunset_hits on every post-sunset request, labelled with version and sunset. Unlike the warn-event, this counter advances on every hit — its purpose is rate-of-arrival visibility, not signal-per-incident paging. With the feature off (default), the framework takes zero dependency on the metrics crate; the constitutional 0.4.0 secure defaults are byte-identical for non-opting-in consumers.

No-deny on post-sunset: the comparator is observability-only. The framework continues to serve every request past sunset; if you want denial after a date, add your own middleware. A first-class deprecated_with_enforcement(...) opt-in is on the roadmap but not shipped at 0.7.0.

Per-request budget: the comparator’s common path runs in well under 200 ns on the CI reference runner and is informational-tier under 100 ns. The framework’s first build-gating performance contract enforces this: a regression past 200 ns fails the build (cargo run -p xtask --bin check_sunset_ceiling against cargo bench --bench sunset_comparator). The two-tier discipline is documented in ADR-0039 as the pattern for future hot-path additions.

Public-default docs and the protected variant

.with_docs() exposes the documentation surface unauthenticated by default. This is a deliberate, documented departure from Ferra’s model-route default-deny posture (Q1 in the 0.5.0 specification, arbitrated in ADR-0024). The reasoning: the docs surface describes the API but does not serve resource data; gating it would block the constitutional zero-to-documented-API standard for every new consumer.

For any publicly-reachable network surface, switch to .with_docs_protected(verifier). The verifier closure receives the inbound request and returns bool; a false produces an RFC 7807 401 Unauthorized response with type: "https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized":

use axum::http::header::AUTHORIZATION;
use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
// Constant time: `==` on a secret stops at the first differing byte, and the delay tells it.
fn same(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> bool {
    a.len() == b.len() && a.iter().zip(b).fold(0u8, |acc, (x, y)| acc | (x ^ y)) == 0
}
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .mount::<Film>()
    .with_docs_protected(|req: &axum::extract::Request| {
        let sent = req.headers().get(AUTHORIZATION).map_or(&[][..], |v| v.as_bytes());
        same(sent, b"Bearer secret")
    })
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

The verifier runs synchronously and MUST NOT perform I/O — the underlying primitive does not yet integrate with the ferra-auth provider chain (that landing is scheduled for 0.8.5 beta). The current API accepts any Fn(&Request) -> bool + Send + Sync + 'static; the future Provider arm of DocsAuthVerifier will be additive.

Layer-ordering invariance

Every resource mounted through Foundry carries the per-resource Tower stack: CORS (restrictive default), the 413-mapping middleware, the 1 MiB body limit, tracing with body sampling off, and per-route rate limiting on mutation endpoints. Foundry does not reorder, replace, or remove any of these layers.

Consumer-added .layer(...) calls on the value Foundry::build() returns land outside the framework’s stack — the standard Tower composition rule. If you need a layer to wrap framework layers, add it on the returned router. Beneath the framework layers, each model’s routes accept only the knobs of .mount_with_layer::<M>(layer) (see §“Transport-layer overrides”): there is no hook to insert an arbitrary layer inside a model’s stack.

Cross-reference: ferra-http.md §“Tower layer-ordering notation” documents the exact stack order.

Transport-layer overrides

Reader contract. This section stands on its own. A reader with only this page plus standard Rust knowledge produces a correct per-app or per-model override on the first attempt. Every knob, default, fallback, and validation rule is spelled out below — no ADR and no framework source is required.

The framework’s secure Tower stack (CORS deny-by-default, 1 MiB body cap, { per_second: 2, burst_size: 5 } mutation rate-limit, tracing of one INFO event per request) is the right default for the vast majority of APIs. Some shapes — file uploads, high-volume mutation endpoints, sub-path deployments behind a reverse proxy — need narrow overrides. Use the FerraLayer builder for those.

FerraLayer is a single value carrying overrides for five knobs:

KnobDefaultOverride surface
CORSCorsLayer::new() (deny by default).cors(cors_layer)
Body cap1 MiB.body_limit(bytes)
Rate-limit (mutations only)2/sec, burst 5.rate_limit(RateLimitRule::new(per_second, burst_size)?)
Tracingnone by default: the request span and the ferra_http::request line come from build()’s observation layer and are not set here; your own TraceLayer runs beside them.trace_layer(layer)
Base path for _linksnone.base_path("/api")

A FerraLayer whose every knob is left at its None default (FerraLayer::new().build()) reproduces the framework stack byte-for-byte — the override surface is silent when unused.

RateLimitRule construction. Build a rule with RateLimitRule::new(per_second, burst_size)? (or RateLimitRule::default(), 2 per second, burst 5) and read it with .per_second() and .burst_size(). The fields are private: a checked rule cannot be changed into an invalid one afterwards.

Per-app vs per-model — REPLACE not merge

FerraLayer applies at two scopes:

  • Per-application default — Foundry::new(conn).layer(global) — every model mounted afterwards inherits global’s settings.
  • Per-model override — Foundry::new(conn).mount_with_layer::<M>(M_layer) — only M’s routes use M_layer.

The per-model layer REPLACES (does NOT merge with) the per-app layer for the affected model. Critically, a knob left at None on the per-model layer falls back to the framework default — NOT to the per-app setting. The intent is per-model auditability in isolation: every mount_with_layer::<M>(...) site is fully inspectable on its own, without chasing a per-app default the reader may not have on screen, and without the security surprise of inheriting a permissive per-app override the per-model author did not intend.

Security posture. The REPLACE-not-merge rule means that an unset knob on a per-model override cannot silently inherit a permissive per-app value. If the per-app layer raises the body cap to 5 MiB and the per-model layer for Document does NOT explicitly call .body_limit(...), Document routes use the 1 MiB framework default, not the 5 MiB per-app value. The rule is auditable by grep: every override is explicit at its declaration site.

use ferra::{FerraLayer, Foundry};
use tower_http::cors::CorsLayer;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
mod document {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "documents")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use document::Model as Document;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection, permissive_cors: CorsLayer) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let global = FerraLayer::new()
    .body_limit(5 * 1024 * 1024)         // 5 MiB
    .build();
let document = FerraLayer::new()
    .cors(permissive_cors)
    .build();

let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .layer(global)                       // 5 MiB on every model …
    .mount_with_layer::<Document>(document) // … EXCEPT Document
    .mount::<Film>()
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Observable behaviour:

  • Film routes: body limit 5 MiB (from global), CORS deny-by-default (global did not set .cors(...)).
  • Document routes: body limit 1 MiB (the framework default — document did not set .body_limit(...), so the per-model layer does NOT inherit global’s 5 MiB), permissive CORS (the per-model setting).

Body-limit override + verbatim 413 detail

When the configured cap is exceeded, the framework’s standard 413 application/problem+json response carries the verbatim configured limit in the detail field:

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_large",
  "title": "Payload Too Large",
  "status": 413,
  "detail": "request body exceeds 5242880 bytes"
}

Operators tracing 413s in logs can map the byte cap in the response back to the originating FerraLayer::body_limit(...) call site without consulting source code.

Sub-path mount — base_path

A common deployment shape: serve Ferra at /api/ behind a reverse proxy that strips the prefix before forwarding. Configure the framework’s hypermedia links to include the publicly visible prefix via .base_path("/api"):

Static prefix only. base_path is a static &'static str declared at framework-assembly time. Ferra deliberately does NOT consume the X-Forwarded-Prefix request header (the dynamic-prefix convention used by FastAPI’s root_path_in_servers + Traefik). Reasons: (a) request-time prefix discovery breaks _links URL stability — two requests through different proxies could yield different _links.self.href for the same row; (b) the closed, const-evaluable contract enables the validation grammar below to fire at compile time, not at proc-macro time. If your deployment needs multiple prefixes simultaneously, declare a separate FerraLayer per-deployment-target.

use ferra::{FerraLayer, Foundry};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .layer(FerraLayer::new().base_path("/api").build())
    .mount::<Film>()
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Every _links.*.href (self, collection, and restore on a soft-delete model) now carries the /api prefix:

  • _links.self.href → https://api.example.com/api/films/42
  • _links.collection.href → https://api.example.com/api/films

.base_path is validated at proc-macro-equivalent time: the prefix MUST start with / and MUST NOT end with /. Malformed literals produce a compile error at the call site when the value is reachable in const context:

.base_path("api")        // compile error — no leading `/`    (FRG-340)
.base_path("/api/")      // compile error — trailing `/`      (FRG-341)
.base_path("")           // compile error — empty             (FRG-342)

Each is a section of the diagnostics page, with its bad example compiled and its good one: FRG-340, FRG-341, FRG-342.

The base_path declaration applies only to hypermedia link generation. The framework does not assume the prefix is present in the inbound request URI — if the reverse proxy strips /api before forwarding, no further configuration is needed. To mount under the prefix internally as well, compose with axum::Router::nest("/api", foundry.build()).

Rate-limit override

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{FerraLayer, RateLimitError, RateLimitRule};

fn layer() -> Result<ferra::FerraLayer, RateLimitError> {
    Ok(FerraLayer::new()
        .rate_limit(RateLimitRule::new(10, 20)?) // 10/sec, burst 20
        .build())
}
}

The constructor signature is RateLimitRule::new(per_second: u32, burst_size: u32) -> Result<RateLimitRule, RateLimitError>. burst_size is the bucket depth (peak concurrent mutations); per_second is the steady-state refill rate: one token every 1 / per_second seconds. At RateLimitRule::new(10, 20) a client may issue 20 mutations in burst, then 10/second steady-state. A zero per_second or burst_size is refused with RateLimitError::ZeroRate or RateLimitError::ZeroBurst (such a rule would never let a mutation through), and a per_second above 1 000 000 000 with RateLimitError::RateTooHigh. A throttled request gets 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After of at least 1 second.

FerraLayer::new().no_rate_limit().build() disables both the governor and its 429 mapper, so mutations need no ConnectInfo, and the OpenAPI document declares no 429 on the model’s mutations. It is const-callable; the last rate_limit or no_rate_limit call wins. Per-model replacement still applies: an unchanged per-model layer restores the framework default.

Choose the application-wide key before the first mount:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{Foundry, RateLimitKey, TrustedProxies, TrustedProxiesError};
fn proxy(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), TrustedProxiesError> {
    let _foundry = Foundry::new(conn).rate_limit_key(
        RateLimitKey::forwarded_for(TrustedProxies::new(["10.0.0.0/8", "192.0.2.7"])?),
    );
    Ok(())
}
}

The default RateLimitKey::PeerAddr needs into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>(); a missing peer with an enabled limiter answers 500. Forwarded extraction reads X-Forwarded-For only from a trusted peer, walks all header lines right to left, and chooses the first untrusted IP. A malformed or empty entry before that IP, an all-trusted chain, or an untrusted peer falls back to the socket IP. Ports/brackets are stripped and IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses normalized. An empty trust list ignores the header. Name another header with RateLimitKey::forwarded_for(trusted).header(HeaderName::from_static("x-real-chain")).

RateLimitKey::from_fn accepts fn(&http::request::Parts) -> Option<IpAddr>. Its use case is a platform that gives the client address otherwise: Lambda Web Adapter relays requestContext.http.sourceIp in the x-amzn-request-context header. Parse only the deployment’s verified header shape and return the client IP; None shares one bucket (0.0.0.0), so extraction failures remain throttled. Ferra does not check where such a header comes from: a client can set x-amzn-request-context itself, so a from_fn reading it is forgeable unless every request reaches the service through the adapter that overwrites it.

On Lambda the buckets belong to one execution environment, not the whole API. Disable the in-process limiter and configure API Gateway throttling; the Lambda template uses burst 20, rate 10 requests/second.

Custom CORS + tracing layers

.cors(cors_layer) and .trace_layer(trace_layer) accept the underlying [tower_http] types verbatim — the framework does not wrap them. To configure CORS for a specific allowed origin:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraLayer;
use tower_http::cors::{AllowOrigin, CorsLayer};

let cors = CorsLayer::new()
    .allow_origin(AllowOrigin::list(["https://app.example.com".parse().unwrap()]))
    .allow_methods(tower_http::cors::AllowMethods::list([
        axum::http::Method::GET,
        axum::http::Method::POST,
    ]));
let layer = FerraLayer::new().cors(cors).build();
let _ = layer;
}

The trace slot accepts any TraceLayer shape (0.8.0)

Through 0.7.x the trace slot held one concrete type — the TraceLayer<HttpMakeClassifier> that TraceLayer::new_for_http() returns — so a custom classifier or custom span fields could not reach it without forking the builder.

The slot is now a type-erased closure (Arc<dyn Fn(Router) -> Router + Send + Sync>), and FerraLayer stays non-generic. .trace_layer(...) is generic over the full TraceLayer<C, M, OnReq, OnResp, OnBody, OnEos, OnFail> shape: pass your configured layer verbatim, whatever its classifier, make_span_with, or on_request / on_response / on_failure handlers, and the builder boxes it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraLayer;
use tower_http::trace::TraceLayer;
use tracing::Level;

let custom_trace = TraceLayer::new_for_http().make_span_with(
    |req: &axum::http::Request<axum::body::Body>| {
        tracing::span!(Level::INFO, "http_request", method = %req.method())
    },
);
let layer = FerraLayer::new().trace_layer(custom_trace).build();
}

Two consequences of the erasure worth knowing:

  • FerraLayer carries no static evidence of which trace shape is mounted. Reading the type alone will not tell you whether your layer is in the slot. Debug renders the slot as Some("<trace closure>") or None.
  • The slot is empty by default, and an empty slot adds nothing. It defaults to None: the request span and the one ferra_http::request line of every response are written by the observation layer of build(), outside the whole stack, not by this slot. Your layer is an addition, with its own span and events inside the request span. An empty slot is also what keeps build() callable from a const context:
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraLayer;

const APP_LAYER: FerraLayer = FerraLayer::new()
    .body_limit(7 * 1024 * 1024)
    .base_path("/api")
    .build();
}

A const layer makes every builder validation run during rustc rather than at startup — a malformed base_path becomes a compile error at the literal, not a panic on the first request.

Composition order — preserved

The constitutional Tower stack order is preserved regardless of which knobs are overridden:

CorsLayer                                       (outermost of these; the whole stack: ferra-http.md § Layer ordering)
  JWT / API key layer (when the model's rules need one)
    body_limit_mapper   (413 → problem+json with verbatim detail)
      RequestBodyLimitLayer({bytes})
        trace slot          (empty unless `trace_layer` fills it)
          DefaultBodyLimit::disable
            [on mutation sub-router only:]
              rate_limit_mapper   (429 → problem+json)
                GovernorLayer(per_second, burst_size)
                  <handlers>
            [on read sub-router:]
              <handlers>

FerraLayer does not reorder, add, or remove layers — only swaps the parameters / values that flow into the existing slots.

Typestate guard — .layer(...) before .mount(...)

.layer(...) carries the same typestate bound as .api_version(...) and .with_auth(...). Calling it after a model has been mounted produces the compile error documented in §“The no-mixed-mode rule” above.

.mount_with_layer::<M>(layer) follows the same no-duplicate-mount rule as .mount::<M>().

Request time budget

Call .request_budget(Duration::from_secs(10)) before the first mount. No budget applies by default. The setting survives .with_auth() and .api_version() in either order. Choose a value under your infrastructure’s timeout (a gateway, a proxy, a platform limit): 10 s plus the 1 s Ferra may spend after a commit stays under the lowest common default, Envoy’s 15 s route timeout (API Gateway allows 29 s, Heroku 30 s, ALB and nginx 60 s). It is a margin, not a maximum: a slow COMMIT is not cut, and for a model with a BelongsTo the read of the written row’s parents after the commit is under no deadline either (acquire_timeout bounds the wait for the connection, statement_timeout the query).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::Foundry;
use std::time::Duration;

fn configure(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
    let _router = Foundry::new(conn)
        .request_budget(Duration::from_secs(10))
        .route("/live", axum::routing::get(|| async { "ok" }))
        .build();
}
}

If the budget expires before a Ferra repository commit starts, the request answers 503 application/problem+json, with type https://ferra.rs/errors/timeout and no Retry-After. Its unfinished transaction rolls back. Create, update, delete, soft delete and restore all use this boundary.

The budget also bounds the retry of a transient conflict. A write the database aborts with 40001 or 40P01 is run again, up to three attempts; the deadline bounds every attempt as it bounds the first. No attempt starts once it has passed and no wait ends past it, and each of these answers the same 503 timeout, with no Retry-After and nothing written. A COMMIT the database refuses with 40001 or 40P01 committed nothing, so it is not a started commit: the gate below is taken back, and the attempts that follow are cut at the deadline until their own commit starts. Without a budget only the three attempts bound the work, and the answer past them is the 503 retry_exhausted, with Retry-After: 1.

Once any commit starts, the commit is never cancelled and never answered 503 timeout: the handler finishes and returns its own response. The gate stays set until the request ends, so your own work in that handler is not cut. The work Ferra itself runs after the commit is bounded: a model’s after_commit hook, which runs after the commit and before the response, and the computed fields served after it, share one post-commit deadline per request, max(deadline, first post-commit work + 1 s), so a slow COMMIT does not leave them no time. When it runs out the work is dropped and the request answers 500 internal; the commit stands (see Behaviors). A gateway or process timeout can still interrupt the connection; choose a budget below that infrastructure timeout.

Generated routes use the budget automatically. To include your own Resource<M> route, obtain its handle with .mount_and_handle::<M>(), then declare the route on the builder before .build(): .route("/films/{id}/publish", post(publish).with_state(films)). Call .route once per path, every method of the path in one MethodRouter (get(a).post(b)); a path declared twice panics. Nested routers and nest_service are not accepted. Merging routes into the finished router afterwards (axum’s .merge or .route on the value build() returns) does not give those routes the budget, and escapes the conflict check below too. Writes through an application-owned raw DatabaseConnection are outside this guarantee.

Declared routes mount at the root, outside the .api_version(...) prefix: a /live probe or a webhook keeps its URL when the version changes, and gets no Deprecation or Sunset header. They receive only the chain-wide layers: the request budget and the cache default (Cache-Control: no-store, a merged Vary). To cache one of them, set its own Cache-Control with a layer on its MethodRouter: see ferra-http.md § Caching.

Ferra does not authenticate a declared route by itself. Ferra’s JWT authentication, authorization, mutation rate limiter, body limit and CORS apply to model routes only. A declared route that reads no caller answers a request that carries no token, and ignores every credential: a webhook with its own Authorization scheme, or two of them, is the handler’s own answer. Declared routes appear neither in the OpenAPI document nor in route_table().

Who is calling a declared route

A handler that wants the caller says so with an extractor, and the extractor reads the credential itself, with the rules of the model routes, before the handler body runs:

  • Principal<Claims> is the JWT’s claims or the API key’s identity; CurrentUser<Claims> is the JWT only, and answers 401 on a key; Resource<M> binds the caller for M’s rules.
  • Two credentials answer 400 multiple_credentials; one that is invalid answers 401; an identity source out of reach (key set, key store) answers 503 identity_unavailable.
  • Option<Principal<Claims>> and Option<CurrentUser<Claims>> are None only when no credential was sent: an invalid one is still a 401, never an anonymous request.
  • The credential is verified once per request: Resource<M> and Principal<Claims> in one handler share one API key lookup.
  • The request span’s credential field is recorded where Ferra verifies the credential: by the credential layer on a model route, and by the Principal<Claims> or Resource<M> extractor on a declared route. A declared route that extracts neither verifies nothing, so the span carries no credential, whatever the request sent.

On a chain without .with_auth() there is no credential to read: Principal and CurrentUser answer 401 and their Option forms are None.

A declared path that overlaps a model route or the docs page (same path, or a {param} segment that matches it), whatever the method, makes .build() panic at startup with a message naming both paths, for example the route `/films/{key}` declared with `FoundryBuilder::route` conflicts with `/films/{id}` . A custom PATCH /films/{id} beside a films model is refused too. Give the declared route a path no model and no docs page use. A root catch-all /{*rest} and any path under the docs page (/docs/...) are refused as well; for a SPA fallback, call Router::fallback on the router build() returns (outside the budget) or serve the SPA under a dedicated prefix such as /app/{*rest}. The check compares a chain’s declared routes with that chain’s models only: in an assembly merged from two chains, a route declared on one is not compared with the models of the other.

.build() also panics at startup, with a message that says how to fix it:

  • when the key-set fetch timeout (JwtConfig::with_key_set_timeout) is not below the request budget: the fetch runs inside the request, so lower the timeout or raise .request_budget(...);
  • when the cookie credential is configured and a custom FerraLayer::cors sits on the chain’s .layer(...) or on a mount_with_layer: the origins given to JwtConfig::with_cookie drive CORS, so remove the custom CORS layer;
  • with .with_docs*(), when a pass over the OpenAPI document finds the part it edits missing: build() panics with “the OpenAPI document lost the part the <stage> pass edits, so it would be served without that content — this is a Ferra bug, please report it”. It is a Ferra bug, not something to fix in your chain. The server does not start with a document that silently lost part of its content; please report it.

Entity-tag key

One line every application adds, before the first .mount(...) (ADR-0077):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::Foundry;

fn configure(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let _chain = Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?;
    Ok(())
}
}

.etag_key(secret) is the key that signs the entity tags of a row. Five rules:

  • At least 32 bytes. Generate one with openssl rand -base64 32. A shorter key is refused by .etag_key(...) itself with EtagKeyError::TooShort { len, min }, whose text gives the length and the minimum, never a byte of the key.
  • The same on every replica. Read it from the environment or a secret store, never from a literal in the source. Two replicas with two keys compute two tags for one row.
  • Rotating it changes every tag. Each client’s next conditional write on a row answers 412 once; it reads the row again and retries with the new tag.
  • Never the JWT secret. .try_build() returns BuildError::EtagKeyEqualsJwtSecret when the key equals any HMAC secret of .with_auth(...) (the comparison runs in constant time), and .build() panics with the same text. A key-set (EdDSA) configuration has no HMAC secret to compare with.
  • Never printed. Debug of the builder shows the key as [REDACTED], in a log line or in a tracing event.

Like .with_auth(...), .etag_key(...) is callable only before the first mount.

What the key signs. A tag is HMAC-SHA256 over the table, the primary key and the row’s PostgreSQL version (xmin). So, for the operator:

  • Rewriting a row with identical values still gives it a new version, so a client holding the old tag gets a 412 it could not have avoided.
  • A logical replica, or a dump and restore, gives every row a new xmin; as with a rotation, each outstanding tag is stale once. A physical standby keeps it.
  • VACUUM FREEZE changes nothing: PostgreSQL 9.4 and later do not rewrite xmin when they freeze a row.
  • xmin wraparound is accepted. After 2^32 transactions a stale tag could match again, with probability 2^-32 per stale tag and no leverage without the key.

try_build

.build() panics at startup when the chain is misconfigured. .try_build() does the same checks and returns the refusal as a ferra::BuildError instead, for a launcher that reports it its own way or a test that asserts it. .build() is .try_build() that panics with the error’s Display, so the two never disagree.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{BuildError, Foundry};
use std::time::Duration;

fn configure(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<axum::Router, BuildError> {
    Foundry::new(conn)
        .request_budget(Duration::from_secs(10))
        .route("/live", axum::routing::get(|| async { "ok" }))
        .try_build()
}
}

BuildError is #[non_exhaustive]; give the match a catch-all arm. One variant per refusal:

VariantThe refusal
ProjectionPrefixestwo projections resolve to the same URL prefix (FRG-310), a projection’s prefix collides with another model’s resource (FRG-312), or an OpenAPI name is produced twice (FRG-153)
Policiesa mounted model leaves an operation without an authorization rule (FRG-150), or GET /me is not held to one model
KeySetTimeoutExceedsBudget { timeout, budget }the key-set fetch timeout is not below the request budget
CookieWithCustomCors { culprit }the cookie credential is configured next to a custom FerraLayer::cors
RouteOverlap { path, owned }a route declared with .route overlaps a route Ferra mounts, or the docs page
EtagKeyMissinga model is mounted and the chain has no .etag_key(...); a chain with only .route(..) needs none (see Entity-tag key)
EtagKeyEqualsJwtSecretthe entity-tag key equals an HMAC secret of .with_auth(...)
Docsthe OpenAPI document cannot be finished: a Ferra bug, please report it

Each Display says what is wrong, where and how to fix it. Docs wraps the opaque ferra::InternalError: the document error is behind source(), in the error chain, and its type is not part of the contract.

The duplicate-path panics of .route(...) and .mount(...) are raised where the call is made, not by try_build.

Escape hatches

  • mount_and_handle::<M>() — mount as mount::<M>() does and get the ResourceHandle<M> a route of your own extracts Resource<M> from. mount_with (a caller-built FerraState) is gone since 0.10.0: there is no way to hand Foundry a repository.
  • with_docs_at(path) / with_docs_protected_at(path, verifier) — override the /docs mount point. Useful when a reverse proxy serves Ferra under a sub-path.
  • Another docs UI (Redoc, RapiDoc, Swagger UI) — serve it yourself and point it at /docs/openapi.json, which with_docs() mounts. ferra-openapi has no public API since 0.9.0: the document is reached through the running router, not through a function call.

When Foundry is the wrong tool

There is no lower-level way to mount a model: a model is always served by Foundry, because Foundry is what applies its authorization rules. Per-model transport settings go through .mount_with_layer::<M>(layer) (see §“Transport-layer overrides” above).

  • Apps that mount the docs surface from a different process than the API itself. The ferra-openapi free functions stand alone.
  • Apps with a non-Sea-ORM persistence layer. Foundry takes a sea_orm::DatabaseConnection; there is no way to substitute another backend behind a mounted model.

For the bare CRUD case — the framework’s zero-to-documented-API target — Foundry::new(conn).mount::<M>().with_docs().build() is the right shape.

Cross-references (for the curious reader)

  • ADR-0024 — ferra-openapi crate scope, public-default docs deviation, Foundry → ferra-openapi edge.
  • ADR-0025 — Foundry typestate strategy (#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]; since 0.9.0 the typestate has two states, Empty and Mounted, and the duplicate-mount check runs at assembly time).
