  • ADR-0026 — closed ERROR_TYPES URI namespace; the https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized URI used by .with_docs_protected(...).
  • ADR-0027 — x-sunset vendor extension + deprecated: true mirror.
  • ADR-0002 — Axum 0.8 framework choice and the Foundry::build() -> axum::Router single-leak rule.

These are pointers for readers tracing decisions back to their arbitration; they are not required reading for correct use of the APIs above.

ferra-core

ferra-core is the zero-I/O contract layer that every other Ferra crate depends on. An application does not declare it: it reaches what is public through the ferra facade (ferra::meta, ferra::model, ferra::error, ferra::Id, ferra::DateTime, ferra::Date, ferra::Time, ferra::date!). What the facade exports is the contract (stability.md, api/ferra-core.txt); the rest of the crate is #[doc(hidden)] and may change without notice.

ModuleItems an application reads
metaFieldType, FieldMeta, ModelMeta, and the rest of the description of a model
modelFerraModel
idId
errorIdParseError
timeDateTime, Date, Time, plus the date! macro

The crate performs no I/O and talks to no database. Its runtime dependencies are serde, uuid and jiff; utoipa (the OpenAPI schemas of the date types) and Sea-ORM’s value traits (so that Id and the date types are columns) sit behind the openapi and sea-orm Cargo features, which ferra-openapi and ferra-db enable for you: do not enable them yourself (Architecture).

Model metadata (FieldMeta / FieldType / ModelMeta)

The types of ferra::meta describe a resource precisely enough for downstream crates to derive HTTP routes, SQL, OpenAPI and hypermedia links from a single source of truth. #[derive(FerraModel)] writes them; an application reads them. FieldMeta and ModelMeta are #[non_exhaustive] and have no public constructor, so a description cannot be written by hand: a model is a Sea-ORM entity with the derive.

FieldType

A tag identifying the Rust type of a field. Option variants are spelled out so every field’s nullability is visible without indirection. FieldType is #[non_exhaustive]: a match on it needs a _ => arm to stay forward-compatible. This function names every variant of 0.9, and compiles:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::meta::FieldType;

fn label(ty: FieldType) -> &'static str {
    match ty {
        FieldType::String | FieldType::OptionString => "text",
        FieldType::I32 | FieldType::OptionI32 => "32-bit integer",
        FieldType::I64 | FieldType::OptionI64 => "64-bit integer",
        FieldType::F64 | FieldType::OptionF64 => "float",
        FieldType::Bool | FieldType::OptionBool => "boolean",
        FieldType::Uuid | FieldType::OptionUuid => "uuid",
        FieldType::Timestamp | FieldType::OptionTimestamp => "instant (DateTime)",
        FieldType::Date | FieldType::OptionDate => "calendar date",
        FieldType::Time | FieldType::OptionTime => "time of day",
        FieldType::ComputedUserNamed => "a type of the user's, on a `#[ferra(computed)]` field",
        _ => "a type added after 0.9",
    }
}
}

See the recognised field types table in ferra-forge.md for the end-user surface.

FieldMeta

The description of one field. Its public members are name, wire_name (the JSON name, which differs from name under #[ferra(rename_all = ...)]), ty, required, mode, filterable, sortable, cursor_key and validation_rules. The six flags readable, writable, skip_api, read_only, write_only and computed, and is_id, were removed in 0.15.0: mode replaces them, see Migrating to 0.15. There is no groups member since 0.14.0: groups had no effect and is a compile error (see FRG-137).

A field carries mode, one FieldMode that says how it meets the API, and four const fn methods read it: is_id(), readable(), writable() and is_read_only() (the OpenAPI readOnly). FieldMode is #[non_exhaustive]; its variants answer as follows.

modeis_id()readable()writable()is_read_only()
Key { read_only }truetruefalseread_only
ReadWritefalsetruetruefalse
ReadOnlyfalsetruefalsetrue
WriteOnlyfalsefalsetruefalse
Computedfalsetruefalsetrue
Hidden (skip)falsefalsefalsefalse

A field has one mode: skip together with read_only is Hidden.

writable() answers the mode, not the write set. The owner field (#[field(owner)]) is ReadWrite (or WriteOnly), yet no generated body accepts it: the server sets it. A projection narrows the set further; read ProjectionMeta::write_fields for what a route accepts.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::meta::{FieldMeta, FieldMode};

fn describe(field: &FieldMeta) -> &'static str {
    match field.mode {
        FieldMode::Key { .. } => "key",
        FieldMode::Computed => "computed",
        FieldMode::Hidden => "hidden",
        _ if field.readable() && field.writable() => "read and write",
        _ if field.readable() => "read only",
        _ => "write only",
    }
}
}

validation_rules is a &'static [ValidationRule], the #[field(...)] rules of the field in declaration order (since 0.15.0; it was a slice of encoded strings, see Migrating to 0.15). ValidationRule is #[non_exhaustive]: MinLength(u64), MaxLength(u64), Min(Bound), Max(Bound), Pattern(&'static str), Email, Url and Required, with Bound either Int(i64) or Float(f64). The request validator and the validation_rules slice come from one parse of the attribute, and ValidationRule::schema_keyword() gives the JSON Schema keyword the OpenAPI document carries for a rule, as Some((keyword, KeywordValue)): minLength, maxLength, minimum, maximum, pattern, format ("email" or "uri"). Required answers None: it is an entry of the schema’s required list, not a property keyword. An integral float bound is an integer keyword (min = 0 on an f64 field gives minimum: 0).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::meta::{FieldMeta, KeywordValue, ValidationRule};

fn min_length(field: &FieldMeta) -> Option<u64> {
    field.validation_rules.iter().find_map(|rule| match rule {
        ValidationRule::MinLength(n) => Some(*n),
        _ => None,
    })
}

fn documented_keywords(field: &FieldMeta) -> Vec<(&'static str, KeywordValue)> {
    field
        .validation_rules
        .iter()
        .filter_map(ValidationRule::schema_keyword)
        .collect()
}
}

ModelMeta

The description of one resource: resource_name (the URL segment, "films"), table_name, primary_key_fields, fields, projections, behaviors, actions, pagination_mode, owner_field, auth_posture, authorize_rules and client_pk. It also answers field_by_wire_name, wire_name_of and renames_fields.

pagination_mode is a PaginationMode: Page, Cursor { key, ty } or Both { key, ty } (#[non_exhaustive]). The cursor modes carry the #[field(cursor_key)] field’s Rust name and its FieldType; pagination_mode.cursor_key() answers Some((key, ty)) for them and None for Page. A page-mode model has no cursor key in its description, even when a field carries #[field(cursor_key)].

actions lists the actions the model declares with #[ferra(action(...))], in declaration order, and is empty for a model that declares none. Each ActionMeta has its name, its target (ActionTarget::Row or ActionTarget::Collection), has_body and rule, the authorize rule the action declared. That rule is the action’s own: the model’s #[authorize] block and its posture neither supply nor replace it, and a model without a block keeps its posture rules for its other operations. The routes, the links and the OpenAPI operations of the actions are in Declared actions.

A ModelMeta built by hand, through the #[doc(hidden)] constructors, is outside the checks of the derive, which are the only checks of these combinations. Two examples of what a hand-built description can hold and the derive never emits: a FieldMode::Computed field marked filterable, and a PaginationMode::Cursor { key, .. } whose key names a hidden or write-only column. Trust a description only when #[derive(FerraModel)] produced it.

primary_key_fields carries the primary-key column names in declaration order. A single-key model holds a one-element slice and the route shape is /{resource}/{<pk>}; a composite-key model holds several and the route becomes /{resource}/{<pk1>}/{<pk2>}/….

Reading a description is what FerraModel::meta() is for:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::meta::FieldMode;
use ferra::model::FerraModel;

fn describe<M: FerraModel>() {
    let meta = M::meta();
    println!("{} is served at /{}", meta.table_name, meta.resource_name);
    for field in meta.fields {
        let kind = if field.is_id() {
            "key"
        } else if matches!(field.mode, FieldMode::Computed) {
            "computed"
        } else {
            "column"
        };
        println!("  {} ({:?}): {kind}, wire name {}", field.name, field.ty, field.wire_name);
    }
}
}

The FerraModel trait

FerraModel binds a Rust struct to its static ModelMeta. #[derive(FerraModel)] implements it; do not implement it by hand (its description cannot be built outside the framework, and the derive is what declares the model’s authorization posture).

pub trait FerraModel: serde::Serialize + serde::de::DeserializeOwned + Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn meta() -> &'static ModelMeta;
}

Every bound is load-bearing:

BoundWhy it’s required
SerializeResponses are rendered from the model.
DeserializeOwnedRequest bodies are deserialised into it (no borrowed 'de).
Send + SyncModels participate in async handlers on a multi-threaded Tokio runtime.
'staticFerra models are owned values, never borrowed from request state.

A field whose type is not Send or Sync is reported in Ferra’s words, at the field (Compile-time diagnostics).

Id — the identifier primitive

Id is the identifier type every Ferra model uses. It is a 16-byte newtype wrapping uuid::Uuid.

Construction

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::Id;

let a = Id::new();        // fresh UUID v7: time-ordered, collision-resistant
let b = Id::default();    // same as Id::new()
let n = Id::nil();        // all-zero sentinel — TEST FIXTURE ONLY
let _ = (a, b, n);
}

Id::nil() is explicitly a test fixture: it is distinguishable from any Id::new() output, which makes it useful as a sentinel in unit tests. Do not store or return Id::nil() from production code.

Wire format

Display emits the RFC 4122 hyphenated lowercase form (for example, "67e55044-10b1-426f-9247-bb680e5fe0c8"). FromStr accepts any of the four canonical UUID forms: hyphenated, simple (no hyphens), URN (urn:uuid:...), and braced ({...}). The serde impls delegate to Display / FromStr, so the wire representation is consistent across JSON, MessagePack, and every serde-backed format.

Full round-trip example

The same assertions run as a doctest of Id in crates/ferra-core/src/id.rs; this one is compiled with the guide.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::str::FromStr;
use ferra::Id;

// Construction.
let id = Id::new();

// Text round-trip.
let text = id.to_string();
let parsed = Id::from_str(&text)?;
assert_eq!(id, parsed);

// JSON round-trip.
let json = serde_json::to_string(&id)?;
let back: Id = serde_json::from_str(&json)?;
assert_eq!(id, back);

// Equality and the nil sentinel.
let nil = Id::nil();
assert_eq!(nil, Id::nil());
assert_ne!(nil, id);

// Parsing failure is typed, never a panic.
let err = Id::from_str("not a uuid").unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(err.to_string(), "failed to parse Id as a UUID");

// Id is Copy — passing by value is free.
fn takes_id(_x: Id) {}
takes_id(id);
takes_id(id);       // still valid, the previous call didn't move it.
Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
}

Why a newtype

Wrapping uuid::Uuid rather than exposing it directly lets Ferra swap the inner representation later without churning every caller. The 16-byte payload is Copy; passing Id through the HTTP pipeline costs nothing at runtime.

Id is not PartialOrd / Ord. UUID v7 values sort by creation time at millisecond precision, but two ids created in the same millisecond have no defined order; order rows by a column you control. Id is also a column type: a ferra::Id field maps to a Postgres uuid column.

IdParseError

<Id as FromStr>::Err is IdParseError, a hand-written unit struct with a Display impl and a std::error::Error impl. Its inner is pub(crate), so you can only obtain an IdParseError by a parse failure — never by direct construction.

In later phases, IdParseError may grow variants distinguishing “wrong length” from “invalid character”. Because external code only ever matches it as an opaque error, adding variants will be a non-breaking change.

Time vocabulary (DateTime / Date / date!)

Ferra exposes one typed time vocabulary across the framework. Three #[repr(transparent)] newtypes — ferra::DateTime (an instant), ferra::Date (a calendar date) and ferra::Time (a time of day) — wrap the underlying time library so the framework can swap that library in a future release without a consumer-facing signature change. Reach the types through ferra::DateTime / ferra::Date / ferra::Time (or via ferra::prelude::*); never import the underlying time library directly.

DateTime — timestamp

DateTime represents a precise instant anchored to UTC. Wire format: RFC 3339 timestamp text ("2023-11-14T22:13:20Z").

ConstructorReturnsNotes
DateTime::from_second(seconds: i64)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>seconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_millisecond(milliseconds: i64)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>milliseconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_microsecond(microseconds: i64)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>microseconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_nanosecond(nanoseconds: i128)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>nanoseconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_duration(duration: jiff::SignedDuration)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>epoch-relative duration
DateTime::now()DateTimereads the system clock; not const

The constructor names mirror the underlying time library verbatim; they are not invented. Names that do not exist on DateTime and will not be added: from_unix_timestamp, from_unix_nanos.

Each from_* constructor returns a Result and propagates an out-of-range argument as the underlying time library’s error type. The methods are not const fn — call sites use the standard ? operator, not const-context evaluation.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::DateTime;

fn epoch_seconds(seconds: i64) -> Result<DateTime, jiff::Error> {
    DateTime::from_second(seconds)
}

let now = DateTime::now();
let later = epoch_seconds(1_700_000_000)?;
let _ = (now, later);
Ok::<(), jiff::Error>(())
}

Date — calendar date

Date represents a time-zone-free calendar date. Wire format: RFC 3339 calendar date text ("YYYY-MM-DD").

ConstructorReturnsNotes
Date::new(year: i16, month: i8, day: i8)Dateconst fn; out-of-range triple is a const-eval error

Date::new is const fn — an out-of-range (year, month, day) triple is rejected at cargo build time, not at runtime:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::Date;

const RELEASED: Date = Date::new(2027, 1, 1);
// const INVALID: Date = Date::new(2027, 13, 1); // would not compile
}

date! macro — hyphen-literal calendar dates

ferra::date!(YYYY-MM-DD) re-tokenises a hyphen-literal into Date::new(year, month, day). Same compile-time validation as Date::new:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{Date, date};

const SUNSET: Date = date!(2027-01-01);
// const INVALID: Date = date!(2027-13-01); // const-eval error
}

The macro is the recommended call site for fixed dates (release sunsets, scheduled migrations) because the literal form is most readable. Use Date::new(...) directly when the inputs are computed or come from configuration.

Time — time of day

Time is a time of day without date or time zone. Wire format: "HH:MM:SS", with an optional fraction ("09:30:00", "23:59:59.5").

ConstructorReturnsNotes
Time::new(hour: i8, minute: i8, second: i8)Timeconst fn; an out-of-range triple is a const-eval error
"09:30:00".parse::<Time>()Result<Time, jiff::Error>FromStr

DateTime and Date implement FromStr too (RFC 3339 text).

Use as model fields

The three types are column types. Each maps to one Postgres type and round-trips through the database and through JSON:

Field typePostgres columnJSON
ferra::DateTimetimestamptz"2026-10-01T09:30:00Z" (RFC 3339, UTC)
ferra::Datedate"2026-10-01"
ferra::Timetime"09:30:00"

Option<T> of each is a nullable column. Postgres stores microseconds: a DateTime or a Time is rounded down to the microsecond when written, so what you read back is the written value truncated to microseconds.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{Date, DateTime, FerraModel, Time};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "events")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub at: DateTime,          // timestamptz NOT NULL
    pub day: Date,             // date NOT NULL
    pub opens: Time,           // time NOT NULL
    pub ends_at: Option<DateTime>, // timestamptz NULL
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Import the three from ferra, not from Sea-ORM’s prelude, which has types of the same names: an explicit use ferra::{Date, DateTime, Time}; takes precedence over the glob (and use ferra::prelude::* does the same for an application that declares no sea-orm). There is no timetz, no zone-less date-time and no duration type yet.

These types are columns because ferra-core implements Sea-ORM’s value traits for them, behind its sea-orm Cargo feature. Do not enable that feature yourself: ferra-db enables it, so it is on in every application that uses the ferra facade. It is tied to Sea-ORM 2.x and adds no I/O dependency to ferra-core.

Use as deprecation dates

FoundryBuilder::deprecated(since, sunset) takes two Dates and returns Result<_, DeprecationError>: a sunset earlier than since is refused. Every response under the deprecated version carries Deprecation: @<seconds> (RFC 9745: the start of since, UTC) and Sunset: <HTTP-date> (RFC 8594: the last second of sunset, for example Tue, 05 Jan 2027 23:59:59 GMT):

use ferra::{Foundry, date};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .api_version("v1")?
    .mount::<Film>()
    .deprecated(date!(2026-07-01), date!(2027-01-05))?
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Banned imports

A field typed with another time library does not compile: #[derive(FerraModel)] rejects a field whose type path starts with chrono::, time:: or jiff::, and names the Ferra type to use instead:

error: field type uses the `chrono` time crate; a Ferra model types time values with `ferra::DateTime` (an instant), `ferra::Date` (a calendar date) or `ferra::Time` (a time of day)
         help: replace it with `ferra::DateTime`, `ferra::Date` or `ferra::Time` (Postgres `timestamptz`, `date`, `time`); the wire format is RFC 3339
         note: docs/user-guide/ferra-core.md § Time vocabulary

cargo deny check also bans the chrono and time crates from the dependency graph, except where the Sea-ORM ecosystem and Ferra’s own column adapter use them.

Why newtypes

The three newtypes are #[repr(transparent)] over the underlying library’s value types. The layout is identical to the inner type, so a future release that replaces the underlying library does so at the ferra-core::time module boundary alone — consumer-facing signatures stay stable. The inner field is pub(crate); consumers reach the value only through ferra::DateTime / ferra::Date.

The OpenAPI schema emission is encapsulated in the same module: DateTime and Date emit {type: "string", format: "date-time"} and {type: "string", format: "date"}; Time emits {type: "string", pattern: "^([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:[0-5][0-9](\.[0-9]{1,9})?$"} (JSON Schema’s time format requires a time-zone offset, which a time of day does not have). Consumers and downstream crates never write the schema literal — the typed-newtype contract preserves the framework’s “single source of truth” rule.

Public surface

RequestContext

RequestContext (canonical path: ferra::request_context::RequestContext) is the request-scoped handle the framework hands to application code: the ctx parameter of FerraComputed::compute_field and FerraComputed::compute_field_batch (the request’s own since 0.15, for the rows and fields served to the caller), and the context of the authorities and hooks that read it. It answers who the caller is and what the request carried:

AccessorAnswers
subject() -> Option<&str>the caller’s FerraIdentity::id(), None when anonymous
is_authenticated() -> boola verified identity is present
has_role(&str) -> boolthe identity’s FerraIdentity::has_role
claims::<C>() -> Option<&C>the typed claims of a bearer or cookie token; None for an API key, an anonymous request, or when C is not the type given to .with_auth::<C>()
api_key() -> Option<&ApiKeyIdentity>the identity of the API key that authenticated the request
header(&str) -> Option<&str>the first value of a request header, case-insensitive; None when absent or not UTF-8

A model with none of an authority, hooks, owner(from), a computed field or a declared action gets RequestContext::empty(): every accessor answers None or false. A model with a computed field gets the request’s own context in its hooks, which run only for the rows and fields served to the caller (computed-fields.md).

A hook receives the context of the model it is declared on, and tx.resource::<N>() hands that same context to the authority of N and to the computed-field hooks of N (not a context built for N).

  • Credentials never reach it. Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie and the Foundry’s API key header are dropped when the context is built, in any case, so header() answers None for them, and Clone and Debug cannot carry them. Debug prints the subject and the header names, never a value.
  • Every other header is client-supplied. header("X-Forwarded-For") returns what the client sent, as is: do not authorize on X-Forwarded-*, Forwarded, Host or Origin unless your own trusted proxy sets them.
  • Not Copy. Since 0.13.0 the type owns an Arc and a header list: it is Clone, no longer Copy, UnwindSafe or RefUnwindSafe (migration note).

For the consumer-facing usage of the surrounding pipeline, see computed-fields.md.

JSON documents

serde_json::Value, bare Value, Sea-ORM’s prelude alias Json, and their Option forms are JSON fields. A typed Serialize + Deserialize struct stored with Sea-ORM’s FromJsonQueryResult opts in with #[field(json)]. sea_orm::Value is a SQL value enum and is not a JSON document type.

Before typed deserialization, a JSON field allows at most 32 container levels and 65,536 compact serialized bytes. Overrides use #[field(json(max_depth = 8, max_bytes = 4096))]; max_depth accepts 1–126, max_bytes a positive integer. Exceeding a limit returns 422 json_too_deep or json_too_large before any write. The JSON parser’s own 128-level limit returns 400 invalid_json first. An optional field accepts null. JSON fields cannot be filtered, sorted, or cursor keys (FRG-355).

An application declaring Sea-ORM with default-features = false must enable "with-json" beside "macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", and "sqlx-postgres". ferra::meta::FieldMeta::json exposes the compiled JsonBounds description.

ferra-db — the database layer

The repository layer (PgRepository, FerraRepository, FerraDbError) is internal to Ferra and outside the contract: the ferra facade does not export it, and an application does not declare ferra-db. What an application reaches from this layer is Page, CursorPage, CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, PkValue and DatabaseConnection, all exported by ferra.

To read and write a model from a route of your own, take a Resource<M> extractor (from the ResourceHandle<M> that mount_and_handle::<M>() returns): get, list, list_cursor, create, update, delete, each returning FerraError (Custom Handlers). Behaviour that used to be read on the repository (SQLSTATE 23505 becomes a 409 Conflict, a missing row a 404, an undecodable cursor a 400) is read on the HTTP side and on FerraError (ferra-http.md). For raw access, use your own DatabaseConnection, outside the contract: see Custom Handlers § Raw database access, outside the contract. Transactions are the same: begin one on your own connection with conn.begin() (below).

Dependencies. The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

Queries and pages

CollectionQuery and CursorQuery are #[non_exhaustive]: build one with CollectionQuery::new(page, per_page) and the with_filter / with_sort methods, CursorQuery::new(per_page) and with_after / with_filter. A filter key the model does not declare #[field(filterable)] is refused, never ignored (Pagination). PkValue<M> is the Sea-ORM primary-key value type of M: a plain i32 / i64 / Uuid, or a tuple for a composite key (ferra-forge.md § Composite primary keys).

A filter key is the field name for equality, or field[op] for a comparison (gt, gte, lt, lte) on a ferra::DateTime, Date or Time field, as filter[field][op] is on the wire; a comparison on another type is refused (400 unsupported_operator). A CursorQuery walks ascending unless with_direction(SortDirection::Desc) says otherwise; a cursor issued for the other direction is refused as an invalid cursor, and Resource::list_cursor applies the same checks as the generated route.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{CursorQuery, SortDirection};

let newest_first = CursorQuery::new(20)
    .with_direction(SortDirection::Desc)
    .with_filter("created_at[gte]", "2026-10-03T00:00:00Z");
assert_eq!(newest_first.direction, SortDirection::Desc);
}

Logging and tracing of database activity

sea_orm::Database::connect(&database_url) — the connection form used throughout this guide — accepts anything that converts Into<ConnectOptions>, including a bare &str. When you pass a bare URL, Sea-ORM builds a ConnectOptions with its own defaults, and those defaults are logging-on:

SettingDefaultWhat it emits
sqlx_loggingtrueThe SQL text of every executed statement, with its placeholders and not its bound values, is logged via the log/tracing bridge, at the level below.
sqlx_logging_levellog::LevelFilter::InfoThe level statements above are logged at (ignored if sqlx_logging is false).
record_stmt_in_spanstrueThe SQL text of the statement, with its placeholders and not its bound values, is attached to the tracing span for that query. Only under sea-orm’s non-default tracing-spans feature; without it the setting does nothing.
sqlx_slow_statements_logging_settings(LevelFilter::Off, _)Off by default; when enabled, statements slower than a threshold you set log at a separate level.

Neither setter logs a bound value (sea-orm 2.0.4, sqlx-core 0.9.0): sqlx’s statement log and the span field carry the SQL text with its placeholders, so a query binding a user’s email address or a password-reset token logs $1, not the address or the token. The text still tells a reader of your logs which tables, columns and filters your API touches, which is what the two setters cut. Bound values reach a log by one path: sea-orm’s debug-print feature, which logs every statement with its values at debug level whatever these setters say. It is off by default; never enable it outside development.

A reader of this section alone can now answer: does query text reach my logs and traces by default, and how do I change that? Yes for statement logging; for spans, only if sea-orm’s tracing-spans feature is on. To change it, build a ConnectOptions explicitly instead of passing a bare URL string, and connect with that:

use ferra::sea_orm::{ConnectOptions, Database};

async fn demo(database_url: String) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let mut opt = ConnectOptions::new(database_url);
opt.sqlx_logging(false)           // stop logging statements entirely, or...
   .record_stmt_in_spans(false);  // ...keep statement-shape logging but never
                                   // attach the SQL text to a span.

let conn = Database::connect(opt).await?;
let _ = conn;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

ConnectOptions’s setters take &mut self and return &mut Self, so they chain on an existing let mut binding as shown — they are not a consuming builder, and ConnectOptions::new(url) must be bound to a variable before you call a setter on it.

Recommended production posture. Disable sqlx_logging (or drop the level to a value your production log pipeline filters out) and disable record_stmt_in_spans to keep statement text out of your logs and spans. Never enable sea-orm’s debug-print feature outside development: it logs every statement with its values whatever these setters say. Keep both settings enabled in local development, where seeing the generated SQL is a debugging aid and the log sink is your own terminal. There is no framework-level override that does this for you today — ferra-db accepts whatever sea_orm::DatabaseConnection you construct and does not itself configure ConnectOptions — so the setting is entirely in your hands at the Database::connect(...) call site.

A connection for a permanent server

Ferra configures no ConnectOptions itself, so a server that stays up chooses its own. This recipe takes the URL from the environment, bounds the pool under the request budget, and keeps statement text out of the logs and spans (it never carries a bound value; see the debug-print bullet below):

use ferra::sea_orm::{ConnectOptions, Database, DatabaseConnection};
use std::time::Duration;

/// `budget` is the value you give `FoundryBuilder::request_budget`.
fn options(url: String, budget: Duration) -> ConnectOptions {
    let mut options = ConnectOptions::new(url);
    options
        .max_connections(20) // under the database's `max_connections`, divided by your instances
        .acquire_timeout(budget / 3) // under the budget: a full pool answers its own 503
        .idle_timeout(Duration::from_secs(300))
        .sqlx_logging(false) // no statement text in sqlx's logs
        .record_stmt_in_spans(false); // no statement text in a span (`tracing-spans` feature only)
    options
}

async fn connect(budget: Duration) -> Result<DatabaseConnection, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // From the environment or a secret store, never a literal, test fixtures included.
    let url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?;
    Ok(Database::connect(options(url, budget)).await?)
}
fn main() {
    let budget = Duration::from_secs(10);
    let o = options("postgres://db.internal/app".to_owned(), budget);
    assert_eq!(o.get_max_connections(), Some(20));
    assert!(o.get_acquire_timeout().is_some_and(|t| t < budget));
    assert!(!o.get_sqlx_logging() && !o.get_record_stmt_in_spans());
    let _ = connect;
}

  • acquire_timeout under the budget. A bare URL leaves it at sqlx’s 30 s, past a 10 s budget, so a full pool would answer the budget’s 503 timeout. Under the budget, it answers 503 service_unavailable (see When no connection can be had). A third of the budget leaves room for a request that needs a connection more than once.

  • Logging off. Both setters default to true; the table above says what each one emits and cuts: the statement text in sqlx’s log lines and, under the tracing-spans feature, in a span. Neither carries a bound value. Turn them back on in local development to see the SQL. sea-orm’s debug-print feature logs every statement with its values whatever these setters say; never enable it outside development.

  • Never enable TRACE for sea_orm in production. sea-orm 2.0.4’s Postgres connect function is #[instrument(level = "trace")] with no skip, so its span records the ConnectOptions through their Debug output, and the url field has no debug skip: a subscriber that enables TRACE for sea_orm records the URL, password included. Database::connect also puts the URL in the DbErr it returns when the URL cannot be parsed. Prefer a password from a secret store over a URL that carries credentials.

  • A lock wait ends on the server, below the budget, set once per role (the role your application connects as; here app_user, 5 s under a 10 s budget):

    ALTER ROLE app_user SET lock_timeout = '5s';

    Postgres applies a role setting when the role starts a session, and only then, so it reaches every server connection a pooler opens for that role and no session already open. A SET in your own connect hook lands on one server connection: in transaction mode PgBouncer releases the server connection after each transaction (PgBouncer pool_mode) and says clients must not use any session-based features (PgBouncer server_reset_query), and Neon lists SET/RESET as unsupported on its pooled endpoint and recommends a role-level setting instead (Neon connection pooling). A lock_timeout sent as a startup parameter is refused by PgBouncer unless track_extra_parameters lists it (then PgBouncer restores it, a pooler-side setup this recipe does not rely on) or ignore_startup_parameters does (then it is ignored and never applies). Below the budget, the wait ends while the request is alive: Postgres aborts the statement and the client’s ROLLBACK ends the transaction (the SQLSTATE is in the log only; the client gets a 500 internal), and the connection goes back to the pool clean. Behind a transaction pooler says what else a pooler forbids.

  • Keep lock_timeout above deadlock_timeout (1 s by default). Otherwise a deadlock surfaces as a 55P03 500 that is never retried, instead of the 40P01 that is.

  • What a timeout answers. A lock wait cut by lock_timeout (55P03) and a statement cut by statement_timeout (57014) are a 500 internal, logged once with the SQLSTATE, never retried (only 40001 and 40P01 are), and never the 503 timeout. A COMMIT refused with either code is classed as rolled back, and is the same 500. The repository pins both answers in crates/ferra-http/tests/lock_timeout.rs; the role form itself is not run there, as it would change a role every test shares. The Lambda page sets lock_timeout the same way: Server-side timeouts.

The Page<M> shape

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::Page;
use ferra::model::FerraModel;

// The four public fields of `Page<M>`; `CursorPage<M>` has `items`, `per_page` and `next_cursor`.
fn summary<M: FerraModel>(page: &Page<M>) -> String {
    format!(
        "page {} of {} per page: {} items, {} in all",
        page.page,
        page.per_page,
        page.items.len(),
        page.total
    )
}
}
  • 1-indexed page by framework convention. page = 0 is treated identically to page = 1 (the repository applies saturating_sub(1) internally to hand Sea-ORM its 0-indexed offset).
  • total: u64 fits any Postgres bigint in the non-negative half — the full-table row count observed by the count query.
  • items.len() <= per_page always. An over-scrolled request is Ok(Page { items: vec![], total, .. }), never NotFound.
  • Concurrent-insert drift. items.len() and total may disagree by ±1 under concurrent inserts — both queries run serially on the same connection (FR-015), not in parallel. Callers that need strict consistency read inside a SERIALIZABLE transaction of their own connection.
  • Serialize, not Deserialize. Page<T>: serde::Serialize whenever T: serde::Serialize. Page<T> and CursorPage<T> accept any T, a model or a view of one, which is what lets a route of your own return a page of views (Page<M> and CursorPage<M> are the same types with T = M). No Deserialize — pages are server-constructed, never parsed from client input.
  • #[non_exhaustive] — a later release may add fields. Construct via Page::new(items, total, page, per_page), not a struct literal.

Transactions

Transactions are Sea-ORM’s: begin one on your own DatabaseConnection (the type of your own sea-orm declaration, also exported as ferra::DatabaseConnection). It needs Sea-ORM’s TransactionTrait in scope. Dropping the transaction without .commit() rolls it back. A Resource<M> call runs on its own connection, not inside your transaction; inside it, write with Sea-ORM.

use ferra::DatabaseConnection;
use sea_orm::TransactionTrait; // import needed for .begin()

async fn demo(conn: DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let tx = conn.begin().await?;
// ... Sea-ORM statements on `&tx` ...
tx.commit().await?; // dropped without commit: rolled back
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Every write Ferra opens runs at READ COMMITTED, whatever the server’s default_transaction_isolation says (0.16.0). PostgreSQL’s own default changes nothing. An application whose connection defaults to REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE loses one detection: a hook that reads a second row through tx.resource().get (no lock), then writes it through tx.resource().update with a value computed from that read, no longer gets a 40001 that the retry of Transient conflicts are retried would have replayed. The update locks the row FOR UPDATE, merges the patch over the fresh row, and the stale value wins. Under a SERIALIZABLE default, read-write anomalies across rows are likewise no longer detected. A write of the row’s own model is unaffected, because before_* hooks receive the locked row. Remedy: compute the new value in the target row’s own hook or action, where the row is locked. tx.resource evaluates no If-Match; HTTP clients keep If-Match. See Migrating from 0.15 to 0.16.

A child’s write locks its parent FOR SHARE before its own row (0.16.0; see Relations). On a hot parent, a stream of children writes can keep the parent’s share lock held: PostgreSQL lets new FOR SHARE lockers pass a waiting FOR UPDATE, so a write of the parent itself may wait longer. That is latency, not a deadlock, and the request budget’s 503 timeout caps it (What Ferra executes states the wait).

A transient error that a hook swallows is not replayed. A hook that catches the error of a tx.resource call (a 40001, a 40P01) and goes on gives the write a 500 internal, with nothing committed: the retry of Transient conflicts are retried only replays an error the hook lets out.

What Ferra executes

(0.16.0.) For each operation of the generated routes, the statements Ferra sends, the locks it holds and the level it runs at. The numbers below are pinned by statement_shapes (crates/ferra-http/tests/statement_shapes.rs), which counts statements and probes the locks from a second connection, and never reads SQL text; a change of one is a change of the other. They hold for the models of that test, a studio (a root, no relation), its films and their reviews (a child through owner(from), with a soft delete and one BelongsTo). Read the tables as shapes: a model with another number of relations runs another number of readable-set statements, one per BelongsTo (Links and foreign keys).

  • Counted: every statement the request sends. BEGIN, the SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED that follows it and COMMIT are not.
  • Isolation: every write runs in one transaction at READ COMMITTED, whatever the server’s default_transaction_isolation says (the test sets it to REPEATABLE READ). A read opens no transaction of Ferra’s: each of its statements runs alone, so a list’s count and its page are not one snapshot.
  • The readable set is one key IN (...) read per BelongsTo, whatever the number of rows: it decides the foreign key and the links of the response (Links and foreign keys). It takes no lock.
  • The target read is the read of the row a BelongsTo key names, which a write that sets the key runs under the caller’s rules, without a lock (Writing a foreign key).

GET an item: 2 statements, no lock, no transaction. The same 2 with an embed.

#StatementLockWith an embed
1the row, under the caller’s rulesnonethe same
2the readable set of the parentnonethe same statement: its rows are the embedded ones

GET a list, offset mode: 3 statements for a page of 1, 10 or 50 rows, no lock, no transaction. The same 3, for 1, 10 or 50 rows, with an embed.

#StatementLockWith an embed
1the countnonethe same
2the pagenonethe same
3the readable set of the parent, for all the rows of the pagenonethe same statement: its rows are the embedded ones

GET a list, cursor mode: 2 statements for a page of 1, 10 or 50 rows, no lock, no transaction. The same 2, for 1, 10 or 50 rows, with an embed.

#StatementLockWith an embed
1the pagenonethe same
2the readable set of the parent, for all the rows of the pagenonethe same statement: its rows are the embedded ones

POST a child: 4 statements. No read of its own row first.

#StatementLock held after it
1the parent, under the create checkthe parent FOR SHARE
2the target read of the foreign keynone
3INSERTthe new row, until the commit
4the readable set of the parentnone

POST a root: 1 statement. The INSERT; a model with no relation has no parent to lock and no readable set.

PUT a child: 7 statements.

#StatementLock held after it
1the row, by keynone
2the readable set of the row’s parent, as stored: it tells which foreign keys the caller may not read, so the body need not carry them (a PUT cannot carry an owner(from) key)none
3the row, under the caller’s rules: a row the caller cannot see answers its 404 here, before any locknone
4the parentFOR SHARE
5the rowFOR UPDATE
6UPDATEthe row
7the readable set of the parentnone

PATCH a child: 6 statements. The PUT without its second statement (the readable set before the lock): a PATCH keeps the stored value of every key its body leaves out, so it need not know beforehand which keys are hidden.

#StatementLock held after it
1the row, by keynone
2the row, under the caller’s rules (the 404 before any lock)none
3the parentFOR SHARE
4the rowFOR UPDATE
5UPDATEthe row
6the readable set of the parentnone

PATCH a root: 3 statements. No parent: the read under the caller’s rules takes the row lock itself.

#StatementLock held after it
1the row, by keynone
2the row, under the caller’s rulesFOR UPDATE
3UPDATEthe row

DELETE a child with a soft delete: 5 statements. The UPDATE sets deleted_at; no body comes back, so no readable set.

#StatementLock held after it
1the row, by keynone
2the row, under the caller’s rules (the 404 before any lock)none
3the parentFOR SHARE
4the rowFOR UPDATE
5UPDATE of deleted_atthe row

POST .../restore a child: 6 statements. As the delete, on a row that is deleted, and the restored row comes back.

#StatementLock held after it
1the deleted row, by keynone
2the deleted row, under the caller’s rules (the 404 before any lock)none
3the parent (a soft-deleted parent is locked too)FOR SHARE
4the deleted rowFOR UPDATE
5UPDATE of deleted_atthe row
6the readable set of the parentnone

A row action on a child: 6 statements of Ferra’s, plus the handler’s.

#StatementLock held after it
1the row, by keynone
2the row, under the caller’s rules (the 404 before any lock)none
3the parentFOR SHARE
4the rowFOR UPDATE
the handler, with the row locked: each tx.resource call it makes runs the statements of the operation it iswhat that operation holds
5UPDATE of the row the handler returnedthe row
6the readable set of the parentnone

The test’s publish of a film with two live reviews lists them (3 statements) and writes each (a child PATCH without the PUT’s second statement: 6 each), so it runs 6 + 3 + 2 × 6 = 21. A hook of your own that calls tx.resource adds its own statements the same way.

A collection action over a child’s rows: 3 statements, then one UPDATE per row. 4 for one row, 5 for two. The three come first, whatever the number of rows.

#StatementLock held after it
1the rows, by keynone
2the distinct parents, in one statement, in key orderFOR SHARE on each
3the rows, in one statement, in key orderFOR UPDATE on each
4…UPDATE, one per row, in key orderthe row

Under contention a statement that asks for a lock a transaction holds incompatibly waits for it, and the request waits with it, at that statement and nowhere else. A write waits at the parent’s FOR SHARE while the parent is held FOR UPDATE (by its own write, action or hook), then at its row’s FOR UPDATE while another write holds the row; a parent’s write waits for the shares of the child writes in flight. PostgreSQL lets new FOR SHARE lockers pass a waiting FOR UPDATE, so a stream of child writes can keep a parent’s own write waiting longer. That is latency: it ends when the holder commits or rolls back, or at the 503 timeout of the request budget when the application set one. A read takes no lock and waits for none. A collection action locks its parents, then its rows, each in key order, so two overlapping batches end without a deadlock between them. Ferra does not promise the absence of deadlocks: a deadlock the protocol cannot order away (two hooks that write each other’s siblings, a trigger of yours that writes the parent) is aborted by PostgreSQL with 40P01, replayed up to the bounded retries and answered 503 retry_exhausted when it keeps coming (Transient conflicts are retried). The locks and the order are stated in Relations.

Behind a transaction pooler

Ferra’s writes run behind a pooler in transaction mode: PgBouncer, or Neon’s pooled endpoint (the hostname with -pooler). A pooler hands a server connection to a client for one transaction only, so nothing a session keeps may matter between two transactions. Ferra keeps nothing:

  • no SET outside a transaction (what a write sets, it sets for its transaction: the isolation level of a model with a write’s READ COMMITTED level, for one), no LISTEN, no SQL-level PREPARE;
  • the advisory locks of a system grant are transaction-level (pg_advisory_xact_lock), released at commit or rollback, never session-level;
  • a write, its replay after a 40001 or a 40P01 (the whole transaction runs again) and its COMMIT each use one transaction on one server connection.

The statements Ferra prepares are protocol-level ones (sqlx’s), which a pooler can carry only if it tracks them: PgBouncer does with max_prepared_statements greater than zero (since 1.21.0; on by default at 200 since 1.24.0). sqlx also sends extra_float_digits at the start of every connection, and a PgBouncer that lists it in neither ignore_startup_parameters nor track_extra_parameters refuses the connection. Your own code is yours: a SET, a LISTEN, a session advisory lock or a WITH HOLD cursor of your own is wrong behind such a pooler, whatever Ferra does.

PgBouncer 1.26.1 or later. Earlier versions have CVE-2026-107350, a bypass of SCRAM authentication between users, fixed in 1.26.1. The repository’s compose.yml and its CI pin edoburu/pgbouncer at 1.26.1, by digest, with AUTH_TYPE=scram-sha-256; run no older one, and no looser authentication mode, in front of a database that holds data.

The repository proves the above on every run of pooler_acceptance (crates/ferra-http/tests/): CRUD, a stale If-Match on PUT, PATCH and DELETE, a forced 40001 replayed to one commit and one after_commit, a second pooled connection that reads the server’s defaults after a write, and two concurrent system appends that end with one chain head each. It needs POOLER_DATABASE_URL (podman compose up -d postgres pgbouncer, then postgres://ferra:ferra@127.0.0.1:6432/ferra_test) and fails under CI without it. #[sqlx::test] drops its database without FORCE, and PgBouncer keeps an idle server connection to it for server_idle_timeout after the client left (10 s in the repository’s test pooler, 600 s by default): the test ends those sessions itself, and a run that fails before that leaves its database undroppable (55006) until they expire.

When no connection can be had

A generated route, or a Resource<M> call, that gets no connection from your pool within its acquire_timeout answers 503 service_unavailable (0.17.0). The answer comes before the operation: nothing of it was applied, no hook ran, and the client may retry it. The detail is one fixed text; it names neither the pool, the database nor a delay (service_unavailable shows the body). It is a 503 and not a 500 because the service could not handle the request in time, whatever the cause: a saturated pool, and also a database that is down or still starting, since sqlx retries a refused connection until the acquire_timeout and the pool then reports a timeout. Say “a connection could not be had”, not “the pool is full”, when you read it. A connection the database refuses at once (a wrong password, an unknown database) stays a 500. Ferra does not retry it: only 40001 and 40P01 are retried, and a retry would add to the saturation.

  • Set acquire_timeout under the request budget. The deadline that comes first answers. With the pool’s timeout at or past the budget left, the budget’s 503 timeout wins; under it, the pool’s 503 service_unavailable wins, and that is the one an operator wants to see, because it says what is saturated. For a write made through Ferra (a generated route or a Resource<M> call), both mean nothing was written; a write on your own connection is outside this (What Ferra does not do in one request). The budget’s side of this is in Behaviors.
use ferra::sea_orm::{ConnectOptions, Database};
use std::time::Duration;

async fn demo(database_url: String) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let mut opt = ConnectOptions::new(database_url);
opt.acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5)); // under a `.request_budget(Duration::from_secs(10))`
let conn = Database::connect(opt).await?;
let _ = conn;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}
  • No Retry-After is sent, because no delay is known. A client or a gateway backs off with full jitter on a 503 without Retry-After and caps its attempts; a fixed delay makes every client retry in step.
  • After a commit it is a 500. A pool that gives no connection once the write is durable (the read of a written row’s parents) is a 500 internal with the write standing, never this 503 (service_unavailable).
  • API keys. An API key request whose store shares the saturated pool is a 503 identity_unavailable, not a service_unavailable: the credential could not be checked, so the handler never runs (API keys). The key store does not go through the path above, so it writes one warn line per refused request, target ferra_http::credential, reason = "store_unavailable", and no ferra_db::pool line. Under a flood of requests that is one line each. Give the key store its own small pool when its 503 must stay distinct from the rest, and, for the volume, put a de-duplicating tracing layer in your subscriber (tracing-throttle or Vector’s tracing_limit) besides the acquire_timeout and the pool size. Ferra does not de-duplicate for you.

Blameable models and the repository

The public FerraRepository write methods (insert, update, soft_delete, restore and their _in_tx forms) take no subject, so on a #[behavior(blameable)] model they return an error and write nothing: the author comes from the caller’s identity, which only the generated routes and Resource<M> hold (0.13.0).

No raw-SQL entry point

The root of the ferra crate publishes NO entry point that accepts a pre-formed SQL string: ferra::Statement, ferra::execute_unprepared and ferra::raw_sql do not resolve (compile-fail fixtures, crates/ferra/tests/ui/no_raw_sql.rs). That is not a limit on your application — ferra::sea_orm is Sea-ORM itself, and your application owns its DatabaseConnection. It is a statement about the routes Ferra generates: they never put request data in SQL text. A filter value is bound as a parameter, a sort key that is not declared #[field(sortable)] is not an identifier of the query, a cursor is decoded before any query is built (crates/ferra-db/tests/hostile_input_is_bound.rs).

Your own SQL

If you need raw SQL (a hand-written migration, an analytics query that defeats Sea-ORM’s builder), use Sea-ORM directly, on the connection you already hold. It is outside the guarantee above — the query is yours:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }

One rule goes with that line: a Ferra project never holds two major versions of Sea-ORM, not even for its tests or an optional feature. A sea-orm = "1" in [dev-dependencies], or behind a feature such as full = ["dep:sea-orm"], next to a model written through the facade, is refused with FRG-400 as soon as the test or the feature is on. Give it the same major as Ferra, or remove it and write ferra::sea_orm::...; cargo tree -d -i sea-orm lists the copies (docs/user-guide/ferra-forge-diagnostics.md section FRG-400).

Your code reads as “I am opting out of Ferra’s SQL-injection-by-construction contract for this query”. Three entry points, in order of preference:

  • sea_orm::raw_sql! (added in Sea-ORM 2.0) — a format!-style macro that still parameterizes every interpolated value, so it carries no injection risk despite the format!-like syntax. This is Sea-ORM’s own recommended entry point for hand-written SQL as of 2.0. SomeEntity::find_by_statement(raw_sql!(DbBackend::Postgres, "SELECT * FROM films WHERE year > {}", min_year)).
  • Statement::from_sql_and_values — construct a Statement with an explicit parameter list (Vec<Value>) bound positionally ($1, $2, …). Use when you need to build the parameter list programmatically rather than at a single macro call site.
  • execute_unprepared (a ConnectionTrait method, e.g. conn.execute_unprepared("...").await?) — runs a literal SQL string with no parameter binding at all. Only ever pass a compile-time-constant string (a migration statement, a DDL command); passing anything containing interpolated request data here reintroduces the exact injection risk Ferra’s core contract exists to foreclose. Statement::from_string (construct-only, no execution) exists for cases where you need a Statement value without binding parameters — pair it with from_sql_and_values rather than execute_unprepared if the statement takes any input.

API keys

ferra::api_key holds the key store contract (ApiKeyStore, PgApiKeyStore), issue, revoke and the schema. How a key is issued, stored hashed and presented is in ferra-auth.md, section API keys.

The ferra facade

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{
    Page, CursorPage, CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, PkValue,
    DatabaseConnection, Id, FerraModel, Resource, ResourceHandle,
};
}

#[derive(FerraModel)] is exported too (and by ferra::prelude): there is no second dependency to declare. The description of a model (ModelMeta, FieldMeta, FieldType) is read through the ferra::meta module.

Entity declaration: two forms

The split form — a Model struct plus a separate enum Relation { ... } naming every relation. Sea-ORM 2.0 also ships a second, terser dense form, and both are valid ways to declare a Ferra entity. This section states which to write and when, rather than leaving you to infer it from the fact that Ferra’s own shipped examples use both.

The split form

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
}

#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}   // names every relation, even when there are none

impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The dense form (Sea-ORM 2.0)

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[sea_orm::model]      // <- layered above the same derive list
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    // relations, if any, are declared inline on the struct — see below —
    // there is no separate `enum Relation` at all in this form.
}

impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The dense form drops the enum Relation { ... } boilerplate entirely — for a model with no relations, that is a pure line-count win. When a model does have relations, the dense form declares them inline instead of in the separate enum, and FerraModel reads such a model since 0.13.0 (see ferra-forge.md § Relations for a compiled example):

// Sea-ORM's own syntax, shown for the shape.
#[sea_orm::model]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "users")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[sea_orm(has_one)]
    pub profile: HasOne<super::profile::Entity>,
    #[sea_orm(has_many)]
    pub posts: HasMany<super::post::Entity>,
}

Relation fields and FerraModel

Before 0.13.0 #[derive(FerraModel)] refused HasOne<...>, HasMany<...> and BelongsTo<...> as field types, so a dense-form model with a relation field had to be written in the split form. It no longer is: #[sea_orm::model] keeps the relation fields off Model (they live on a second struct, ModelEx), Ferra reads Model, and a relation field is never a column or a wire field, and never a projection field of its own, with one exception: a BelongsTo named in a projection’s read list is embedded (Embedding). The practical rule:

Your model has…Write it as…
No relation fieldsEither form. The dense form (#[sea_orm::model]) is shorter — prefer it for new models.
One or more relation fields (has_one / has_many / belongs_to)The dense form. A split-form model gets no relation feature: a model that gains relations moves to the dense form (ADR-0059).

Which shipped example uses which, and why

Every shipped example uses the dense form (ADR-0050):

  • examples/hello-ferra — its one model, Film, has no relations.
  • examples/movie-stars — its six models (Studio, Film, Review, Actor, Director, Genre) are in the dense form; Studio, Film and Review declare their relations (HasMany, BelongsTo) on it.
  • examples/lambda-neon — its one model, Film, has no relations.

The split form is not shown by an example: it stays valid, and the section above documents it, for a model without relations. A model that gains relations moves to the dense form (ADR-0059), and a new model is written in it: copy any shipped example.

Troubleshooting

error[E0277]: the trait bound <M>: sea_orm::ModelTrait is not satisfied

You forgot the DeriveEntityModel derive on the struct. A Ferra model requires BOTH FerraModel AND DeriveEntityModel on the same #[derive(...)] list. Add DeriveEntityModel back and recompile.

error[E0425]: cannot find value Statement in crate ferra

Expected — the root of ferra has no raw-SQL entry point. Use Sea-ORM’s own (sea_orm::Statement), through the sea-orm your application declares; see “Your own SQL”.

ferra::PgRepository, ferra::FerraRepository, ferra::FerraDbError, ferra::DatabaseTransaction do not resolve

Removed from the facade in 0.10.0 (the repository layer is internal). Use Resource<M> or your own DatabaseConnection (see the top of this page).

Stability commitment

What is guaranteed is what ferra exports and api/ferra.txt snapshots; a change of it needs a minor version bump (stability.md).

ItemCommitmentChange requires
CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, Page, CursorPage#[non_exhaustive], built with new and the with_* methodsAdditions are additive
DatabaseConnection re-exportStable name, re-exported from Sea-ORMA minor version
No raw-SQL entry point at the root of ferraStatement / execute_unprepared / raw_sql do not resolve there; ferra::sea_orm is Sea-ORM wholeA minor version

MSRV: rust-version = "1.94" — inherited from the workspace, and set by Sea-ORM itself.

ferra-http — the Axum CRUD handler layer

The HTTP layer: what Foundry mounts for a model, the wire contracts of the routes (RFC 7807 errors, flat and HAL representations, pagination, Prefer:), and the default layer stack. An application reaches it through the ferra facade and does not declare ferra-http; what is public is the list of stability.md, and the signatures are the snapshot api/ferra-http.txt. The response envelopes (ItemResponse, CollectionResponse), the link builders and PaginationParams are not public in 0.9: a route of your own answers with a struct of its own (Custom Handlers).

This page is the authoritative user-guide for ferra-http. A reader with only this page plus standard Rust knowledge produces a compiling Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(key)?.mount::<Film>().build() call site on the first attempt — no ADR, no constitution, and no framework source is required.

Dependencies and URLs

The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

A model’s URL segment ({resource} below) is its table name: table_name = "films" is served at /films. To serve a table under another name, put #[ferra(resource = "movies")] on the model. A model’s table is its own to create (a migration, or Schema::create_table_from_entity in development): Ferra never creates one.

Zero-to-API in five lines

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
async fn demo(database_url: String) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(&database_url).await?;
let app = Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?.mount::<Film>().build();
let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
axum::serve(listener, app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>()).await?;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Film here is declared #[ferra(auth = "none")]. A model that needs an identity (auth = "bearer", or #[authorize] rules other than Anyone) must be mounted on a chain with .with_auth::<YourClaims>(jwt) — see ferra-auth.md. Foundry is the only way to mount a model: it is what applies the model’s authorization rules. There is no lower-level router constructor.

You get GET /films, GET /films/{id}, POST /films, PUT /films/{id} and DELETE /films/{id}, a Location header on creation, and an application/problem+json body on every error. The primary key may be single or composite. Serve with into_make_service_with_connect_info: the rate limiter keys on the peer address.

See examples/hello-ferra/ for the full worked example with PostgreSQL container + Rust-coded migrations.

The routes a model gets

Foundry mounts these routes for every model; the handlers behind them are internal. The HTTP contracts are:

OperationMethodPathRequestSuccessError surfaces
getGET/{resource}/{id}—200 OK + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links)400 on path-extractor rejection · 404 on missing row · 500 on DB error
listGET/{resource}?page={u32}&per_page={u32}200 OK + the collection as JSON (HAL: with _links)500 on DB error
createPOST/{resource}JSON body of the write projection201 Created + Location: {base}/{resource}/{id} + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links); 201 with no body and no Location when the caller may not GET the new row400 on body parse · 401/403 from the rule · 409 on unique violation · 413 on oversized body · 422 on a field outside the write projection or a #[field(...)] rule · 429 on rate limit · 500 · 503 retry_exhausted
updatePUT/{resource}/{id}JSON body of the write projection200 OK + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links); 204 with no body when the caller may not GET the updated row (0.13.0)400 · 401/403 · 404 · 409 · 412 · 413 · 422 · 429 · 500 · 503 retry_exhausted
updatePATCH/{resource}/{id}Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json: a JSON object of the write projection’s fields to change200 OK + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links), 204 under Prefer: return=minimal or when the caller may not GET the updated row400 · 401/403 · 404 · 412 · 413 · 415 · 422 · 429 · 500 · 503 retry_exhausted
deleteDELETE/{resource}/{id}—204 No Content (no body)400 · 401/403 · 404 · 412 · 429 · 500 · 503 retry_exhausted
a declared actionPOST/{resource}/{id}/{name}nothing, or the JSON body the action declares200 OK + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links); 204 under Prefer: return=minimal or when the caller may not GET the written row (0.14.0)400 · 401/403 · 404 · 409 · 412 · 422 · 429 · 500 · 503, and 413 · 415 when the action has a body
a declared collection actionPOST/{resource}/{name}the envelope {"ids": [...], "body": ...}, 1 to 100 ids; body only when the action declares one204 (no body, no ETag)400 · 401/403 · 404 · 409 · 412 · 413 · 415 · 422 · 429 · 500 · 503

Every write above, restore and the actions included, runs in a transaction the framework owns, and answers 503 retry_exhausted (with Retry-After: 1) when the database aborts it on each of its three attempts; nothing is written. See Transient conflicts are retried.

The path names the row on update and delete; a key in the body is refused (422). PATCH is served on the bare path and under every projection prefix, with the update rule of that route as PUT; it takes application/merge-patch+json alone (any other Content-Type, application/json included, is a 415 naming that type). The rule is checked before the body is read. See Projections and routing § Writes for what a write body may contain.

A declared action (#[ferra(action(..))]) is one more route, on the bare path alone: its own rule, its own handler, the write of a PUT. A collection action (collection) is POST /{resource}/{name}: it runs the handler on up to 100 listed rows in one transaction, all or nothing, and answers 204; on a model with a String key it shadows the row whose key is its name (GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE of that path answer 405). Its rows are in Declared actions.

Public reads, protected writes

A model that must be readable without a token but writable only with one says so per operation, and the chain names the claims type. A field is sortable (?sort=-price_cents) or filterable (?filter[name]=…) only if it says so with #[field(sortable)] / #[field(filterable)] (Pagination). The table is shop_products and the URL is /products: #[ferra(resource = "products")] sets the URL segment; without it, the segment is the table name (/shop_products):

use ferra::{ClaimCheck, FerraIdentity, FerraModel, Foundry, HmacAlgorithm, JwtConfig};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

mod product {
    use super::*;

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "shop_products")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer", resource = "products")]
    #[authorize(
        list = Anyone,
        get = Anyone,
        create = Authenticated,
        update = Authenticated,
        delete = Authenticated
    )]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        #[field(filterable)]
        pub name: String,
        #[field(sortable)]
        pub price_cents: i64,
    }

    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Claims {
    sub: String,
}

impl FerraIdentity for Claims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str {
        &self.sub
    }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool {
        false
    }
}

fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let jwt = JwtConfig::single_secret(
    "key-1",                                        // `kid`: every token must carry it
    std::env::var("JWT_SECRET")?,                   // the HMAC secret, from the environment
    HmacAlgorithm::Hs256,
    ClaimCheck::expect("https://auth.example.com/"), // `iss` the token must carry
    ClaimCheck::expect("products-api"),              // `aud` the token must carry
)?;
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .with_auth::<Claims>(jwt)
    .mount::<product::Model>()
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

(Authentication and Authorization has the rest of the JWT configuration.)

A model that carries one or more #[ferra(projection(...))] declarations also mounts a parallel set of routes under each named projection’s URL prefix (e.g. /detail/films/{id}). The wire shape on those routes is the projection’s own: a response is serialized from its read struct, and a body is parsed into its write struct. See Projections and routing for the full URL contract, naming convention, and the path_prefix override.

RFC 7807 error taxonomy

Every error from every handler is rendered as application/problem+json per RFC 7807 §3. FerraError has fourteen variants (the enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match outside the crate needs a wildcard arm; FerraError::error_type() names the wire type of any variant). They map onto twelve of the fourteen type URIs (the others, payload_too_large and rate_limited, come from middleware layers, see Error handling):

VariantHTTP statustype URItitle
FerraError::NotFound { resource, id }404https://ferra.rs/errors/not_foundResource Not Found
FerraError::CollectionNotFound { resource }404https://ferra.rs/errors/not_foundResource Not Found (detail <resource> not found, no id; 0.13.0)
FerraError::Validation(ValidationErrors)400https://ferra.rs/errors/validationValidation Error
FerraError::BadRequest { detail, field, code }400https://ferra.rs/errors/validationValidation Error
FerraError::Unprocessable(ValidationErrors)422https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failedValidation Failed
FerraError::InvalidCursor400https://ferra.rs/errors/invalid_cursorInvalid Cursor
FerraError::Unauthorized401https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorizedUnauthorized (with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer)
FerraError::Forbidden403https://ferra.rs/errors/forbiddenForbidden
FerraError::Conflict(String)409https://ferra.rs/errors/conflictConflict
FerraError::ConflictWith(String)409https://ferra.rs/errors/conflictConflict (your hook’s HookError::conflict; the detail is yours, served as given; see ferra-error-handling.md § Hook errors)
FerraError::UnsupportedMediaType415https://ferra.rs/errors/unsupported_media_typeUnsupported Media Type
FerraError::Internal(InternalError)500https://ferra.rs/errors/internalInternal Server Error (the cause stays in source(), never on the wire; see ferra-error-handling.md § Rust errors and their causes)
FerraError::Timeout503https://ferra.rs/errors/timeoutRequest Timeout Budget Exceeded (no Retry-After; see foundry.md § Request time budget)
FerraError::IdentityUnavailable503https://ferra.rs/errors/identity_unavailableIdentity Unavailable (a key set out of reach with no fresh key cached; no Retry-After; see ferra-auth.md § Key set)
FerraError::ServiceUnavailable(String)503https://ferra.rs/errors/service_unavailableService Unavailable (your hook’s HookError::unavailable, with your detail, or, from 0.17.0, no database connection in time, with a fixed detail and nothing applied; no Retry-After; see ferra-error-handling.md § service_unavailable)
FerraError::RetryExhausted503https://ferra.rs/errors/retry_exhaustedRetries Exhausted (a Resource<M> write aborted on each of its three attempts; Retry-After: 1; answer it as a transient 503, never replay it in a loop; 0.16.0; see ferra-error-handling.md § retry_exhausted)
(middleware)413https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_largePayload Too Large 1
(middleware)429https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limitedToo Many Requests 1

Worked body for a 404:

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found",
  "title":  "Resource Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "films/42 not found"
}

Worked body for a 400 from a malformed JSON request:

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title":  "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "validation failed",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "body", "code": "invalid_json", "message": "expected `,` or `}` at line 1 column 14" }
  ]
}

Internals never leak. The detail field on a 500 is always the literal string "internal server error"; the cause (a sea_orm::DbErr, a failed hook) is kept in the error’s source() chain for your logs and never reaches the HTTP body. A failed COMMIT is the exception: its chain carries only the SQLSTATE and the outcome (rolled back or unknown), never the database error, and its message stays out of the logs (the ferra_db::commit line). The Axum "Failed to deserialize … into the target type: " prefix and any axum::extract::rejection:: substring are stripped at the extractor boundary; only human-readable messages reach errors[*].message.

Worked body for a 429 from the rate-limit mapper:

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited",
  "title":  "Too Many Requests",
  "status": 429,
  "detail": "rate limit exceeded; retry after 3 seconds"
}

The response also carries the Retry-After header (integer seconds, at least 1). A refill shorter than a second is answered as Retry-After: 1, never 0, which would invite an immediate retry that is refused again. If the component ever emitted no Retry-After header, detail would degrade to the literal string "rate limit exceeded" and the header would be absent from the response; the default rule always emits it. The rate-limit mapper mounts only alongside the framework’s default rate-limit component — consumer-provided rate-limiters produce their own error shape (see ADR-0015 for rationale).

Response representations

A successful response comes in two shapes, and the client chooses with Accept: flat (application/json) is the row, or the collection envelope, as plain JSON; HAL (application/hal+json) is the same body plus _links, so an AI agent can navigate the API without prior URL knowledge. Both go through the same query and the same read projection: they show the same rows, the same total and the same keys.

AcceptRepresentation
absent, empty, */*, application/*, only other types, unparseablethe Foundry default: HAL unless you set it
application/jsonflat
application/hal+jsonHAL
both, with different qthe higher q
both, with equal q (or both q=0)the Foundry default
one of the two at q=0, the other absentthe other

Ferra never answers 406: an Accept it cannot satisfy gets the default. An error is application/problem+json and the same body in both modes.

On a 2xxFlatHAL
Content-Typeapplication/jsonapplication/hal+json
VaryAcceptAccept
Location (201)yesyes

A 201 to a caller who may create the row but not GET it is the exception: no body, so no Content-Type, and no Location (0.13.0).

| Link, X-Total-Count | never | never |

Vary: Accept is on every negotiated 2xx, 204 included: configure a cache in front of the API to honor it. Pagination state is in the body only, never in a header.

To serve flat to a client that states no preference, set the default before the first mount:

use ferra::{Foundry, Representation};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .default_representation(Representation::Flat)
    .mount::<Film>()
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Before 0.11.0 the HAL body was served as application/json. A client that sends Accept: application/json now gets the flat body: it no longer has _links. A client that sends no Accept still gets HAL, with the Content-Type application/hal+json.

Flat bodies

{ "id": 1, "title": "Rust en pratique", "director": "Alice", "year": 2025 }

A page list is {"items": [...], "total": 25, "page": 2, "per_page": 10}; a cursor list is {"items": [...], "per_page": 10, "next_cursor": "<token>"}, and next_cursor is null on the last page (the key is always there). Pass next_cursor back as ?cursor= with the same filter[...] and sort.

HAL single-item body

Model fields are flattened at the top level via #[serde(flatten)]. A Film { id: 1, title: "Rust en pratique", director: "Alice", year: Some(2025) } serializes as:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Rust en pratique",
  "director": "Alice",
  "year": 2025,
  "_links": {
    "self":       { "href": "https://api.example.com/films/1" },
    "collection": { "href": "https://api.example.com/films" }
  }
}

HAL paginated collection body

{
  "items": [ /* array of items, each with its own _links */ ],
  "total": 25,
  "page": 2,
  "per_page": 10,
  "_links": {
    "self":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=2&per_page=10" },
    "next":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=3&per_page=10" },
    "prev":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=1&per_page=10" },
    "first": { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=1&per_page=10" },
    "last":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=3&per_page=10" }
  }
}

An item’s _links.self is present only if the caller may GET that row, and _links.collection only if the caller may list the collection: a caller who may list but not read a row gets the row without self, so following a link as the same caller always answers 2xx (0.13.0). Under a projection prefix every link carries it: a page served at /admin/films links to /admin/films?page=…, and its items to /admin/films/{id}. A served row has no restore link (a served row is live).

On boundary pages, next or prev serialize as JSON null (never omitted). On total == 0, last_page == 1 and first == last == self.

Every link repeats the request’s filter[...] and sort (percent-encoded), so following next stays on the same list. A cursor list in HAL also carries next_cursor, the cursor of _links.next.

Links in a route of your own

The link builders are not public in 0.9.0: they know neither the base path, the version prefix nor the configured origin that Foundry applies. A route of your own that returns a resource with links writes the _links object itself — see custom-handlers.md.
