Pagination

0.7.5 Enameling — collection-read parameters widened. The new filter[<field>], sort, and cursor parameters layer on top of page / per_page without changing the existing extractor surface — see pagination.md for the consumer-facing guide (the load-bearing surface for filtering, sorting, and cursor pagination). The handler dispatches on the model’s #[ferra(pagination = …)] posture; the page-mode parameters below continue to work unchanged.

The page-mode parameters are read by the generated routes; the extractor is internal since 0.9.0. A missing page is 1 (and 0 is read as 1), a missing per_page is 20, and per_page is clamped to 1–100, silently: no Warning header (RFC 9111 §5.5 obsoletes it; the body says what applied).

  • Default: page=1, per_page=20.
  • Cap: per_page ≤ 100 (hard limit). Values below 1 or above 100 are clamped, with no Warning header (RFC 9111 §5.5 obsoletes it; before 0.12.0 the response carried Warning: 214).
  • The response body’s per_page field reports the clamped value, so a client detects a clamp by comparing it with what it asked.
  • A page or per_page that is not a non-negative integer (page=abc) is a 400 with the code invalid_parameter; it is not read as the default.

Worked curl:

$ curl -D - 'http://localhost:3000/films?per_page=500'
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: no-store
content-type: application/hal+json
vary: Accept
vary: Authorization, Cookie
...
{"items":[...],"total":523,"page":1,"per_page":100,"_links":{...}}

Links and Location

Hypermedia links (_links, HAL-inspired) and the Location header are relative by default: /films/42, or /api/films/42 under a FerraLayer base_path. Resolve them against the URL you called, as an HTTP client does for Location. The request’s Host, X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto headers are never read: a client cannot make the API emit links to another origin.

Location on a 201 is the self link of the new row (the same href a HAL read gives it), under a projection prefix as on the bare path. It is present only if self is: a caller who may create but not GET the row gets 201 Created with no body and no Location, with or without Prefer: return=minimal, so no id, stamp or author reaches a caller who may not read them (0.13.0).

A row also links to each parent the caller may read, named after the relation, and leaves the foreign key and the link out for a parent the caller may not read: see Links and foreign keys.

It links to each sub-collection too ("reviews": {"href": "/films/42/reviews"}, the bare {item}/{relation}), when the child is mounted and the caller may list it.

To emit absolute links, configure the public origin once:

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?
    .with_base_url("https://api.example.com")? // Result<_, BaseUrlError>
    .mount::<Film>()
    .build();
// Location: https://api.example.com/films/42
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

The value must be an http or https origin — scheme, host and optional port; a trailing / is dropped — with no path, query, fragment, userinfo (https://user:password@host) or whitespace; otherwise BaseUrlError::NotHttp, NoHost or NotAnOrigin. A path prefix is not part of the origin: declare it with FerraLayer::base_path (for instance behind a proxy that serves the API under /api).

On a versioned chain (.api_version("v1")), links carry the version prefix the routes are served under, relative or absolute: /v1/films/42, or https://api.example.com/v1/films/42 with an origin. The order is origin, then base_path, then the version prefix.

Resource<M> — a model’s rows from a route of your own

A route of your own reaches a model’s rows through Resource<M>, an axum extractor. Foundry::mount_and_handle::<M>() mounts the model and issues a ResourceHandle<M> (Foundry); the handle goes in the router state — .with_state(handle), or a field of an application state that derives axum::extract::FromRef — and the handler takes Resource<M>.

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
use axum::{Json, Router, extract::Path, routing::get};
use ferra::model::FerraViews;
use ferra::{FerraError, Foundry, Resource};

async fn one(films: Resource<Film>, Path(id): Path<i32>)
    -> Result<Json<<Film as FerraViews>::Read>, FerraError>
{
    Ok(Json(films.get(id).await?))
}

fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let (foundry, films) = Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?.mount_and_handle::<Film>();
let app: Router = foundry
    .build()
    .merge(Router::new().route("/films/{id}/mine", get(one)).with_state(films));
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}
MethodDoes whatTakesReturns
getGET /{resource}/{id}the key<M as FerraViews>::Read
listGET /{resource}, page modea CollectionQueryPage<Read>
list_cursorGET /{resource}, cursor modea CursorQueryCursorPage<Read>
createPOST /{resource}<M as FerraViews>::WriteRead
updatePUT /{resource}/{id} for the fields it setsthe key, <M as FerraViews>::PatchRead
deleteDELETE /{resource}/{id}, soft on a soft-delete modelthe key()

All of them answer with a FerraError, so the refusals are those of the generated routes.

Who the caller is, and the order of refusals

The caller is bound when Resource<M> is extracted: the identity the JWT layer verified, if the request went through it; else the bearer token of the Authorization header, verified with the chain’s own JWT configuration; else nobody.

  1. A token that is present and invalid — an Authorization header that is not a well-formed Bearer credential included — is refused at extraction with the 401 the JWT layer gives, before any database statement.
  2. On a chain without .with_auth() no token is read, and the caller is anonymous: a rule that needs an identity answers 401.
  3. Your route’s own extractors (FerraPath, FerraJson) run before you call a method, so a malformed path or body can be answered 400 before the access answers 401 or 403. What the access then refuses — 401, 403, 404, 422 — is what the generated route refuses, because it is the same code: another caller’s row under IsOwner is a 404, indistinguishable from a missing row.

What it hands back

get and list return the model’s read view, <M as FerraViews>::Read (create and update return an Option of it, below): the {Model}ReadProjection struct #[derive(FerraModel)] generates (or the projection promoted with default = true). A #[ferra(write_only)] or #[ferra(skip)] field is not a member of that type, so a route that serializes it cannot leak it. update takes <M as FerraViews>::Patch, the generated {Model}Patch: one Option<T> per field of the write projection, None meaning “leave the column” (and Option<Option<T>> for a nullable column, Some(None) writing null). Only the set columns reach the UPDATE; a write-only column is writable and never read back.

create and update return Result<Option<Read>, FerraError>. Some is the row they wrote with the field read rules applied. None means the row is written and the caller may not read it under the generated route’s rule (the get rule on the row, then the can(Get) of the model’s #[ferra(authority)]; an authority that panics or fails counts as “may not read”, with one error! on ferra_http::policy, and panic = "abort" defeats that catch): the route sends such a caller no body, and a handler of yours should send none either, with no Location and no id. The authority’s filter is not consulted, as for the body of the generated write: keep filter equal to can(Get). None comes only after a successful write: a refusal, a validation error or a row the caller cannot reach for update is an Err, the absent row’s 404 included. A caller allowed to update but not to read tells None from that 404, so it learns the row exists, as it does from the route’s bodiless 204. The same holds for tx.resource::<N>() inside a hook, mounted or not. Computed fields are computed only for a caller who may read the row (see Computed fields); for one who may not, nothing is computed.

Limits, by design:

  • The access serves the bare route’s projections. Selecting a named projection comes with per-projection authorization, later.
  • restore is not offered.
  • A write through Resource<M> evaluates no If-Match or If-None-Match in 0.14.0, and a route of your own cannot compute the entity tag of the row; see Preconditions on a write.
  • The read view carries the model’s Rust field names; #[ferra(rename_all = "camelCase")] is applied by the generated routes when they serialize, not by the struct. A route of your own answers with a struct of its own.
  • A filter you put in a CollectionQuery or a CursorQuery is held to the route’s safelist: only #[field(filterable)] fields, by their Rust names, with a value of the field’s type. Under IsOwner the list holds the caller’s rows whatever filter you pass.

A handler that extracts Resource<M> from a state that carries no handle for M does not compile; see FRG-152 in the diagnostics.

Custom extractors

See custom-handlers.md — the rationale for FerraJson<T> / FerraPath<T> (RFC 7807 error continuity), the FromRequest vs FromRequestParts ordering rule, the Send + Sync + 'static cheat-sheet, and a worked end-to-end POST /films/{id}/publish custom handler. A declared action is in Declared actions.

Security defaults

Every route Foundry mounts carries a deny-by-default Tower layer stack:

LayerDefaultOverride path
tower_http::cors::CorsLayer::new()Deny all cross-origin; with JwtConfig::with_cookie, the listed origins only, with credentials, exposing ETag and Location (see CORS with the cookie)FerraLayer::cors(...), refused with the cookie
413 body-limit mapperRewrites stock text/plain → application/problem+json with type: .../payload_too_large— (permanent)
tower_http::limit::RequestBodyLimitLayer1 MiBFerraLayer::body_limit(...)
Trace slotEmpty: it adds nothing. A request has one span (request) and one INFO/WARN/ERROR event (target ferra_http::request: method, route, status, ferra.error.type, latency in ms), both written by the observation layer, outside everything below; the span records the kind of credential Ferra verified (credential = token, cookie or api_key) and url.path without the query. Never headers, bodies, a token, a key or its prefix.FerraLayer::trace_layer (your own TraceLayer, beside them)
tower_governor::GovernorLayer on mutation endpoints2 mutations per second, burst 5 (RateLimitRule::new(2, 5)) + peer-socket-IP keyFerraLayer::rate_limit(RateLimitRule::new(per_second, burst))
Cache default (outermost layer of build() but the observation layer, which adds no header)Cache-Control: no-store when the response has none; Vary merged with Accept, Authorization, Cookiea route’s own Cache-Control, see Caching
per_page clamp (FR-017)Clamped to [1, 100]; the body’s per_page is the applied value (no Warning header since 0.12.0)— (constitutional)

429 wire format — the framework’s default rate-limit component’s 429 responses are rewritten to application/problem+json with type: https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited, with a Retry-After of at least 1 second. See the worked body in §“RFC 7807 error taxonomy” above. Oversized bodies produce the same application/problem+json shape — a client parsing type never sees a mixed wire format.

FerraLayer::new().no_rate_limit().build() removes mutation throttling and its mapper; no ConnectInfo is needed. Otherwise the default peer-IP key requires into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>(); a missing peer answers 500. Foundry::rate_limit_key selects trusted-proxy or custom keying before mounting (see foundry.md § Rate-limit override). On Lambda quotas are per execution environment: use no_rate_limit with API Gateway throttling (the example uses burst 20, rate 10 requests/second).

Rate-limit observability event. Each time the rate-limit mapper rewrites a 429, it emits a single structured tracing::warn! event so an operator tailing logs can see rate-limit rejections without reading the framework source:

  • Target: ferra_http::rate_limit — namespaced so an operator can isolate it via EnvFilter (RUST_LOG=ferra_http::rate_limit=warn).
  • Message: rate limit exceeded.
  • Severity: WARN.
  • Fields (deliberately minimal):
    • http.method — the request HTTP method (e.g. "POST"). Always present.
    • http.target — the request path, never the query string (e.g. "/films" for POST /films?page=2; ADR-0076). Always present.
    • http.retry_after_seconds — integer seconds parsed from the inbound Retry-After header. Present only when the header parses as a non-negative integer; genuinely absent otherwise (not recorded as 0).

Request and response body content never appear in this event — only the three fields listed above. The schema is pinned minimal so the framework’s dedicated observability phase at 0.12.0 Sheen can absorb it into span-based telemetry (adding trace_id, span_id, and peer-IP once the trusted-proxy story lands) without breaking a consumer’s existing EnvFilter or custom tracing::Layer.

Wire up a subscriber in your host binary’s main to surface these events:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
tracing_subscriber::fmt()
    .with_env_filter("ferra_http::rate_limit=warn")
    .init();
}

Layer placement (FR-006). The rate-limit mapper mounts as the outer layer of the mutation sub-router only, wrapping tower_governor::GovernorLayer from the outside (the last .layer() call on that sub-router). Consumer-added middleware appended to Foundry::…build() wraps the mapper from further outside — see §“Layer ordering — how .layer() composes” below for the full diagram.

Overriding the defaults. Every default in the table above is overridable via the FerraLayer builder applied to a Foundry chain — body cap, CORS, mutation rate-limit rule, tracing layer, and a base_path prefix on hypermedia links. The override surface is documented in foundry.md § “Transport-layer overrides” with the full worked example and the REPLACE-not-merge rule for per-model overrides.

CORS with the cookie

When the JwtConfig has with_cookie(name, origins) (ferra-auth.md § Cookie), each model’s CORS layer is built from that origin list instead of the deny-all default: a listed origin gets its exact Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, any other origin gets no Access-Control-Allow-* header, and a preflight needs no credential. The same list is the CSRF guard of a write the cookie authenticates. CORS wraps the authentication layer, so what that layer answers (the 401 of an expired cookie, the 400 of two credentials, the 403 of the CSRF guard) carries the CORS headers too: a listed app can read it and tell that its session expired.

Do not set FerraLayer::cors(...) with the cookie. build() panics: “a custom CORS layer cannot be combined with the cookie credential: remove FerraLayer::cors; the origins given to JwtConfig::with_cookie drive CORS”. Two policies would leave one silently ignored, and a custom layer with allow_credentials(true) answers every origin. A chain without the cookie keeps FerraLayer::cors as it was.

What the cookie CORS layer exposes (0.14.0). A browser script reads only the response headers a CORS answer exposes, so the layer lists ETag and Location in Access-Control-Expose-Headers for a listed origin: the app reads the tag of a row to send it back in If-Match, and the URL of a created row. It allows If-Match and If-None-Match among the request headers of a preflight, next to Content-Type, Accept and Prefer. A foreign origin gets no Access-Control-Expose-Headers, as it gets no Access-Control-Allow-* (tower-http adds the exposed headers to every answer whatever the origin; Ferra strips them from the answers it does not allow).

Your own FerraLayer::cors(...) (a chain without the cookie) does its own exposure: Ferra adds nothing to it. List the origins, the request headers a write may carry and the response headers the app reads, and never use CorsLayer::permissive(), which allows every origin and every header:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraLayer;
use tower_http::cors::{AllowHeaders, AllowMethods, AllowOrigin, CorsLayer};
use axum::http::{
    Method,
    header::{ACCEPT, CONTENT_TYPE, ETAG, IF_MATCH, IF_NONE_MATCH, LOCATION},
};

let cors = CorsLayer::new()
    .allow_origin(AllowOrigin::list(["https://app.example.com".parse().unwrap()]))
    .allow_methods(AllowMethods::list([
        Method::GET,
        Method::POST,
        Method::PUT,
        Method::PATCH,
        Method::DELETE,
    ]))
    .allow_headers(AllowHeaders::list([
        CONTENT_TYPE,
        ACCEPT,
        IF_MATCH,
        IF_NONE_MATCH,
    ]))
    .expose_headers([ETAG, LOCATION]);
let layer = FerraLayer::new().cors(cors).build();
let _ = layer;
}

Layer ordering — how .layer() composes

Tower’s .layer() wraps the current router as the inner service, so the last .layer() call becomes the outermost layer. A .layer(MyCustomLayer::new()) appended to Foundry::…build() therefore wraps every Ferra-provided layer from the outside.

The stack Foundry::…build() returns, from the outermost layer (a request enters here) to the handler. Rows 1 to 5 wrap the whole application once; rows 6 to 15 are built for each mounted model:

#LayerWhat it does
1Observation layerRecords the request (span, request line, metrics under observability); adds and changes no header. See observability.md
2Cache defaultsCache-Control and Vary on every response
3Request budgetThe 503 timeout, when a budget is set
4ETag layer, and the extensionsThe ETag key, the base URL, the default representation and the mounted models, which the handlers read
5Version prefix (with .api_version)The VersionPrefix extension and, with .deprecated, the middleware that adds Sunset/Deprecation and the post-sunset warn and counter
6Base pathThe FerraLayer::base_path prefix of hypermedia links
7Cookie origin checkOnly with JwtConfig::with_cookie (see CORS with the cookie)
8CORSFerraLayer::cors, or the cookie origins
9JWT / API key authenticationAlso the ApiKeyHeader extension (innermost on the chain), which tells the handlers which header carries API keys
10body_limit_mapperRewrites the 413 to application/problem+json
11RequestBodyLimitLayer1 MiB by default
12Trace slotEmpty: it holds a layer only if you passed trace_layer
13DefaultBodyLimit::disable
14rate_limit_mapper (mutations only)Rewrites the 429 to application/problem+json
15GovernorLayer (mutations only)The rate limit
16Handler

A request enters at row 1 and traverses down to the handler; the response retraces the stack back out. In the source, the call order is inverted: the first .layer() call is the innermost layer, and the last .layer() call is the outermost.

Mutation sub-router subtlety. GovernorLayer (rate-limit) and rate_limit_mapper (the 429 RFC 7807 wrapper) mount on the mutation sub-router only — never on the merged router and never on read routes. rate_limit_mapper is the last .layer() call on that sub-router, so it wraps GovernorLayer from the outside and sees the 429s that layer produces. Placing a layer of your own that watches requests is a decision about which sub-router you wrap — consumers who want to watch only mutations attach to a sub-router; consumers who want to watch everything attach to the merged router returned by Foundry::…build().

Worked consumer example. A consumer appending two custom layers on top of the framework stack:

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
use axum::{extract::Request, middleware::{from_fn, Next}, response::Response};
async fn audit(request: Request, next: Next) -> Response { next.run(request).await }
async fn shed_load(request: Request, next: Next) -> Response { next.run(request).await }
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app = Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?.mount::<Film>().build()
    .layer(from_fn(audit))        // outer: sees requests before the framework
    .layer(from_fn(shed_load));   // appended AFTER → now the TRUE outermost
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

On incoming requests: shed_load runs first, then audit, then the framework stack (the table above, from the observation layer to the handler). Ferra’s observation layer does not see what the two layers you appended answer: a 503 from shed_load is not in the metrics, the request line or a span. On the way back out, responses traverse the stack in reverse.

See also §“RFC 7807 error taxonomy” for the 429 wire body the rate_limit_mapper produces.

Caching

Every response a Foundry router gives, errors included, carries Cache-Control: no-store and a Vary that names Accept, Authorization and Cookie (and the configured API key header when API keys are configured). This covers the generated routes, your .route(...) routes, /docs, a 404 or 405 before any route, the 503 of the request budget, the 413, the 429 and a CORS preflight answer. A shared cache (CDN, API gateway, proxy) therefore stores nothing and cannot replay an authenticated answer to another caller (RFC 9111 §3.5 protects Authorization only, and a 200 or 404 is cacheable with no header at all, §4.2.2).

  • Cache-Control is inserted only when the response has none: a route that sets its own Cache-Control, whatever its directives, keeps it.
  • Vary is merged, never replaced: the names the route already sent stay, the missing ones among the three are added, case-insensitively. A Vary: * is left as it is. A route that opts into caching still carries Vary: Authorization, Cookie: the entries are keyed on them (over-keying is safe).

A public route that may be cached. Declare it with .route(...) and give its MethodRouter a layer that sets Cache-Control; the default only inserts when the header is absent, so this route alone keeps its directive:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use axum::{http::{HeaderValue, header}, response::Response, routing::get};
use ferra::Foundry;

fn configure(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
    let cacheable = get(|| async { "a public page" }).layer(
        axum::middleware::map_response(|mut response: Response| async move {
            response.headers_mut().insert(
                header::CACHE_CONTROL,
                HeaderValue::from_static("public, max-age=60"),
            );
            response
        }),
    );
    let _router = Foundry::new(conn).route("/public", cacheable).build();
}
}

tower_http::set_header::SetResponseHeaderLayer::overriding does the same; it needs the set-header feature of tower-http, which Ferra does not enable, so your application declares it. A generated model route has no such knob before 1.0.

Warning. Do not add a layer that overwrites Cache-Control to the Router that build() returns: it wraps Ferra’s default and replaces no-store on every route, authenticated ones included. Ferra cannot see it and does not refuse it. FoundryBuilder::layer takes a FerraLayer, which cannot set Cache-Control: its knobs are CORS, body limit, rate limit, trace and base path, and trace_layer takes a TraceLayer, which does not set response headers. Only a layer added to the Router after build() can override no-store.

Responses that depend on the caller

A response whose content depends on who asks carries no-store and the full Vary above. Tests prove it on each such surface: a field only some roles read, a list scoped to the caller’s own rows, a list narrowed by an authority and GET /me. No generated response carries public or s-maxage, whatever the model, the operation or the identity.

What the guarantee does not cover is yours: the responses of your .route(...) handlers, which keep any Cache-Control they set, and a layer you add after build(). A public or s-maxage there lets a shared cache replay a caller’s answer to another (OWASP API8, security misconfiguration).

Entity tags are not cache validators here

Every response that serves one row carries a strong ETag (see Entity tags and preconditions), and a row response is still no-store: a GET with If-None-Match is not answered 304 Not Modified, whatever the tag. The tag serves writes, not caches.

Entity tags and preconditions

A caller that reads a row and later rewrites it needs a way to say “only if nobody changed it meanwhile”. The ETag response header is the read half of it: an opaque version of one row, issued by the server and given back by the client.

The tag

GET /films/1 HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "k3Qm0u8bW1xHn7c9sFqYtA2R5eJvZ_dLw4iUoPgXaBE"
  • Opaque and strong. The value is a quoted base64url text, never W/. Compare it as a whole and send it back as it came; do not parse it, it has no structure a client may rely on and its length may change.
  • One tag per row. The same row gives the same tag on every projection URL (/films/1, /summary/films/1, a version prefix) and on GET /me; the tag changes when the stored row changes. The key of a composite-key row is part of it, so two rows never share a tag.
  • Where it is sent. On every response that serves one row: GET of an item (every projection, /me), 201 Created (with Location), PUT, PATCH, POST /{resource}/{id}/restore, and the 204 of a write under Prefer: return=minimal. The DELETE of a soft-delete model answers its 204 with the tag of the row as deleted, so that a restore has a current tag to send.
  • Where it is not. On a collection or any row inside one, on the DELETE of a model without soft delete (the row is gone), and on any refusal (401, 403, 404, 422, …).
  • It follows Location. A response that withholds the body and Location from a caller who may write a row but not GET it (a 201 with no body, the 204 of a write-only authority, the DELETE of a row the caller may not read) withholds the tag too: a tag is a statement about a row the caller may read.
  • Never cached, never a 304. A GET carrying If-None-Match is not answered 304 Not Modified: row responses are no-store (see Caching) and the tag serves writes.
  • It follows the row only. The tag is computed from the row’s table, key and version (xmin). A response that embeds a parent carries the child’s tag, so the parent can change while the tag stays the same. Ferra never answers 304, so it serves nothing stale from it. A cache in front of Ferra that stores the response despite no-store and revalidates on the ETag can keep a stale embed: do not give such a cache a route whose projection embeds.

What the tag reveals, and does not

The tag is keyed by the server’s entity-tag key, which also covers rotation, restores and the other operational cases. Without the key nobody can compute a tag, test a guess about a field they may not read, nor tell that two rows were written in the same transaction.

The residual signal. Any stored change of the row changes its tag, hidden fields included. A caller who cannot read a field therefore learns that something changed when its tag moves, one bit per observation, never the value. This is accepted: it is the price of one tag per row whatever the projection.

Preconditions on a write

PUT, PATCH, DELETE, POST /{resource}/{id}/restore and a declared row action (POST /{resource}/{id}/{name}, Declared actions) accept If-Match and If-None-Match. A client that read a row and sends its tag back says “only if nobody changed it meanwhile”:

PUT /films/1 HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "k3Qm0u8bW1xHn7c9sFqYtA2R5eJvZ_dLw4iUoPgXaBE"
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Aliens"}

HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/problem+json
  • If-Match is optional. A write without it goes through as it always did: there is no 428 Precondition Required, and no setting that asks for one. A create (POST /{resource}) ignores both headers.
  • The tag must be current. If-Match passes when * is sent or when one of the listed tags is the row’s current tag. The comparison is strong: a W/ tag never matches. Ferra only issues strong tags, but an intermediary can weaken them; send the tag as the server issued it.
  • If-None-Match is the reverse. The write is refused when * is sent, or when a listed tag is the row’s current tag. Here the comparison is weak, as RFC 9110 §13.1.2 defines it: the W/ prefix is ignored and the opaque-tag decides, so If-None-Match: W/"<current>" is refused too. It is evaluated after If-Match.
  • Lists. Several header lines are one list (RFC 9110 §5.3), so a row’s tag may sit on any of them. A list holds at most 32 entries. A value that is no list of entity-tags (a missing quote, a bare word), an empty list, * beside a tag, or a list of 33 tags is a 412 for both headers: it is never ignored, and never read as “no match”, so a mangled If-None-Match cannot let a write through.
  • If-Unmodified-Since is ignored. The tag is the only validator a write reads; a date has a one-second resolution and a row can change twice within it.
  • The decision is the locked row’s. It is taken inside the write’s transaction, after the row is locked, so two writers that hold the same tag cannot both win: the second one gets the 412, its write is not applied, and the first writer’s change stays. A 412 is also decided before the early return of an empty patch: {} with a stale If-Match, or with If-None-Match: *, is a 412, not a no-op 200.
  • The order. A precondition never tells a caller anything about a row they may not see: the row is looked up first, and a row that is absent, soft-deleted or hidden from the caller is a 404 whatever the headers, * included. For a row the caller may write, the 412 comes after the 415 and before everything the body can provoke (400, 422 unknown_field, the 403 of a field rule, the 422 on values): a stale If-Match with a forbidden field in the body is a 412, with a wrong Content-Type a 415. The full order is in What a patch is refused with.
  • The 412 says nothing. Its detail is one fixed text. It does not repeat the header, does not carry the current tag, and the response has no ETag. The client GETs the row again, redoes its change on what it reads, and writes with the new tag.
  • restore compares against the row’s tag. The DELETE of a soft-delete model answers the tag of the row as deleted, and that is the tag restore expects: the tag from before the delete is stale and gets a 412, and If-Match: * passes.
DELETE /films/1 HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "<tag read before>"

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
ETag: "<tag of the row as deleted>"

POST /films/1/restore HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "<tag of the row as deleted>"

Known limitation: a route of your own. A write route you write by hand on Resource<M> evaluates no precondition in 0.14.0, and returns no tag. An If-Match sent to such a route is ignored and its write is unconditional; the response you build carries no ETag. If clients of that write need to avoid lost updates, route them through the generated PUT or PATCH. A typed precondition on Resource<M> can be added later without breaking the API.

PUT and RFC 9110 §9.3.4: a deliberate deviation

RFC 9110 §9.3.4 forbids a validator on a successful PUT response unless the stored representation is byte-identical to the content the client sent, so that the client knows whether the copy it sent is the result. Ferra’s PUT never stores the content as received (an absent optional field is cleared, the stamps and the key are the server’s), so the letter of §9.3.4 forbids the tag, and Ferra sends it anyway: the tag of a successful PUT names the stored row, never the sent content. The 200 response carries that row, and it is the row to keep. A client must not cache its PUT body under that tag; a client that chose Prefer: return=minimal holds no representation of the stored row at all, and caches nothing under the tag. This is what OData 4.01 §11.4.3 requires and the Azure REST API Guidelines prescribe (ADR-0077 § Consequences).

Transient conflicts are retried

Two writes that touch the same rows can make PostgreSQL abort one of them: SQLSTATE 40P01 (deadlock detected), and 40001 (serialization failure). The request is valid, so since 0.14.0 Ferra runs the write again instead of answering a 500. Every write Ferra opens runs at READ COMMITTED whatever the server’s default says (since 0.16.0), so the isolation level itself no longer produces a 40001.

  • What is rerun. The whole operation, decided again on the new state of the database, hooks included (Hooks can run more than once).
  • Only two codes. 40001 and 40P01, a failure at COMMIT included. Nothing else is: a failed precondition stays the 412 of the first attempt, a unique violation (23505) stays a 409, and an error a hook chose stays what it chose.
  • Only an operation that owns its transaction. The generated routes and the writes of Resource<M>. A tx.resource call inside a hook borrows the transaction of the write: its abort goes up to the loop of the write, which reruns everything.
  • The constants. 3 attempts (one plus two retries). Before retry k the wait is uniform in [0, min(100 ms, 10 ms × 2^(k−1))]: at most 10 ms before the first retry and 20 ms before the second, so at most 30 ms are added. These are constants of the crate, not settings.
  • Exhaustion. A write aborted on all three attempts answers 503 https://ferra.rs/errors/retry_exhausted with Retry-After: 1 (whole seconds). That write was not applied, so the client may retry it; the detail is one fixed text that speaks for that write and names no SQLSTATE, table or constraint. An aborted attempt logs one line with its number and its SQLSTATE, never a value. A Resource<M> write returns it as Err(FerraError::RetryExhausted) (0.16.0; before, an Internal over a private cause): return it to answer the 503, and never replay the write in a loop of your own, since the three attempts already ran. A hook’s tx.resource write reaches the caller as the same variant, through the outer write.
  • The request budget. With .request_budget(..) the deadline bounds every attempt as it bounds the first: no attempt starts once it has passed, no wait ends past it, and a COMMIT the database refused with 40001 or 40P01 committed nothing, so it is not a started commit. Each of these answers 503 timeout, without Retry-After, with nothing written. Without a budget only the three attempts bound the work.
  • A route of your own. Only the operation is rerun. In a handler that calls Resource::update, the code around the call (your extractors, what you did before it, what you do after it) runs once, however many attempts the write takes; two calls are two operations, each with its own attempts. Keep the effect of a handler after the call, or in after_commit (see Hooks can run more than once). A write that was given up after an earlier Resource<M> write of the same handler is Err(FerraError::RetryExhausted), answered retry_exhausted while that earlier write stands: the detail speaks for the write that failed, not for the request; do not retry a non-idempotent request blindly (RFC 9110 § 9.2.2).
  • The cost. A request under conflict does up to three times its work.

Write bodies reject unknown fields

Both write paths now refuse a request body carrying a field the model does not declare, with HTTP 422 and an application/problem+json body naming every offending field.

Since 0.8.0 (a break from 0.7). Through 0.7.x the two paths disagreed: projection-routed writes were already strict, while bare-path (POST /films, PUT /films/{id}) writes silently dropped unknown fields and returned 201 / 200. The same model therefore enforced two different postures depending on which URL a consumer addressed. That divergence is closed; the bare path is now strict too.

Why strict. The model’s field set is the safelist. A typed model surface that silently discards consumer-supplied fields is the silent-tolerance shape adjacent to mass assignment — a client sends {"role": "admin"}, receives 200, and has no signal that the field went nowhere. The industry is genuinely split here (Stripe and OWASP allowlisting on one side, Postel’s-law tolerant-reader on the other); Ferra picks strict as a deliberate security-over-convenience arbitration, not as a claim of consensus.

Migrating. Request bodies must match the model’s declared field set.

  • Remove fields your model does not declare. If a client was sending them and relying on the drop, that reliance was silent and is now visible — which is the point.
  • A field you want accepted must exist on the model, or on the projection’s write = [...] set for a projection-routed write.
  • Every offending field is reported in one response; the framework does not stop at the first.
  • Since 0.9.0 the bare path reads the model’s default write projection, which leaves out the primary key, the owner, read-only, skipped and computed fields, and the behavior columns: a body carrying any of them is a 422 too (see Projections and routing § Writes).

The OpenAPI document says so. It carries additionalProperties: false on every write-body schema, so generated clients and API-discovering agents see the same strictness the server enforces.

Partial updates with PATCH

PUT replaces a row; PATCH changes the fields it names and leaves the others as they are. The body is a JSON merge patch (RFC 7396): a JSON object, sent as application/merge-patch+json.

PATCH /films/1 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json

{"title": "Aliens", "year": null}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "k3Qm0u8bW1xHn7c9sFqYtA2R5eJvZ_dLw4iUoPgXaBE"

See The routes a model gets for where PATCH is served.

What a patch means

In the patchEffect
a key with a valuethe field is set to it, under the rules PUT applies to that value
a key with nulla nullable field is cleared; a field that cannot be null is the 422 required
a key that is absentthe field is untouched, whatever it is
{}nothing is written; the answer is the row (a stale precondition is a 412)

PUT is a replacement and answers the same body differently: it writes every write field, so an optional field without a read or write rule that the body leaves out becomes NULL, a field with such a rule is kept, and a #[field(required)] field that is missing is the 422 required. A client that wants to change one field sends a PATCH; one that sends a PUT sends the whole row.

  • Only the fields the patch sets are judged. Each value gets what PUT gives it (its type, the #[field(...)] rules, the write rule of the field, the JSON bounds), so a PATCH never stores a value a PUT refuses. A field the patch does not set is neither typed, nor judged, nor named in an error: a row stored before a rule was tightened, or before a JSON bound was lowered, can still be patched elsewhere, and the stored value stays as it was, byte for byte.
  • A JSON field is merged. When the stored value and the patch value are both objects, the patch is merged into the stored one member by member, and a null member removes its key. Stored {"a": 1, "b": 2} patched with {"a": 3} is {"a": 3, "b": 2}; patched with {"a": 3, "b": null} it is {"a": 3}. Any other patch value (an array, a scalar, null) replaces the field or clears it, and an object patched onto a stored value that is not an object is merged into {}. The max_bytes and max_depth bounds apply to the merged document.
  • The key, the owner and the parent key are not patchable. A patch that names the primary key, the owner column, the foreign key of an owner(from) model (0.16.0: it is immutable) or any key outside the write set is a 422 unknown_field, nothing written, as for PUT; so is a key the caller may not read, so that the answer does not tell a field that exists from one that does not.

What a patch is refused with

AnswerWhen
415 unsupported_media_typethe Content-Type is not application/merge-patch+json, application/json included; the detail names the type to send
400 validation, code invalid_jsonthe body is not a JSON object, a key is repeated in it at any depth (a JSON field included: a key is repeated at line L column C), or a value is of the wrong type for a field the caller may read
404 not_foundthe row does not exist, is soft-deleted, or is one the caller may not see: the same answer, byte for byte. It comes before the 415, 400 and 422 of the body when a rule, an authority, an owner field or a precondition header reads the row; see the order below
403 forbiddena key the caller may read but not write (a write rule of the field)
422 validation_failedunknown_field (above); required for a null on a field that cannot be null; a #[field(...)] rule of a value the patch sets (min_length, max, pattern…); json_too_large or json_too_deep for the merged document

Every errors[] entry names its field and its code (Validation codes). A refused PATCH writes nothing, computes no field and runs no hook.

The refusals come in the order every row write follows (PUT, PATCH, DELETE, restore): 401, 403 for a rule that reads no row, 404, 403 for the row-dependent part of the rule, 415, 412 (the If-Match and If-None-Match preconditions, see Entity tags and preconditions), 413, 400 (the body is decoded once: a repeated key, a wrong type on a key the caller may read), 422 unknown_field, 403 for a field write rule, then 422 on the values, and last the 400 of a required key the body omits. A caller who is not allowed to touch a row therefore learns nothing from the body it sent, and a key the caller may not read is never judged by the 400: it is an unknown key. An unknown key next to a wrong-typed value on a readable key is the 400. A PATCH types the keys it sets after the merge, on the locked row: where nothing reads the row before the body (no rule, authority, owner field or precondition header does), its unknown and unwritable keys are still judged first, before the 404, so there an unknown key beside a wrong-typed value is the 422.

That order holds whenever something reads the row before the body is judged: a rule of the model, a projection, an authority or an owner field, or an If-Match or If-None-Match header; for a model nothing reads the row of, see Update-vs-create symmetry.

Prefer and the ETag

PATCH honours Prefer as PUT does (below): return=minimal answers 204 No Content with no body and Preference-Applied: return=minimal; return=representation, or no Prefer at all, answers 200 OK with the projected row. The 200 and the 204 of a PATCH carry the ETag of the stored row, which is not the tag the row had before the write (a caller who may not GET the row gets a 204 with no body and no tag, as for PUT).

From Rust

Resource::update with a {Model}Patch does what PATCH does, with the same merge and the same refusals; in the patch, None is an absent key and Some(None) is a null. See Custom handlers and ferra-forge.md § Generated items.

Content negotiation — RFC 7240 Prefer: header

Every mutation endpoint (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) recognises the RFC 7240 Prefer: request header and branches the response shape accordingly. Consumers that do not send the header observe the default shape.

Recognised tokens

Prefer: valueEffectResulting statusResponse body
(header absent)default mutation shapePOST → 201 Created, PUT → 200 OK, PATCH → 200 OK, DELETE → 204full resource body on POST/PUT/PATCH; empty on DELETE
return=minimalomit the response bodyPOST → 204 No Content (Location preserved, for a caller who may GET the new row; one who may not gets 201 with no body and no Location), PUT → 204, PATCH → 204, DELETE → 204 unchangedempty
return=representationexplicit form of the defaultPOST → 201, PUT → 200, PATCH → 200, DELETE → 204 unchangedfull resource body
respond-asyncparse-only — recognised so clients can probe the header without being broken, but has no effect on the response shape. Reserved for a future async-jobs cohort.unchangedunchanged

A caller who may PUT, PATCH or restore a row but not GET it gets 204 No Content with no body whatever it asked, as a create gets its 201 with no body (0.13.0): the write is done, nothing of the row leaves. Preference-Applied: return=minimal is echoed only when return=minimal was asked, never return=representation. A hand-written route on Resource::update serves what it chooses.

The parser is case-insensitive, whitespace-tolerant, and silently drops unrecognised tokens and ;-delimited parameters per RFC 7240 §2 (“recipients SHOULD ignore preferences they do not understand”):

Prefer: Return=Minimal, respond-async; wait=10

…parses as return=minimal + respond-async (the ; wait=10 parameter is dropped).

Preference-Applied: response header

Per RFC 7240 §3, the framework echoes honoured preferences via the Preference-Applied: response header. The header is absent when no preference was honoured — including the no-header case (table row 1) and the unrecognised-token case.

Request Prefer:Response Preference-Applied:
(absent)absent
return=minimalreturn=minimal (also for a caller who may not GET the row: it gets no body whatever it asked, and the echo says only what it asked)
return=representationreturn=representation (echoed even though the body is unchanged — the standard binds the echo to “preferences that were honoured”, not to “preferences that changed the response”), except for a caller who may not GET the row it just created, updated or restored: it gets no body, so return=representation is not honoured and not echoed (0.13.0)
respond-asyncabsent (parse-only — no observable change)
return=minimal, respond-asyncreturn=minimal (only the honoured preference is echoed)
handling=lenient (unrecognised)absent

Interaction with the 422 validation path

When a mutation request fails declarative validation (the application/problem+json 422 path), the Prefer: header is recognised but does not change the response. The 422 body is mandated by the framework’s closed-namespace contract; Preference-Applied: is not emitted on the 422 path (no preference was honoured that changed observable behaviour).

Worked example

# Default — full body returned.
curl -i -X POST https://api.example.com/films \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title": "Inception", "director": "Christopher Nolan", "year": 2010}'

# HTTP/1.1 201 Created
# Content-Type: application/json
# Location: /films/42
# { "id": 42, "title": "Inception", ... }

# `return=minimal` — body omitted, Location preserved.
curl -i -X POST https://api.example.com/films \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Prefer: return=minimal' \
  -d '{"title": "Inception", "director": "Christopher Nolan", "year": 2010}'

# HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
# Location: /films/43
# Preference-Applied: return=minimal

Batch-processing consumers gain bandwidth and JSON-parse savings on every mutation.

The ferra facade

[dependencies] ferra = { git = "…", tag = "…" } is the entry point (the facade package is ferra; nothing is published on crates.io). Resource, FerraError, FerraJson, FerraPath and Foundry are named from this single dependency, alongside the #[derive(FerraModel)] macro (use ferra::{FerraModel, Foundry};; use ferra::prelude::*; opens them all, for an application that declares no sea-orm of its own). The exact list of what ferra exports is stability.md.

Consumers do not depend on ferra-core, ferra-db, ferra-forge, or ferra-http directly. A compile-fail fixture pins ferra::Statement, ferra::execute_unprepared and ferra::raw_sql as unreachable: the root of the facade has no raw-SQL entry point. ferra::sea_orm is Sea-ORM itself; what Ferra guarantees is about the routes it generates.

Worked end-to-end example

use ferra::{FerraModel, Foundry};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

mod film {
    use super::*;

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")] // deliberately public: this example has no JWT
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        #[sea_orm(unique)]
        pub title: String,
        pub director: String,
        pub year: Option<i32>,
    }

    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

pub use film::Model as Film;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let database_url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?;
    let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(&database_url).await?;
    let app = Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?)?.mount::<Film>().build();
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>()).await?;
    Ok(())
}

See examples/hello-ferra/ for the full three-command boot sequence (docker compose up -d postgres or podman compose up -d postgres → sea-orm-cli migrate up → cargo run -p hello-ferra) and the smoke.sh script that exercises all seven wire-format contracts.

Troubleshooting

413 vs 400 on oversized bodies

A request whose body exceeds the 1 MiB default cap is rejected either with 413 Payload Too Large or with 400 Bad Request, depending on a single precondition: whether the request declares a Content-Length header.

RequestResponse codetype URIResponsible mapper
Body > 1 MiB with Content-Length declared413https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_largebody_limit_mapper (FR-033a)
Body > 1 MiB without Content-Length (streaming / chunked)400https://ferra.rs/errors/validation (single errors[0].code = "invalid_json")FerraJson<T>::from_request surfacing as FerraError::Validation

When Content-Length is present, RequestBodyLimitLayer short-circuits at the layer level before the stream is consumed — hence the early 413. When the header is absent, the stream is consumed up to the cap, the read fails, and the JSON extractor rejects the request as a parse error (still machine-readable, still RFC 7807, still parseable via the same generic type-dispatch path you use for the other validation failures).

Both outcomes are semantically correct — the oversized input is rejected either way. The divergence is intentional; a regression test pins the 400 fallback, so any change to it is visible. If you can set Content-Length on your client, do — your clients then see a single, predictable 413.

Other diagnostics

  • 413 with application/problem+json body — request body exceeds 1 MiB. Split the request or raise the limit via FerraLayer::body_limit(...) (Foundry).
  • 429 with Retry-After — peer IP hit the mutation rate limit (2 per second, burst 5 by default). Back off for the number of seconds in Retry-After.
  • problem+json with type: ".../validation" and errors[0].code = "invalid_path_param" — the path segment after /{resource}/ is not a valid primary key for M (e.g. GET /films/abc when Film.id: i32). The built-in path extractor rejects before the handler runs.
  • 500 with detail: "internal server error" — the DB surfaced an error the framework does not map. Inspect logs / tracing for the Debug form of FerraError::Internal; the HTTP body intentionally says nothing more.
  • CORS preflight fails — CorsLayer::new() denies all cross-origin by default. Open it with FerraLayer::cors(...) (Foundry § Transport-layer overrides).

  1. emitted by a middleware mapper (the 413 body-limit mapper or the 429 rate-limit mapper), not by FerraError::IntoResponse. The wire shape is identical to the handler-produced variants — a client that handles one type URI handles them all through the same generic RFC 7807 code path. ↩ ↩2

Projections and routing

The 0.6.5 Chasing deliverable. A #[derive(FerraModel)] struct can expose multiple distinct read/write shapes — projections — by adding a single attribute. Each named projection auto-mounts under its own URL prefix and surfaces as a distinct path in the OpenAPI document, a distinct call in the generated SDK, and a distinct HAL _links.self.href target.

This page is the authoritative user-guide for projection-driven routing. A reader with only this page plus standard Rust knowledge produces a working projection declaration on the first attempt — no ADR and no framework source is required.

Mental model

A projection is a content variant of a resource — not an access-control mechanism. The same underlying row can be served through several projections, each one a deliberate slice of the row’s fields plus a deliberate stance on which fields a client may submit.

The defining property is that every projection is a distinct callable entity at every layer of the stack: a distinct URL path, a distinct OpenAPI operationId, a distinct generated-SDK method, a distinct HAL self link. A consumer that has the URL has, by construction, also fixed the wire shape — there is no header, no query parameter, and no out-of-band negotiation required.

A response is serialized from the projection’s own read struct ({Model}{Name}ReadProjection), not from the row with some keys removed afterwards: a field the projection does not list is not in that struct, so it cannot be in the response. A write_only field and the deletion column of a soft-delete model are in no read struct, and the dispatcher refuses an object that holds the deletion column’s name (0.13.0).

The links of a row follow the route that served it (0.13.0): a row served under /admin/films links to /admin/films/{id} and /admin/films, a page under that prefix links to its own pages, and no link ever points at another projection. POST /admin/films answers with Location: /admin/films/{id}, the row’s self link; a caller who may create but not read the row gets 201 with no body and no Location. A link is present only if following it, as the same caller, answers 2xx; a served row is live, so it has no restore link.

Authorisation is enforced separately — by middleware on the route or by per-operation guards. A detail projection is not an admin-only projection; it is a more detailed projection that a developer may choose to gate behind an authorisation layer if they wish.

The routing contract

SurfaceURLWire shape
Default read (always emitted)GET /{resource}/{id} and GET /{resource}Every readable field of M
Default write (always emitted)POST /{resource}, PUT /{resource}/{id}, PATCH /{resource}/{id}Every writable field of M (a PATCH names the ones it changes)
Named projection — auto-derived prefixGET /{name}/{resource}/{id} (etc.)Exactly the fields the projection’s read/write lists declare
Named projection — explicit path_prefixGET /{path_prefix}/{resource}/{id} (etc.)As above; the auto-derived /{name}/ is suspended
Default replacement (default = true)GET /{resource}/{id} (the bare path now serves the named projection’s shape)The named projection’s read/write lists

A model that declares zero named projections observes byte-identical 0.5.x / 0.6.0 routing — the bare resource path is unchanged. This is the SC-007 baseline: introducing a named projection on a model is strictly additive to its URL surface, never a silent breaking change.

Field idents must resolve

Each ident of a projection’s read = [...] list is a field of the struct (FRG-301 otherwise, ferra-forge-diagnostics.md), or, on a model written with #[sea_orm::model], the name of one of its BelongsTo relations (0.16.0, FR-040). A relation name is not a field of the projection: it adds the parent’s row to the response, under the relation’s name, in the parent’s projection of the same name, when the caller may read both. read = [id, body, film] on a review embeds its film. The parent’s own rules decide (a parent the caller may not read gives neither embed nor link), and its projection needs its own path_prefix when the two projections share a name. The whole contract, with a compiled example, is Embedding. A HasMany or HasOne is never embedded: it is the link to its sub-collection.

A worked example

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
// Sea-ORM entity scaffolding (the `Relation` enum + `ActiveModelBehavior`
// impl) is required alongside every `DeriveEntityModel` — see
// `examples/hello-ferra/src/main.rs` for the canonical shape.
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
#[derive(
    Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize,
)]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "detail",
    read = [id, title, director, cost_price],
    write = [title, director, cost_price],
))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[sea_orm(unique)]
    pub title: String,
    pub director: String,
    pub cost_price: Option<f64>,
}
}

This declaration auto-mounts two parallel route groups:

VerbBare pathDetail path
Read itemGET /films/{id}GET /detail/films/{id}
Read collectionGET /filmsGET /detail/films
CreatePOST /filmsPOST /detail/films
UpdatePUT /films/{id}PUT /detail/films/{id}
Partial updatePATCH /films/{id}PATCH /detail/films/{id}
DeleteDELETE /films/{id}DELETE /detail/films/{id}

A model marked #[ferra(system_only)] serves the two read rows only, under the bare path and under every prefix: Ferra registers no create, update, delete or restore route for it (see Behaviors).

The bare-path responses carry every readable field of Model (the default-read set). The /detail/... responses are filtered to the projection’s read list — fields not in that list never appear in the response body, ever.

For the OpenAPI document, the paths map gains entries for /films/{id} and /detail/films/{id}, each operation referencing a distinct schema (Film vs FilmDetail). SDK generators driving off the document produce distinct method names per surface (client.films.get(id) vs client.films.getDetail(id)).

Overriding the URL prefix

By default the projection’s name is lower-cased and used as the URL prefix segment. To pin the URL surface to something different — for example, a versioned segment or a developer-friendly synonym — add a path_prefix:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "detail",
    path_prefix = "/v2/detail",
    read = [id, title, director, cost_price],
    write = [title, director, cost_price],
))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    pub director: String,
    pub cost_price: Option<f64>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

This mounts /v2/detail/films/{id} (and parallel verbs). The auto-derived /detail/... URL is NOT also registered — exactly one URL surface exists per projection.

The leading / is part of the literal; the framework appends the trailing / and the resource segment.

Naming convention — shape first, audience in authorize

Projection names should describe the shape of the variant — what fields it exposes — rather than the audience it serves.

Preferred (shape)Audience name (declare the matching authorize)
"detail""admin"
"summary""staff"
"compact""backoffice"
"full""internal"

A name tells a reader what the variant shows; a rule tells them who may use it, and they are two declarations. Since 0.13.0 a projection can carry its own rule (authorize = <rule>), so a name that says an audience ("admin", "staff") is no longer a misleading promise: it is accurate if the projection declares the matching rule, and it is wrong if it does not. Prefer the shape name, and put the audience in authorize; if an audience name is the clearest URL for your consumers, declare the rule next to it (see § Authorization on projection routes).

Promoting a projection — default replacement and the silent-break problem

Setting default = true on a named projection makes that projection’s shape the one served at the bare resource path. The auto-default read/write surface is suppressed; consumers requesting /films/{id} get the named projection’s shape without any URL change to signal the difference. This is a silent breaking change to the public API contract.

To force the change to be visible, the framework requires two attestation attributes alongside default = true:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "detail",
    default = true,
    promotes_from = "auto-derived",      // attestation of the previous default
    breaking_change_version = "2.0.0",   // app version in which the promotion lands
    read = [id, title, director, cost_price],
    write = [title, director, cost_price],
))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    pub director: String,
    pub cost_price: Option<f64>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Missing either attestation produces compile-time FRG-316. The value of promotes_from is checked: auto-derived, or named:<another projection> with that projection declared in the same model, never the projection itself; any other value is refused at the value, and promotes_from on a projection without default = true is refused at the key. The macro never checks it against repository history. Its purpose is to force the developer to name what is being replaced, which is the part the silent-flip case skips entirely. breaking_change_version surfaces in the OpenAPI document as the x-ferra-promoted-in vendor extension on every operation under the bare resource path, so SDK consumers and downstream tooling can detect the silent break.

A second defence (the .ferra/projection-defaults.lock file with schema-hash drift detection) is not scheduled and does not exist; the Layer-1 attestation is the sole defence.

Worked example — promotion replaces the bare path

The default-promoting projection serves at the bare resource path and no prefixed mirror is published. A model whose v2 projection is the default has exactly one URL surface for the projection’s shape: /films / /films/{id}. The would-be auto-derived /v2/... prefix is not registered, so GET /v2/films/{id} returns 404. This is what makes the promotion a REPLACE, not an ADD.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
#[derive(
    Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize,
)]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "v2",
    default = true,
    promotes_from = "auto-derived",
    breaking_change_version = "2.0.0",
    read = [id, title],
    write = [title],
))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
}
}

Wire-shape contract:

RequestResponse
POST /films body {"title": "X"}201 Created — accepted, named projection’s write_fields
POST /films body {"title": "X", "unknown": "y"}422 Unprocessable Entity — unknown field rejected
GET /films/{id}200 OK body {"id": ..., "title": "X", "_links": {...}}
GET /v2/films/{id}404 Not Found — the prefixed mirror is NOT published

Worked example — x-ferra-promoted-in in the OpenAPI document

The breaking_change_version attestation surfaces as the x-ferra-promoted-in vendor extension on every operation under the bare resource path. SDK generators and tools like ferra anvil read this extension to detect the silent breaking change.

For the Film model above, fetching GET /docs/openapi.json returns a document containing:

paths:
  /films:
    get:
      x-ferra-promoted-in: "2.0.0"
      # ... rest of operation ...
    post:
      x-ferra-promoted-in: "2.0.0"
      # ...
  /films/{id}:
    get:
      x-ferra-promoted-in: "2.0.0"
      # ...
    put:
      x-ferra-promoted-in: "2.0.0"
      # ...
    delete:
      x-ferra-promoted-in: "2.0.0"
      # ...

The extension is per-operation under the bare path. A non-default named projection (one with an auto-derived /admin/ prefix or an explicit path_prefix = "/...") does not emit the extension on its prefixed operations — the extension is the signal that the model’s bare-path wire shape has shifted, not a per-model badge.

Writes — how the body reaches the database

Every write route — the bare path and every projection prefix — reads its body through a write projection: the projection’s write = [...] list, or, at the bare path, the model’s default write projection. The default write projection is every field except:

  • the primary key (the server chooses it — see below);
  • the #[field(owner)] field (the server writes the caller — see ferra-auth.md § Ownership);
  • #[ferra(read_only)], #[ferra(skip)] and #[ferra(computed)] fields;
  • the columns a behavior manages (created_at, updated_at, deleted_at).

The authorization check runs before the body is parsed: a caller the rule refuses gets 401 or 403 (404 under a prefix whose projection rule refuses it) whatever its body, and never learns the body’s shape from a validation error. (The body is still received first, up to the 1 MiB cap: a larger body gets 413 before any rule is checked.)

A field with its own rule (#[field(read = …, write = …)], 0.13.0) is judged on top of the projection: a key the caller may not read is refused like an unknown one (422), and a readable key whose write rule refuses the caller is a 403; see ferra-auth.md § Field rules.

The body is strict. A field outside the write projection — an unknown name, the key, the owner, a read-only field — is refused with 422, listing every offending field. A body that is not JSON of the right shape is a 400. A projection’s own write = [...] list cannot name a read_only, skip or computed field (FRG-324), the key (FRG-318) or the owner (FRG-115).

Columns outside the write projection are not written. The INSERT binds exactly the columns the projection writes; the database’s DEFAULT / SERIAL fills the others. A NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT outside the write set makes the insert fail, correctly — the framework does not invent a value. An update writes the projection’s columns and leaves every other column as stored. #[field(...)] rules run on the projection’s fields only.

The update’s target row comes from the URL. The key is never in an update body.

Primary keys of new rows

KeyWho chooses it
one i32 / i64 columnthe database (SERIAL / identity default)
one Uuid / ferra::Id columnFerra: a UUID v7
a composite or natural keythe client, on models that declare #[ferra(client_pk)] (see ferra-forge.md § Primary keys)

A create body that carries a server-chosen key is refused with 422.

The names default, collection and hal

default names the model’s own read and write projections, served at the bare path. A projection named default does not compile (FRG-317); to replace the bare path’s shapes, give your projection its own name and default = true (see § Promoting a projection below). collection and hal do not compile either (FRG-317): the projection’s schemas in the OpenAPI document are {Model} then its name, so they would overwrite the model’s own {Model}Collection and {Model}Hal.

Authorization on projection routes

Every projection route passes the same authorization checkpoint as the bare resource path, with the model’s #[authorize(...)] rules, or its auth posture when there is no block. A projection may add a rule of its own, authorize = <rule> (or authorize = inherit), and must when it shows or accepts more than the bare path, or when the projection promoted with default = true carries a rule that restricts callers (that rule protects the bare path, not the routes under the other projections’ prefixes) (FRG-117).

The rule is added to the model’s rule of each operation (both must pass), and it is checked first, from the caller alone, before the body is read and before any statement. A caller it refuses learns nothing of the projection:

Request under the prefixAnonymous callerCaller the rule refuses
GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE /{prefix}/{resource}/{id}, POST …/{id}/restore401404, byte for byte the answer for a row that does not exist
GET, POST /{prefix}/{resource}401404 with the fixed detail <resource> not found (no id, no count)

The refusals come in one order under a prefix: 401 (no or invalid credential), 400 (a malformed path key, the same for every caller that is not anonymous), 404 (the projection, then an absent or someone else’s row), 403 (the model’s own rule). A link to the projection is present only on a row the projection served, and a row served under a prefix links to that prefix.

A projection promoted with default = true binds the bare path with its rule, in the same order, and Resource<M> (which reads the default view) answers a caller it refuses with the same NotFound.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "admin",
    read = [id, title, cost],
    write = [title, cost],
    authorize = HasRole("finance"),
))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    pub cost: f64,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The authority of a #[ferra(authority)] model and the parent chain of an owner(from = …) model are checked on a projection route as on the bare path: see ferra-auth.md § Programmatic authority and § Ownership through a parent.

See ferra-auth.md § Projections and authorization.

Prefix collisions

Two collision classes are rejected by the framework — one at compile time, one at Foundry::build().

FRG-310 — same prefix on two projections

Two projections (on the same model or across two mounted models) that resolve to the same effective URL prefix produce ambiguous routing. The compile-time channel catches the intra-model case; the Foundry::build() channel catches the cross-model case.

// Both projections declare path_prefix = "/staff" → FRG-310 at compile time.
#[ferra(projection(name = "admin", path_prefix = "/staff", read = [id, title]))]
#[ferra(projection(name = "manager", path_prefix = "/staff", read = [id, title]))]

(The complete models, bad and good, compiled: FRG-310.)

Resolution: rename one of the projections, or set a distinct path_prefix on one of them.

FRG-312 — projection prefix collides with another resource

A named projection’s auto-derived prefix that matches another mounted model’s resource_name is rejected at Foundry::build(). For example, model A with projection name = "admin" (auto-deriving /admin/) cannot be mounted on the same Foundry as model B with resource_name = "admin" (mounting at /admin).

Resolution: rename the projection to a shape descriptor that does not match any mounted resource name, or set an explicit path_prefix to disambiguate.

Nested resources (the sub-collection)

When a parent and its child are both mounted on the same Foundry (a HasMany or HasOne field and the two .mount; ADR-0084 decision 1, ADR-0030 as amended), only the sub-collection is served: GET and POST {parent item}/{relation}, for example /films/{id}/reviews. See Sub-collections for the rules it follows.

  • It is served at the bare path, in the child’s default representation (its promoted projection, if it has one). A named projection’s prefix does not get it: /detail/films/{id}/reviews is not served.
  • The item stays canonical at its own path, /reviews/{rid}. There is no nested item path (/films/{id}/reviews/{rid}), and Location and self name /reviews/{rid}.
  • The projection prefix does not propagate across models. /detail/films/{id} is the detail projection of Film only; a child’s projection is reached at its own prefixed path (/summary/reviews).
  • A model’s own path_prefix is its own. FRG-315 stays unbuilt: no nested path takes a prefix, so there is nothing to reject.

A developer who needs a different shape of the children declares a projection on the child and reads it at the child’s own prefixed path (/summary/reviews), narrowed by a #[field(filterable)] foreign key.

Versioning composition

Ferra takes no position on API versioning — that is an application-level concern. The framework provides two complementary mechanisms that compose with the projection surface:

  1. Application-level prefix (canonical). Mount the entire API under a version segment:

    use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let key = std::env::var("ETAG_KEY")?;
let app = ferra::Foundry::new(conn).etag_key(key)?.api_version("v1")?.mount::<Film>().build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

    When a breaking change requires bumping /v1 → /v2, the developer bumps the prefix in the application code. The framework provides the signal (the FRG-316 attestation requirement on default = true); the developer decides when to bump and how to communicate the bump (Deprecation: header, sunset date, parallel-run period).

  2. Per-projection versioning (escape hatch via path_prefix). A single projection can be versioned independently of the application by embedding the version in its path_prefix:

    #[ferra(projection(name = "detail", path_prefix = "/v2/detail", read = [id, title]))]

    This composes naturally with .api_version("v1") — the final URL becomes /v1/v2/detail/films/{id}.

The framework deliberately does NOT introduce a separate version = N attribute; path_prefix is sufficient for the escape-hatch case and avoids growing the projection surface for what is fundamentally an application concern.

/me

GET /me (and HEAD) answers the caller’s own row, so a client does not need to know its id. Declare it on the model that holds one row per user:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "profiles")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer", me)]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[sea_orm(unique)]
    #[field(owner)]
    pub user_id: Uuid,
    pub display_name: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
  • One model per Foundry. A second #[ferra(me)] model, or a model whose resource is me, makes build() panic with a message that names both. The resource of a model is its URL segment (/profiles): its table_name, unless #[ferra(resource = "...")] sets another (ferra-forge.md), so a table called me is served at /me and clashes; give it another resource.
  • PUT /me does not exist: the item route (/profiles/{id}) serves writes. A client learns the id from the id of the row GET /me answers, or from its _links.self. Whether a caller may write that row is the update rule of the model, not /me: put IsOwner in it to let a caller write only the row they own (Ownership).
  • A unique owner. The model needs a root #[field(owner)] (the field of the model itself, not the owner(from = ...) that copies the owner from a parent) that identifies one row: #[sea_orm(unique)], or the single-column primary key (FRG-131). The owner’s type is Id, Uuid, i32 or i64; Uuid is sea-orm’s with-uuid feature, which a default-features = false dependency (the block of Getting started) does not enable: add it. The attribute declares the index to Ferra, it does not create it: a unique index declared only in a migration is refused the same way (add the attribute), and an attribute without the index in the database lets two rows share an owner. Then /me answers 500 internal and logs it (tracing, target ferra_http::operations); find the rows with SELECT owner_column FROM table GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1.
  • .with_auth() is required. The model does not compile without it (FRG-151), whatever its auth posture, auth = "none" included: a call with no credential is a 401.
  • The subject compared with the owner is FerraIdentity::id() of the caller’s identity (Identity), for every credential kind: the sub of a bearer token or of the cookie’s JWT, the subject recorded when an API key was issued. To make an API key’s subject match an owner, issue the key with the id the owner column holds (API keys).
  • The path follows the version prefix: /v1/me under .api_version("v1"). A .route on /me makes build() panic too, as on any path Ferra serves.
  • One SELECT, under the model’s read field rules, the soft-delete filter and the authority’s filter. _links.self is the item’s URL (/profiles/{id}).
  • Soft delete keeps the owner. On a soft-deletable model, a soft-deleted row still holds its unique owner value. /me answers 404 (the row is hidden), and a new POST for the same owner hits the unique constraint and answers 409 until the row is restored.
CaseStatus
no credential401, before any statement
the get rule refuses the caller before any row is read (see below)403, before the SELECT, the same whether the caller owns a row or not
no row, a soft-deleted row, a row the authority’s filter leaves out, can(Get, row) refused, a get rule that depends on the row refused on it, or a default = true projection whose authorize refuses the caller404 not_found, detail "profiles not found", with no id
one row200
