The key, the owner, the foreign key behind owner(from = ..), a computed field and a skip field cannot be listed: that is FRG-146, at compile time, and so is a field that anyone who may write the row can already write, or a name the model does not have.

The answer

  • 200 with the row, as GET serves it to this caller: the read projection of the bare path, the ETag of the new state, the _links. No Location.
  • 204 with the ETag under Prefer: return=minimal.
  • 204 with no body, no ETag and no Location when the caller may not GET the row as written: the write stands, and nothing of the row is told.

Retries and the request budget

When the database aborts the write with 40001 or 40P01 (at the statement or at COMMIT), Ferra runs the whole action again: the lock, the preconditions, the handler, the hooks. Three attempts, then a 503 retry_exhausted with Retry-After: 1, and the action was not applied. Details and constants: Transient conflicts are retried.

So a handler must be re-runnable:

  • No external I/O before the commit. A message, an HTTP call or a file written from the handler goes out once per attempt, and for an action that is then rolled back. Work on the database through tx, which the abort rolls back; send effects from after_commit, which runs once, for the attempt that committed.
  • Keep no state between attempts. A counter or a flag changed in the application is changed once per attempt.
  • A precondition is decided again. If another writer committed between two attempts, the new attempt locks the new row, and a stale If-Match is a 412.

Set a request budget. Without one, only the three attempts bound the work. With one, the deadline cuts a handler at its next .await before the commit starts (503 timeout, nothing written); a handler that blocks the thread without awaiting is not cut, and neither is a commit once it has started. After the commit, the after_commit hooks run under the request’s one post-commit deadline, shared by every row of a batch (the three phases).

Sending the same request twice

Ferra does not deduplicate a request, and there is no Idempotency-Key. If-Match is the guard against running an action twice:

  • A client that sends the ETag it read as If-Match and gets no answer can send the same request again. If the first one committed a change, the row has a new tag and the replay is a 412: it ran once.
  • An action that changed nothing leaves the tag as it was, so the replay passes and the handler runs again.
  • Without If-Match, the handler runs again.

Write the handler so that running it twice on the same row is harmless, or make the client send If-Match.

_links.<name>

A served row carries _links.<name> for each action the caller may run on that row, only when self is present: the action’s rule and can(Action(name), row) both pass, judged in memory from the row in hand, with no statement. The href is the action’s bare path (/jobs/1/mark_seen), whatever projection prefix served the row. A link is a hint: following it is judged again by the route.

{
  "id": 1,
  "seen": false,
  "_links": {
    "self": { "href": "/jobs/1" },
    "collection": { "href": "/jobs" },
    "mark_seen": { "href": "/jobs/1/mark_seen" }
  }
}

Collection actions

collection in the attribute serves the action on POST /{resource}/{name} (POST /jobs/mark_all_seen): one request runs the handler on up to 100 rows of the model, in one transaction. The rule, the handler, the typed body and writes are those of a row action; the handler runs once per row, in the order of the keys. A model with a composite key cannot declare one (FRG-143).

The request is an envelope, a JSON object with the Content-Type application/json:

{ "ids": [3, 7, 12], "body": { "progress": 40 } }
  • ids is required: one to 100 distinct keys of the model’s key type, in any order. An empty list is 422 min_items, a key listed twice is 422 unique_items and a list over 100 is 422 max_items; a missing ids is 422 required; an id of the wrong JSON type or that does not parse as the key is 400 invalid_json. The message never holds an id.
  • body is the typed body, required when the action declares one (422 required) and the same for every row. An error of the typed body names its key body.<key> (body.progress). A key other than ids and body is 422 unknown_field, and so is body on an action that declares none.
  • A key repeated in the envelope (ids twice) or in the typed body is 400 invalid_json.
  • If-Match: * passes and If-Match with a tag is a 412: no tag is served for a batch. If-None-Match: * is a 412 and If-None-Match with tags passes. Prefer is ignored.

The order of refusals is the row action’s, with the envelope judged first: 401, then 413 for an announced Content-Length over the cap, 403 (a rule that reads no row), 415, 412, 413 for a body read over the cap, 400, the 422 of the envelope and of the typed body, then the rows. None of them calls the handler.

  • One 404, naming no id. If any listed row is absent, soft-deleted or hidden from the caller (IsOwner, the authority’s filter, can(Action(name))), the answer is one 404 with the status, type, title and headers of an absent row’s, and the detail <resource> not found, whatever the number of rows or which one: the rows are locked in one read, in key order, so the number of statements does not tell either.
  • All or nothing. A 403 on one row (the part of the rule that reads the row, a field the action may not write, can(Action(name)) on the row as written), a handler error, a failed validator: the whole batch is rolled back and nothing is written. The first error is the answer. The checks of What the handler may change run on every row.
  • after_commit once per row, after the commit of the batch, for each row that was committed, even if the hook of one row fails (the answer is then the first error).
  • The batch is the retried unit. On 40001 or 40P01 the whole batch runs again, the handlers and hooks of every row with it (Retries and the request budget). The rows are locked in key order, so two batches that list the same rows in opposite orders do not deadlock. On a model with owner(from = ..) the distinct parents are locked FOR SHARE first, in key order, so a batch and a child write do not either (Relations). Set a request budget: without one, a batch of 100 rows holds its locks as long as its handlers run.

The answer is 204, with no body, no ETag and no _links: a batch serves no row. A collection action never appears in _links.

On a model whose key is a String, POST /{resource}/{name} is a literal route: GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE /{resource}/{name} answer 405, and a row whose key equals the action’s name is unreachable on those methods. Pick a name no row will have as a key.

OpenAPI

Each action is one POST operation on the bare path, in the document exactly as the router serves it: /{resource}/{id}/{name} for a row action, /{resource}/{name} for a collection action. The operationId is the name in lower camel case followed by the model (mark_seen on Job is markSeenJob); the suffix of a promoted default projection, and the version prefix, are added as for restore. A body is a component named {Pascal(operationId)}Input (SetProgressJobInput), additionalProperties: false. The responses of a row action are 200 and 204, 400, 401 where the model reads tokens, 403, 404, 409, 412, 422, 429 unless the limiter is off, 500 and 503; 413 and 415 only for an action with a body. A collection action answers 204 (no ETag) and the same errors, 413, 415 and 422 included, since its envelope is a body, the component {Pascal(operationId)}Request (AckAllJobRequest): minItems: 1, maxItems: 100, uniqueItems: true on ids, and body a $ref to the component when the action declares one. The details are in Ferra OpenAPI.

Under a projection prefix

An action is served on the bare path only. /{prefix}/{resource}/{id}/{name} (/{prefix}/{resource}/{name} for a collection action) under a projection prefix answers 404 or 405, and the handler does not run.

Relations

A model with owner(from = ..) is the child of another model: its rows live under a parent’s owner. This page states what Ferra guarantees when a parent and its children are written at the same time. It grows with the release.

Declaring relations

A model written with #[sea_orm::model] (Sea-ORM’s dense form) may declare its relations inline, as HasMany<..>, HasOne<..> or BelongsTo<..> fields. The macro expands the struct twice: Model keeps the scalar fields, a second struct ModelEx keeps all of them. #[derive(FerraModel)] runs on both. On Model it reads the columns as ever, so a relation field is never a column or a wire field, and never a projection field of its own, with one exception: a BelongsTo named in a projection’s read list is embedded (Embedding). On ModelEx it emits one typed marker per relation (name, kind, foreign key, both models), which Foundry reads at .mount.

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod client {
    use super::*;

    #[sea_orm::model]
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "clients")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub name: String,
        #[sea_orm(has_many)]
        pub contexts: HasMany<super::context::Entity>,
    }

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

mod context {
    use super::*;

    #[sea_orm::model]
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "contexts")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub client_id: i32,
        #[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "client_id", to = "id")]
        pub client: BelongsTo<super::client::Entity>,
    }

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
fn main() {}

A relation field is only valid in this form. On a struct that is not an expansion of #[sea_orm::model], such as a hand-written Model with an enum Relation, it is refused (FRG-125, see ferra-forge-diagnostics.md). The split form stays valid for a model without relation fields.

The three kinds. The kind comes from the attribute, not from the field’s type:

  • BelongsTo: the field carries #[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "..", to = "..")]. Its foreign key is the column from names. A nullable key is written HasOne<..> in Sea-ORM 2.0, and is still a BelongsTo here.
  • HasMany: the rows of another model that point back at this one.
  • HasOne: the same, for at most one row.

The back key. The foreign key of a HasMany or a HasOne is the one BelongsTo its target has back to this model. Ferra does not guess it. When both models are mounted on the same Foundry, build() (and try_build()) refuses a target with none, or with two or more, naming both models and the relations:

`films.reviews` is a `HasMany` to `reviews`, but `reviews` has two `BelongsTo` back to `films` (film, other_film); keep exactly one, or do not mount both

Keep one BelongsTo, or mount only one of the two models: a pair with a single side mounted is not checked.

The target must be a Ferra model. A relation whose target does not derive FerraModel fails to compile at .mount, with FRG-136: “<Target> is not a Ferra model that Foundry can serve, yet a relation points at it”.

Sub-collections

A HasMany or HasOne whose target is mounted on the same Foundry serves its rows under the parent (0.16.0). With films having reviews: HasMany<review::Entity> and both models mounted:

GET  /films/{id}/reviews
POST /films/{id}/reviews

There is nothing to switch on and no method to call: the two .mount and the relation field are the declaration, as for restore and the row actions. The routes appear in the OpenAPI document (listFilmReviews, createFilmReview: list or create, the parent’s name, the relation’s name) and are listed, with the parent’s path parameters, next to the routes of the child. A pair with a single side mounted serves nothing. A parent with a composite key has no sub-collection: a foreign key is one column.

A sub-collection is the child’s own path with one more term. POST /films/1/reviews allows nothing that POST /reviews with film_id = 1 does not, and GET /films/1/reviews lists what GET /reviews?filter[film_id]=1 lists:

  • It runs the child’s own list and create, with the child’s own rules, projections, field rules, hooks, soft-delete state, pagination mode, count and cursors. The parent’s term is added to the child’s authority, so a client’s filter[film_id]=2 cannot widen it: it narrows to nothing.
  • It goes through the child’s layers: its mount_with_layer, rate limit, body limit, CORS, JWT and cookie guard. Its rate-limit bucket is its own, as that of each route family of a model is. The JWT layer follows the stricter of the two policies, because the parent is judged on this route: a public child under a parent that needs an identity still reads the caller’s token. So do the child’s own routes, because they judge the parent too (the key, the parent link, a POST naming the parent): under .with_auth(), a model reads a credential (the Authorization header, the cookie, an API key) when a model one of its relations targets needs an identity, so a valid token is seen and a broken one is a 401. Such a model read no token before, and a request that carries the cookie may now meet the CSRF guard. A request with no token still reaches the child’s Anyone rules, with the key and the link hidden.
  • The representation is the child’s default one. A named projection’s prefix does not get sub-collections (/summary/films/1/reviews is not served).
  • The parent’s key comes from the URL and wins over the body’s film_id. The created review is canonical at /reviews/{id} (Location, self); the links of a page of the sub-collection (next, prev) stay on the sub-collection.

What the parent adds. Only refusals, in this order:

  1. The parent, judged exactly as GET /films/{id} judges it for this caller. A parent that is absent, soft-deleted or unreadable answers the 404 of an absent parent, byte for byte, and so does a key that is no key of the parent (/films/not-a-key/reviews: the 400 of GET /films/not-a-key would tell a caller that the key’s format is wrong, where no row would tell it anything).
  2. For POST, the parent’s update right: a parent the caller can read and may not update answers 403, before the child’s body is looked at.
  3. The child’s own refusals, in their own order. A parent the caller can read with a child list rule that refuses the caller answers the child’s 403 on GET. For an owner(from) child the create judges the parent again under its FOR SHARE lock; a parent that lost the right in between is that path’s 422 reference_not_found, which only a race can reach.

For a plain BelongsTo child (no owner(from)) Ferra takes no lock on the parent: its update right is read without one, like any plain BelongsTo (The aggregate protocol). The database still has a say: a Ferra write of film 1 holds it FOR UPDATE, and the INSERT of a POST /films/1/tags takes FOR KEY SHARE on film 1 through the foreign-key constraint, so it waits for that write to commit. A hold that does not conflict with FOR KEY SHARE (FOR NO KEY UPDATE, the mode of an UPDATE that leaves the key alone) does not make it wait.

A soft-deleted parent. Its children stay served on their own path (ADR-0059 limitation); a POST /reviews naming it is the 422 reference_not_found; a POST under it (/films/{id}/reviews) is the absent parent’s 404.

A relation that shares its name with a route. A HasMany or HasOne named like a row action, or restore, of its own model would take the path of that route: build() refuses it, naming the model and both names (BuildError::RelationNameCollision). Rename the relation or the action.

To serve none of them, write the parent in the split form (it declares no relation) or do not mount the child. There is no per-relation opt-out yet.

The aggregate protocol

A parent’s check (a film is published only when it has a live review, a studio’s rows are counted) is valid only if no child can be written behind its back. Ferra enforces that with locks, on by default, with nothing to switch on.

  • FR-001. Every write of a child (PUT, PATCH, delete, restore and row action, through the generated routes, Resource<M> and tx.resource alike) takes FOR SHARE on its direct parent, then locks its own row FOR UPDATE, whether or not the foreign key changes. The parent lock judges no rule and no authority, and it locks a soft-deleted parent too. A row the caller cannot see answers its 404 before any lock, so it never locks its parent. Creating a child keeps its parent check (FOR SHARE, judged under the parent’s update rule).
  • FR-002. Every write or action of a parent holds the parent’s row FOR UPDATE. A child write waits for it, and it waits for the child writes in flight. The children a parent writes from its hook or action are locked FOR UPDATE when they are written.
  • FR-004. Every write opens at READ COMMITTED (see Transactions).
  • FR-005. The lock order is total: the parent, then the row. Along a chain each level’s write is its own transaction, so the root is locked first.
  • FR-006. A plain BelongsTo (no owner(from)) locks nothing.
  • FR-007. Residual deadlocks go to the bounded retries of Transient conflicts are retried, and end at the 503 retry_exhausted. Ferra does not promise the absence of deadlocks: two child writes whose hooks write each other’s siblings can still cross.

A foreign key that changes between the read of the row and its lock (only a raw statement can do that) makes the attempt transient: it is rolled back and retried, and ends at the 503 retry_exhausted if the key keeps moving.

An empty collection under publish. A parent whose action reads “no review yet” holds the parent FOR UPDATE; a concurrent POST /reviews for that film waits for the parent’s lock, so the review cannot appear between the check and the commit.

A three-level chain. For studio, film and review, a review write locks its film only, and a film write locks its studio only. The ancestors are locked root first because each level’s write is its own transaction.

A collection action over several parents. A model with owner(from = ..) reads the keys of its rows without a lock, then locks the distinct parents FOR SHARE in one statement in key order, then the rows FOR UPDATE in key order, and checks that each row still has the key it was read with. A row the caller cannot see is the batch’s 404 before any parent is locked; a parent that no longer exists is that 404 too.

A plain BelongsTo locks nothing. Reading the target is enough: a PATCH of a tag whose film is held FOR UPDATE does not wait.

A raw INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE is outside the protocol. A raw INSERT into the child table waits on the parent’s FOR UPDATE when the table carries the foreign-key constraint (its check takes FOR KEY SHARE). A raw UPDATE or DELETE of an existing child does not wait: only the writes Ferra makes take the parent lock.

The protocol needs the database foreign-key constraint. It locks the parent row the key names; without a FOREIGN KEY on the child table nothing stops a parent from being deleted under its children. A child whose parent row is gone answers 404 to every write (PUT, PATCH, delete, restore and row action): there is no row to lock.

Hooks and the parent

A child’s hook runs with its parent held FOR SHARE. Its tx.resource may read the parent, create a sibling and write a row of another parent, but an update or a delete of the held parent is refused: 500 internal, one error! with both resource names and no key, and the write commits nothing even when the hook swallows the error (details). Write the parent from its own action, which holds it FOR UPDATE.

Across aggregates, write from the root’s action: a child’s hook that writes a grandparent can cross another write’s locks, and ends at the 503 retry_exhausted rather than waiting forever.

A database trigger that writes the parent on a child’s insert deadlocks the same way, and Ferra cannot see it: keep a counter on the parent in the parent’s action, or compute it on read.

Moving a child

The foreign key of a model with owner(from = ..) is set when the row is created and never changes (0.16.0, FR-010):

  • A PUT or a PATCH that names it is the 422 unknown_field of any key outside the write set, whatever value it names and whatever the caller may read, with nothing written. The key is not in the PUT and PATCH request schemas of the OpenAPI document, and it stays in the POST one.
  • A PUT that leaves it out keeps the row under its parent: the stored value fills in before the body is decoded.
  • A row action or a hook that changes it is a bug of yours: the action answers 500 internal, and a hook’s tx.resource().update naming it is refused with the same 422, and the hook that returns it rolls the whole write back; a hook that swallows it commits nothing either.

To move a child, delete it and create it again.

A delete then a create is not a move. The new row has a new identity: references to the old one (links, other tables, a client’s cached id), its history and its created_at do not follow it. A move protocol is post-1.0.

Links and foreign keys

A row never reveals a parent its caller cannot read. For each BelongsTo, the foreign key and the link to the parent follow the parent’s readability (0.16.0, FR-030):

ParentNon-nullable keyNullable key
readablethe value, and a linkthe value, and a link
none (NULL)null, no link
unreadableabsent, no linkabsent, no link
 
"_links": {
  "self": {"href": "/reviews/5"},
  "collection": {"href": "/reviews"},
  "film": {"href": "/films/1"}
}
  • The link is named after the relation and is the parent’s bare item path (no projection prefix), under the same origin and version prefix as self. HAL only. It is present if and only if the caller may GET that parent, so following it never answers a refusal.
  • The link to a sub-collection is named after the HasMany or HasOne relation and is the bare {item}/{relation} ("reviews": {"href": "/films/1/reviews"}), under the same origin and version prefix as self and whatever projection prefix served the row. It is present if and only if the sub-collection is served (the child is mounted on the same Foundry) and the caller may list the child, by the child’s own list rule and projection rule, so following it never answers a refusal. A HasOne is linked as a sub-collection too, never to the item. HAL only.
  • Readable is exactly what GET {parent item} judges: the get rule, the authority’s filter and can, the owner condition and soft delete. One statement per BelongsTo per page decides it for all the rows (key IN (...)), whatever the page size. It fails closed: an authority that fails or panics hides every key and link of the page and is logged, and a parent that is not mounted on the Foundry is hidden for everyone, with no statement.
  • Every response that serializes the row follows it: item, list, cursor page, /me, the write responses, each projection prefix, Resource<M> and a hook’s tx.resource. In FerraViews::Read the key is an Option.
  • Never required. The OpenAPI read schema leaves the key out of required and says it is absent when the caller may not read it; the Hal schema lists the parent and sub-collection links as optional.
  • A PUT does not need the key when the caller cannot read the parent: the stored value is kept.
  • Accepted residual: on a nullable key, “absent” against “null” tells a caller that the row has a parent it cannot read (one bit). A non-nullable key has none.

Embedding

A projection’s read list may name a BelongsTo relation (0.16.0, FR-040). The response then carries the parent’s row, under the relation’s name, next to the link to it. The row is served in the parent’s projection of the same name: the summary of a review embeds the summary of its film.

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;

    #[sea_orm::model]
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    // The target's `summary` carries its own `path_prefix`: see below.
    #[ferra(projection(name = "summary", path_prefix = "/film-summary", read = [id, title]))]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
        #[sea_orm(has_many)]
        pub reviews: HasMany<super::review::Entity>,
    }

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

mod review {
    use super::*;

    #[sea_orm::model]
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "reviews")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    #[ferra(projection(name = "summary", read = [id, body, film]))]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub film_id: i32,
        pub body: String,
        #[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "film_id", to = "id")]
        pub film: BelongsTo<super::film::Entity>,
    }

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
fn main() {}

GET /summary/reviews/5 answers (HAL; the plain JSON representation has the same members, without _links):

{
  "id": 5,
  "body": "Worth the trip.",
  "film": {"id": 1, "title": "Heat"},
  "_links": {
    "self": {"href": "/summary/reviews/5"},
    "collection": {"href": "/summary/reviews"},
    "film": {"href": "/films/1"}
  }
}
  • Exactly what the parent’s projection answers. The embedded row is what GET /film-summary/films/1 answers that caller, member for member: the projection’s own rule, the field read rules of each row (a field the caller may not read is no member, whatever the other embedded rows show), the computed fields (the hook runs once per computed field for the rows of the page), and the wire names. It is judged per row, so a page may hold an embedded row with a field and another without.
  • Not readable, nothing. A parent the caller may not read, or that is soft-deleted, gives no embed, no link and no key, as in Links and foreign keys. A parent the caller may read but whose projection of that name refuses them (its authorize rule), or a parent with no projection of that name, gives the link alone: the GET of that projection is a 404 for them, and the embed does not say more. No embed without the link: a parent whose bare route refuses the caller (a promoted projection with a stricter rule, say) is not embedded, even when the projection of that name would answer them.
  • One statement. The statement that decides the link (key IN (...), one per BelongsTo per page) returns the parent rows, and the embed serializes those: the number of statements does not depend on the number of rows, nor on the embed. The total, the page numbers and the cursor of a page are those of the same page without the embed.
  • A computed field that fails is a 500 on the whole response. If a computed field of the embedded target fails, the child’s response is the 500 internal of a failing hook, and no part of it is served: the embed is not dropped silently. The log line names the target’s model and the operation get.
  • The tag does not follow the parent. The ETag of the response is the child row’s: the embedded parent can change under the same tag. See The tag.
  • Depth 1. The embedded row carries no _links, no embed of its own and no foreign key of its own: its parents are not read again, so their keys are not served. Follow the film link for the whole row.
  • Every response that serializes the row embeds: item, list, cursor page, /me and the write responses of a projection route (the bare route too, when a promoted projection names the relation). Resource<M> and a hook’s tx.resource never embed: they return the typed read view, which has no member for a parent’s row.
  • Two projections of one name. The summary of reviews and the summary of films would both default to the URL prefix /summary/, and Foundry::build() refuses two projections on one prefix (FRG-310, see projections-and-routing.md). So the target’s projection carries its own path_prefix (/film-summary above), or the embedding one does. There is no syntax to embed a projection of another name.
  • No cycle. If the summary of films embedded a BelongsTo back to reviews and the summary of reviews embedded films, Foundry::build() (and try_build()) refuses the chain with BuildError::EmbedCycle: Embedding cycle: `reviews.summary → films.summary → reviews.summary`; remove one embed from a `read` list. The path is made of resource names, which are the table names unless resource = says otherwise, and starts at the first node the check meets again. Only an embed that is served counts: a relation whose target is not mounted (no key and no link either) or has no projection of that name (the link alone) closes no loop.
  • Only a BelongsTo. A HasMany or a HasOne named in a read list does not compile: it stays the link to its sub-collection, bounded by the pagination of the child.
  • OpenAPI. The projection’s read schema gets the relation as an optional member, a reference to the read schema of the parent’s projection of that name, when the parent is mounted on the same Foundry. The required list does not hold it.

Writing a foreign key

A create, a PUT or a PATCH that sets the key of a plain BelongsTo (no owner(from)) reads the target before it writes (0.16.0, FR-032). The read is the one that decides whether the caller may see the parent: the target’s get rule, its authority, its owner condition and soft delete, judged in the write’s own transaction. It takes no lock, so a plain BelongsTo still waits for nothing.

  • One refusal. A target that is absent, soft-deleted, out of the caller’s reach, or not mounted on the Foundry is the same 422 reference_not_found with field the key, whichever it is. The bytes are those of the parent check of an owner(from) child, and the same for the route, Resource<M> and a hook’s tx.resource. A caller cannot tell a film that does not exist from one it may not read, and nothing is written.
  • A table the API does not serve. A target that is not mounted on the Foundry is refused for every value, one that exists as much as one that does not: nobody can read it through this API, so none of its rows may be pointed at, and an answer that told the two apart would tell which ids exist. Two ways to write such a key:
    • mount the target model: its get rule then says who may point at it, and the key and the link are served;
    • set the key in before_save from another value the body carries, reading the reference through tx.resource (it reaches an unmounted model under its own rules).
  • A key a hook writes is the application’s responsibility: Ferra reads the targets of the keys the body names, before before_save runs, and does not judge what a hook then puts in the draft. The constraint still answers the 422 for an absent target. What an action writes (its changed) is the same: the application’s code and its responsibility, not judged by this read.
  • Several keys. When a body names several refused keys, the 422 names the first in declaration order, whatever the others are.
  • null and silence. null clears the key and reads nothing. A PATCH or a PUT that does not name the key reads nothing and keeps the stored value, even when the parent became unreadable.
  • An owner(from) key keeps its own check (lock_for_child): it is not read twice, and a PATCH naming it is still the 422 unknown_field first.
  • One statement per key named, none for a write that names no key.
  • Before 0.16.0 a target the caller could not read was accepted (201), and an absent one was a 500 (SQLSTATE 23503): the two answers told a caller which ids exist. See Migrating.

Deleting a parent

Whether a parent that still has children can be deleted is the schema’s choice, made in the foreign-key constraint of the child’s table (0.16.0, FR-033). Ferra asks the database and answers what it says.

  • ON DELETE RESTRICT (or the default, NO ACTION): the database refuses the DELETE. Ferra answers the 409 conflict with its fixed detail, nothing is deleted, and the statement is run once (a foreign-key violation is not a transient failure, so it is not retried). The OpenAPI document declares the 409 on the DELETE of every model that a BelongsTo targets. The server log holds the constraint’s name (INFO, target ferra_http::conflict), never the key value that Postgres prints in its detail line.
  • ON DELETE CASCADE: the database deletes the children itself. Ferra does not see them: their before_delete and after_delete hooks do not run, their rules and their soft delete are not applied. Use it only for rows nothing else has an opinion on.
  • A write the database refuses for a foreign key (the target was removed between Ferra’s read and its write) is the 422 reference_not_found of Writing a foreign key, on the key the constraint names, with the same bytes as a target that was absent at the read.
  • Accepted residual. Under RESTRICT a caller who may delete the parent learns, from the 409, that some row references it, including a child that caller cannot read: one bit per parent. When that matters, make the children owner-scoped (owner(from = ...) on the child, so the parent’s owner owns every child) or let the schema CASCADE.
  • A soft delete is an UPDATE: no constraint refuses it, and the children stay as they are.

Computed fields

A computed field is server-derived: it has no column, the client never writes it, and the application’s own code fills it before a response is serialised. An invoice’s total is subtotal + tax; a film’s comment_count is a query on another table.

This page is the page of the feature: the declaration, the two per-field hooks and the enum the derive hands them, what Ferra refuses, when the hooks run, the context they receive, what a failure answers, and how to make a replayed create safe.

Declare the field

A computed field carries #[sea_orm(ignore)] and #[ferra(computed)]:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "invoices")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub subtotal: f64,
    pub tax: f64,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub total: Option<f64>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
impl ferra::compute::FerraComputed for Model {}
}
  • #[sea_orm(ignore)] is required (FRG-360): the table has no such column, no SELECT, INSERT or UPDATE names it, and Sea-ORM builds the field with Default. The field’s type must implement Default.
  • The field is read-only on the wire. A POST, PUT or PATCH body that names it is a 422 unknown_field, and the OpenAPI document marks it readOnly: true on every read schema.
  • It cannot be filtered, sorted or used as a cursor key (FRG-361), and cannot be combined with skip, write_only or a primary key (FRG-359).
  • A model with a computed field must write the impl FerraComputed (FRG-362).

Two edge cases follow from “no column”:

  • Every field computed except the key. The model is still valid. A read selects the stored columns only, here the key alone, and the hooks then fill each computed field, so the computed fields add no column to any statement.
  • A computed field in a projection’s write list is a compile error, FRG-324 (a declared action’s writes list is FRG-146). Neither can let a client write a computed field.

The two hooks, and the field they receive

A model with a computed field writes an impl FerraComputed for Model. The trait has two default-implemented hooks, and each is told which computed field it is to compute:

  • async fn compute_field(&mut self, field: ModelComputed, ctx: &RequestContext) -> Result<(), FerraComputeError> computes one field of one row. Default: nothing.
  • async fn compute_field_batch(rows: &mut [Model], field: ModelComputed, ctx: &RequestContext) -> Result<(), FerraComputeError> computes one field of a slice of rows. Default: compute_field on each row in turn, stopping at the first error. Override it to replace one query per row with one query for the slice.

ModelComputed is an enum the derive writes next to the model, with one variant per computed field, named in PascalCase after the field (total is ModelComputed::Total). The application matches on it and never chooses the type, so the field a hook is asked for is always one the model declares:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use ferra::compute::{FerraComputeError, FerraComputed};
use ferra::request_context::RequestContext;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "invoices")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub subtotal: f64,
    pub tax: f64,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub total: Option<f64>,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub label: Option<String>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}

impl FerraComputed for Model {
    async fn compute_field(
        &mut self,
        field: ModelComputed,
        _ctx: &RequestContext,
    ) -> Result<(), FerraComputeError> {
        match field {
            ModelComputed::Total => self.total = Some(self.subtotal + self.tax),
            ModelComputed::Label => self.label = Some(format!("invoice {}", self.id)),
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
}

A model with a computed field must write the impl, empty or not: the derive writes it only for a model with no computed field. Without it the model does not compile, mounted or not (FRG-362).

Replace N queries with one

A field that needs I/O is computed for the whole slice at once. The slice is the page of a collection read, or one row on an item read, so the same code serves both:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

use ferra::FerraModel;
use ferra::compute::{FerraComputeError, FerraComputed};
use ferra::request_context::RequestContext;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub comment_count: i64,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
// Stands for one query on a pool of your own (`WHERE film_id = ANY($1) GROUP BY film_id`).
async fn comment_counts(ids: &[i32]) -> Result<HashMap<i32, i64>, String> {
    Ok(ids.iter().map(|id| (*id, 0)).collect())
}

impl FerraComputed for Model {
    async fn compute_field_batch(
        rows: &mut [Self],
        field: ModelComputed,
        _ctx: &RequestContext,
    ) -> Result<(), FerraComputeError> {
        match field {
            ModelComputed::CommentCount => {
                let ids: Vec<i32> = rows.iter().map(|row| row.id).collect();
                let counts = comment_counts(&ids).await.map_err(FerraComputeError::new)?;
                for row in rows {
                    row.comment_count = counts.get(&row.id).copied().unwrap_or(0);
                }
            }
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
}

Migrating a 0.14 implementation

Through 0.14 the trait had three methods, compute, compute_async and compute_async_batch, none told which field it computed. A synchronous computation is now written in the async body of compute_field, which matches on the field; compute_async_batch(rows, ctx) becomes compute_field_batch(rows, field, ctx). Migrating from 0.14 to 0.15 has the before and after, and the full list of breaks.

When the hooks run

Each computed field is computed per field, for the rows that serve it to this caller, and for no other row. Ferra calls compute_field_batch once per computed field and per read, with the rows for which both hold:

  • the field is in the read projection of the route (a prefix such as /lean/... that does not list total never computes it, and neither does a bare path whose default projection omits it);
  • the caller may read the field on that row: its read rule passes, with the row’s own owner for IsOwner.

A field whose slice is empty is not computed at all: its hook is not called, not even with an empty slice. A caller served total and refused label on the same row triggers the hook for ModelComputed::Total only. This holds for an item, /me, a page, a cursor page, and for Resource<M> and tx.resource alike: they apply the same gate to the read view they hand back, so a hand-written route computes what the generated route would serve and nothing more.

The hook is called on a clone of each served row, and only the field it was asked for is copied back. A hook that also sets another field, a stored field, the key or the owner changes nothing that is served: the owner the gate reads, the _links, the ETag and any Location are those of the row as it was fetched, before any hook ran.

A request that is refused (401, 403, 404, 422, …) computes nothing.

A write response (a create, a PUT, a PATCH, a restore, a row action) serves the same computed values a GET would, computed after the commit and after after_commit, on the row as written. It computes only when it serves a body: not for Prefer: return=minimal, not for a 201 or 204 sent without a body to a caller who may not GET the row, and not for a DELETE or a collection action. The Location, the ETag and the _links are those of the row as written, before any hook ran. Resource::create and Resource::update compute the row they return the same way.

A value is never computed for a caller who may not Get the row: whether the get rule refuses it or the authority’s can(Get) does, the hook is not called for that caller. That holds for Resource::create and Resource::update too: for a caller who may not read the row they return None, the row written, and no hook is called.

A write made by tx.resource computes inside the open transaction, as its reads do: a hook sees its own transaction’s state, which may still roll back. The after-commit rule governs only what is served to a client.

The write is already committed when a write response computes. If that compute fails, the answer is a 500 and the row stands (see When a hook fails); a client that replays the POST can create a duplicate. Idempotent creates shows how to make a replay safe.

A hook is an output path. It can read any field of the row, including a column the API never serves (skip, write_only) or a field under a stricter read rule, and what it computes is served under the computed field’s own read rule. A computed field derived from a hidden or rule-guarded field therefore needs a read rule at least as strict as the field it derives from: otherwise it hands to any reader what the source would have refused them.

The context

The ctx a hook receives is the request’s own RequestContext: the caller (ctx.subject(), ctx.has_role(..)), the typed claims, the API key identity and the request headers. A model with a computed field gets it filled, as a model with an authority or hooks does; Resource<M> hands the hook the context of the request it was extracted from, and tx.resource the context of the outer write.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use ferra::compute::{FerraComputeError, FerraComputed};
use ferra::request_context::RequestContext;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "invoices")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub subtotal: f64,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub viewed_by: Option<String>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}

impl FerraComputed for Model {
    async fn compute_field(
        &mut self,
        field: ModelComputed,
        ctx: &RequestContext,
    ) -> Result<(), FerraComputeError> {
        match field {
            ModelComputed::ViewedBy => self.viewed_by = ctx.subject().map(str::to_owned),
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
}
  • Credentials never reach it. Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie and the Foundry’s API key header are dropped when the context is built: ctx.header("authorization") answers None. The API key’s identity is there, the key is not.
  • Every other header is client-supplied. Never authorize on Host, X-Forwarded-*, Forwarded or Origin, and never build a URL or a link from them: a computed value is served in the response body, so a value derived from a header the client chose is a value the client chose.
  • Resource<M> and tx.resource apply the gate above. tx.resource reads inside the write’s transaction, so a hook of the write that reads a row of another computed model computes it there, for the caller of the write, with the outer request’s context (not a context built for that other model).

See RequestContext for the accessors.

When a hook fails

A hook that returns Err(FerraComputeError), or panics, fails the request. The answer is 500 internal with the fixed body ("internal server error"), and no part of the response is served: the rows computed before the failing one are dropped, never sent. A panic is caught, so the connection stays up.

Ferra writes one error! line for the request, not one per row, on the target ferra_http::hooks. It names the model (model) and the operation (operation: get, list, create, update, restore or action) and carries your FerraComputeError message as error, as the message of a HookError is logged: it is yours to keep free of values the logs must not hold. Ferra adds no row value of its own. A panic is logged as a computed field panicked, without its payload. The catch needs panic = "unwind": with panic = "abort" a panicking hook ends the process.

When it failsAnswerThe line says
on a read (GET, a list, /me)500computed field failed
on a read, the request budget runs out503 timeout, no partial bodynothing from the compute
on a write response, after the commit500; the write is committedcomputed field failed; the write is committed
on a write response, the post-commit deadline runs out500; the write is committedcommitted; computed field cut by the request budget

On a write the 500 does not undo anything: the row exists, the same as when after_commit fails. A client that replays the request can create a duplicate. From the first commit of the request on, every hook runs under the request’s one post-commit deadline, max(deadline, first post-commit work + 1 s), shared with after_commit (without a budget, nothing bounds it; see Behaviors) and a cut answers 500, never 503 timeout, because that answer says that nothing was written. That holds for a write response, and also for a read of a hand-written route after a Resource::create or an update of the same request, and for a tx.resource write in the hook of a later write. Before any commit the budget layer cuts the request itself with 503 timeout, and the transaction rolls back.

Idempotent creates

Ferra has no generic Idempotency-Key header. A client that cannot tell whether a POST was committed (a timeout, a 500 after the commit, a lost response) replays it, and a replay can create a duplicate. The recipe below makes the replay safe for the creates that carry a request key, with the database’s own UNIQUE constraint and nothing else from Ferra. A generic header would be additive and has its own trigger; it is not tied to the transactional outbox planned for 1.1.0.

The recipe covers creates that carry a request key. An update, a delete or an action that has an unknown outcome is recovered through its own contract (If-Match for a row’s tag, for instance), not through this recipe.

The model

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "keyed_orders")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
#[behavior(soft_delete)]
#[authorize(
    get = IsOwner,
    list = IsOwner,
    create = Authenticated,
    update = IsOwner,
    delete = IsOwner
)]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(owner)]
    pub owner_id: Uuid,
    #[field(filterable)]
    pub request_key: String,
    pub item: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
CREATE TABLE keyed_orders (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id UUID NOT NULL,
  request_key TEXT NOT NULL,
  item TEXT NOT NULL,
  deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL,
  UNIQUE (owner_id, request_key)
);

The client chooses request_key (a UUID per intended order is the usual choice) and sends the same one on every replay. Four parts of the declaration carry the guarantee:

  • request_key is NOT NULL. Postgres treats two NULL as distinct, so a row without a key would never collide with another and the constraint would guarantee nothing for it.
  • owner_id is set by the server. #[field(owner)] stamps it from the caller’s identity; a body that names it is a 422 unknown_field. The client cannot create a row in another owner’s name, nor choose which owner’s keys it collides with.
  • The owner is in the constraint. With UNIQUE (request_key) alone, a key would be global: one owner’s POST would answer 409 because another owner holds the key, an existence oracle across owners, and one owner could take another’s keys. With UNIQUE (owner_id, request_key) two owners can use the same key; each gets their own row, and neither learns that the other exists.
  • The read rules are part of the recipe. #[field(owner)] stamps the owner but does not scope reads. get = IsOwner and list = IsOwner are what keep the recovery GET to the caller’s own rows. Without them the recipe is unsafe: GET /keyed_orders?filter[request_key]=<key> returns another owner’s row, a cross-owner leak that doubles as a key-guessing oracle.

What a replay answers

A POST whose owner and key already hold a row answers 409 conflict, with the fixed detail of every conflict (it names no constraint, column or value), and nothing is written. Two concurrent POSTs with the same key give one 201 and one 409; the database decides, so there is no check-then-insert race.

A 409 is never a success. The constraint compares the owner and the key, never the body. A replay with a different body is a 409 too, and the stored row stays as the first request wrote it. A client that gets a 409 has not learned that its request was applied; it recovers the row and compares.

The recovery GET

GET /keyed_orders?filter[request_key]=<key>

returns the row to its owner, and an empty list to any other caller. A client that gets the 409 (or never saw the first answer) reads it back, checks that the item is what it meant to send, and carries on with that row’s:

  • id;
  • ETag;
  • _links.

A deleted row

  • soft_delete keeps the key. A soft-deleted row stays in the table, so its key stays taken: a replay answers 409, and the recovery GET, which leaves deleted rows out, returns nothing. The client has a 409 and nothing to recover. This is a limit of the recipe, not a bug: pick a new key for a new order, or restore the row (POST /keyed_orders/{id}/restore).
  • A hard delete frees the key. On a model without soft_delete, deleting the row removes the key with it, and a late replay creates a second row. The guarantee lasts as long as the key stays recorded. Use soft_delete for this recipe, or accept and state that window.

Not the same: client_pk

A model with #[ferra(client_pk)] lets the client choose the primary key in the create body, and a client could use it as a request key. It is not equivalent. The primary key is unique across the whole table, with no isolation per owner: a collision answers the same 409 conflict, whoever holds the row, so it tells a caller that some owner already uses the key. It also forces the client’s value into the key of the resource’s URL. Keep the recipe’s request_key column for replays.

What If-Match does not guard

If-Match guards PUT, PATCH, DELETE, restore and row actions. It guards no create (there is no row yet, so no tag to send) and no Resource<M> route of your own: the route creates or updates through Resource<M> under its own contract. A create made by a route of your own needs its own key and its own constraint.

pagination — collection-read parameters

Filterable, sortable, page- and cursor-paginated collection reads derived from a single Sea-ORM entity with the FerraModel derive: declare the safelist in the type system, get parameterised SQL, a documented OpenAPI surface and HAL navigation links for free.

This page is the authoritative user-guide for the collection-read query parameters: filter[<field>], sort, page, per_page, and cursor. A reader with only this page plus standard Rust knowledge produces a working filterable / sortable / cursor-paginated endpoint on the first attempt — no ADR, no constitution, and no framework source is required.

The two related pages — ferra-http.md (the handler layer) and ferra-openapi.md (the API specification surface) — describe the broader CRUD shape and the OpenAPI emission respectively. This page focuses exclusively on the collection-read parameter surface.

Dependencies. The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

Zero-to-filter in two lines

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(filterable)]               // ← that's the whole opt-in
    pub title: String,
    #[field(filterable)]
    pub director: String,
    pub release_year: i32,             // not filterable — no attribute
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Mount the model and issue a filtered request:

GET /films?filter[director]=Alice

You get a parameterised WHERE director = $1 SQL statement (Alice is bound, never interpolated), a 200 response carrying only Alice’s films, and an OpenAPI filter[director] query parameter on /docs/openapi.json describing the surface to consumers.

A request naming a non-safelisted field (?filter[release_year]=1999) returns HTTP 400 with application/problem+json:

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "filter field `release_year` is not filterable; allowed: director, title"
}

No database statement is issued for the rejected request — the safelist gate fires inside the extractor, before the handler runs.

Filtering

The #[field(filterable)] marker

Apply #[field(filterable)] to every field that should accept a filter[<field-name>]=<value> query parameter. The marker is the complete opt-in: a field with no marker accepts no filter. Per Constitution §I, the framework’s default posture is restrictive — a Film model that marks zero fields filterable accepts no filter[...] parameter; every request carrying ?filter[anything]=... returns 400 before any SQL is issued.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(filterable)]
    pub title: String,
    #[field(filterable)]
    pub director: String,
    pub internal_note: String,         // not exposed as a filter
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Multiple filter parameters compose as a single AND-joined WHERE:

GET /films?filter[director]=Alice&filter[title]=Citizen%20Kane

emits

SELECT ... FROM films
 WHERE director = $1 AND title = $2
 ORDER BY id ASC
 LIMIT $3

with $1=Alice and $2=Citizen Kane bound as typed Postgres parameters.

The parameter uses the field’s wire name: on a model that declares #[ferra(rename_all = "camelCase")], write filter[releaseYear]=… and sort=-releaseYear (see ferra-forge.md § Field names on the wire).

Allowed types

The filter wire shape carries a single string value per key, type-coerced at the extractor against the field’s underlying Rust type:

Rust typeAccepted value shapeFailure → rejection
Stringany string (incl. empty)never
i32 / i64base-10 integer literalfield … expects integer, received …
f64base-10 number literalfield … expects number, received …
bool"true" / "false"field … expects boolean, received …
uuid::Uuid / IdRFC 4122 hyphenated UUIDfield … expects uuid, received …
Option<T> (for the above)same as T; empty rejected¹same shape

¹ Empty strings on String / Option<String> are accepted as the empty string. Empty strings on every other type are a type-coercion failure per FR-007a’s closing clause.

ferra::DateTime, ferra::Date and ferra::Time fields (and their Option) are filtered like the others, and also with comparison operators (next section).

Operators and date fields

filter[<field>]=<v> is equality; it is the same as filter[<field>][eq]=<v>. On a ferra::DateTime, Date or Time field (and their Option), four comparison operators are available as well: gt, gte, lt, lte.

GET /events?filter[starts_at][gte]=2026-10-03T00:00:00Z&filter[starts_at][lt]=2026-10-04T00:00:00Z
GET /events?filter[day]=2026-10-03

Two operators on one field are two parameters, so a range is filter[f][gt]=…&filter[f][lt]=…. A comparison on any other type (filter[title][gt]=a), or an operator that does not exist (filter[f][between]=…), is 400 with the code unsupported_operator; so is empty brackets, filter[f][]=v, which is not equality (the error names the declared field, filter[f][], after the filter safelist has accepted f). A NULL matches no comparison.

The values have one spelling each, so a client does not depend on what a date library happens to accept:

TypeAcceptedRefused (400 invalid_date)
DateTimeRFC 3339 in UTC: 2026-10-03T10:00:00Z or 2026-10-03T10:00:00+00:00 (+ is %2B in a URL), with an optional fractionany other offset (+01:00), -00:00, a lowercase t or z, a space for the T, a [Europe/Paris] annotation, a date alone
Date2026-10-03a date-time, a date that does not exist
Time10:00:00 or 10:00:00.25any offset, Z, a missing seconds part

A DateTime is stored to the microsecond, and a filter value is cut to the microsecond, like the values a model writes.

Rejection shapes

The extractor produces one of two rejection shapes, both with application/problem+json content type and type: https://ferra.rs/errors/validation:

Unsafelisted filter field (?filter[release_year]=1999 on a model that does not mark release_year as filterable):

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "filter field `release_year` is not filterable; allowed: director, title"
}

detail names the rejected field AND lists the allowed filterable set in stable alphabetical order. A model that marks zero fields filterable rejects every ?filter[...]= request with "no fields on this resource are filterable".

A field with a #[field(read = …)] rule (0.13.0) is in the allowed set of the callers who may read it only: a caller who may not read salary gets this same rejection for ?filter[salary]=… and for ?sort=salary, with an allowed list that leaves salary out, byte for byte what a model without the field answers. See ferra-auth.md § Field rules.

Filter value type-coercion failure (?filter[release_year]=not-a-number when release_year is i32):

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "field `release_year` expects integer, received `not-a-number`"
}

detail names the field AND the expected JSON-schema type. The framework MUST NOT issue any database statement for either rejection shape — the gate runs inside the extractor.

Compile-time gates

A field marked #[field(filterable)] AND #[ferra(skip)] simultaneously fails to compile with diagnostic FRG-350 (bad and good example, compiled):

error: FRG-350: field `internal_note` cannot be both `#[ferra(skip)]` and `#[field(filterable)]`
         help: remove `#[ferra(skip)]` to expose the field, or remove the `filterable` / `sortable` marker to keep the field internal
         note: a field invisible to the API surface cannot be addressable from the API surface as a filter or sort key; see Spec 011 FR-003
  --> src/models/task.rs:18:9
   |
18 |     pub internal_note: String,
   |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A field invisible to the API surface cannot be addressable from the API surface as a filter key — the contradiction is decidable from the field’s declaration alone, so it lives at compile time per Constitution §III.

OpenAPI surface

Every filterable field surfaces in the generated OpenAPI document as a query parameter on the model’s GET /{resource} operation:

parameters:
  - name: filter[director]
    in: query
    required: false
    schema:
      type: string
    description: Filter on `director` (exact-match equality predicate). See …
  - name: filter[title]
    in: query
    required: false
    schema:
      type: string
    description: Filter on `title` (exact-match equality predicate). See …

Parameters appear in stable alphabetical order by field name. Adding a new #[field(filterable)] to a model automatically widens the OpenAPI parameter set on the next emission — no parallel parameter list to maintain.

Edge cases

  • Duplicate keys: a key Ferra reads (filter[…], sort, page, per_page, cursor) that appears twice, after percent-decoding, is 400 with the code duplicate_parameter, and no statement runs. filter[title] and filter[title][eq] are one key; filter[at][gt] and filter[at][lt] are two. A key Ferra does not read (?utm=a&utm=b) is left alone. Before 0.11.0 the last value won.
  • filter[f][]=v: empty brackets are the operator [], which no field supports: 400 unsupported_operator, raised after the safelist check, naming only the declared field. Before 0.12.0 it read as equality. In Rust, CollectionQuery::with_filter("f[eq]", v) filters by equality like filter[f][eq]=v (it used to fail).
  • page=abc: a page or per_page that is not a non-negative integer is 400 with the code invalid_parameter, naming the parameter. Before 0.11.0 it fell back to the default. A valid number out of range is still clamped (page=0 is 1, per_page above 100 is 100; no Warning header since 0.12.0, the body’s per_page is the applied value).
  • Filter on a cursor-mode model: filter parameters compose with cursor pagination — the §Cursor pagination section (added at US3) describes the composition.
  • Composite-PK models: filter parameters address individual columns, not the composite key. Filtering on a composite PK column works the same as filtering on any other field.

Sorting

The #[field(sortable)] marker

Apply #[field(sortable)] to every field that should accept a sort=<field-name> (ascending) or sort=-<field-name> (descending) query parameter. The marker is the complete opt-in — a field with no marker is not addressable as a sort key. Per Constitution §I, the default posture is restrictive.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(filterable, sortable)]
    pub title: String,
    #[field(sortable)]
    pub release_year: i32,
    pub director: String,           // not sortable
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The parameter uses the field’s wire name: on a model that declares #[ferra(rename_all = "camelCase")], write filter[releaseYear]=… and sort=-releaseYear (see ferra-forge.md § Field names on the wire).

Direction marker

The single sort query parameter encodes both the field name and the direction via a leading-minus convention:

Wire formSQL emission
?sort=titleORDER BY title ASC
?sort=-titleORDER BY title DESC
?sort=-release_yearORDER BY release_year DESC
(omitted)ORDER BY <primary-key> ASC

The omitted-sort default is deterministic: ORDER BY <primary-key-col> ASC. Repeated identical requests return rows in identical order. Two rows whose sort-column values are equal are tiebroken by the primary-key default. Composite-PK models tiebreak on primary_key_fields[0] per the declaration-order rule pinned in ADR-0029.

Where NULL sorts

Ferra writes no NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST, so a nullable sortable field (Option<T>) sorts as PostgreSQL sorts: a row whose value is NULL comes last for ?sort=year and first for ?sort=-year. Rows with equal values, NULL included, are then ordered by primary key ascending. A test pins both directions, so changing this later is a listed change, not a silent one.

A cursor key is never nullable (FRG-352), so a cursor walk has no NULL to place; the rule above is the page-mode one.

One sort criterion

sort names one field. ?sort=title,year is not a list of two criteria: the whole string title,year is looked up as a field name, is not one, and the answer is the 400 not_sortable of the next section. Ties are broken by the primary key, never by a second field of yours.

Resource<M>::list in a route of your own has no 400 to give for a sort the generated route would refuse: a sort on a field that is not #[field(sortable)], or that the caller may not read, keeps the default order (primary key ascending). Name the field by its Rust name there.

Rejection shape

A request naming a non-safelisted sort field (?sort=director when director is not marked sortable) returns HTTP 400 with application/problem+json:

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "sort field `director` is not sortable; allowed: release_year, title"
}

detail names the rejected field AND lists the allowed sortable set in stable alphabetical order. No fuzzy matching — a typo on the field name (?sort=titles) lands here too, not as a closest-match substitution.

Compile-time gate

A field marked #[field(sortable)] AND #[ferra(skip)] simultaneously fails to compile with the same FRG-350 diagnostic the filterable+skip case produces — the two markers share the same gate per FR-003.

OpenAPI surface

Every sortable field surfaces in the generated OpenAPI document as a single enum-constrained sort parameter on the model’s GET /{resource} operation. The enum carries both the bare-name and leading-minus form for every sortable field, alphabetised across field names:

parameters:
  - name: sort
    in: query
    required: false
    schema:
      type: string
      enum:
        - release_year
        - "-release_year"
        - title
        - "-title"
    description: Sort the collection by one of 2 fields (ascending by default; leading `-` selects descending). When omitted, results are ordered by the model's primary-key column ascending. See …

Adding a new #[field(sortable)] to a model automatically widens this enum on the next emission — no parallel enum to maintain.

Composition with filtering

Filter and sort parameters compose in a single SQL statement:

GET /films?filter[director]=Alice&sort=-release_year

emits

SELECT ... FROM films
 WHERE director = $1
 ORDER BY release_year DESC
 LIMIT $2

with $1=Alice bound as a typed parameter. The composition is WHERE <filter-predicates-AND-composed> ORDER BY <sort-col> <direction> in deterministic order.

Order is always total. Without sort, a collection is ordered by primary key. With sort, rows with equal sort values are ordered by primary key. The same request therefore returns the same rows in the same order, page after page.

Filters and sorts name the field; the SQL uses the field’s column, including one renamed with #[sea_orm(column_name = "...")].

Pagination modes

Every Ferra model carries one of three pagination postures, set via the model-level #[ferra(pagination = …)] attribute. The posture controls which query-string parameters the collection endpoint accepts:

ModeAccepted parametersDefault?When to use
page?page=, ?per_page=, ?filter[...], ?sort=yes (absent attribute)Small collections, admin UIs needing page numbers / total counts.
cursor?per_page=, ?cursor=, ?filter[...], ?sort=noDeep-pageable collections, infinite-scroll UIs, AI agents traversing data.
bothAll of the above (mutually exclusive: ?cursor and ?page cannot co-occur)noPublic APIs that need to serve both paging shapes without versioning.

page is the framework default to preserve byte-identical behaviour for collections that existed before 0.7.5. Opting into cursor or both is a single line:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(pagination = "cursor")]    // ← opt-in
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(cursor_key)]            // ← exactly one field
    pub created_id: i64,
    pub title: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The framework rejects mismatched parameters at the extractor boundary — no SQL is issued for the rejected request. Each rejection surfaces with https://ferra.rs/errors/validation:

  • ?cursor=… on a page-mode model → detail: "model effective pagination mode is page; cursor parameter is not accepted".
  • ?page=2 on a cursor-mode model → detail: "model effective pagination mode is cursor; page parameter is not accepted".
  • ?cursor=…&page=2 on a both-mode model → detail: "cursor and page are mutually exclusive on this collection".

Page size

per_page defaults to 20 and is held to 1..100 silently: ?per_page=500 answers 200 with at most 100 rows, ?per_page=0 answers one row per page, and neither answers a 400 or a Warning header (RFC 9111 §5.5 obsoletes Warning). The applied size is the one to read: a page-mode body carries per_page: 100, and, in the HAL representation, each of its links (self, first, prev, next, last) repeats per_page=100. Only a per_page that is not a non-negative integer, or does not fit 32 bits (above 4294967295), is refused (invalid_parameter, see Edge cases). Resource<M>::list and list_cursor hold the same bounds.

Cursor pagination

Cursor pagination (also called keyset pagination) tracks the boundary of the previous page via an opaque cursor token instead of an offset. It has two qualities page pagination lacks:

  1. O(log N) on every page. The SQL emits WHERE <cursor-key> > $1 OR (<cursor-key> = $1 AND <pk> > $2) ORDER BY <cursor-key> ASC, <pk> ASC LIMIT N, which traverses the cursor-key index directly. A cursor read walks the collection in cursor-key order, ascending or, with sort=-<key>, descending; a descending walk emits WHERE <cursor-key> < $1 OR (<cursor-key> = $1 AND <pk> < $2) ORDER BY <cursor-key> DESC, <pk> DESC LIMIT N. Deep pages cost the same as the first page — no OFFSET cliff.
  2. Stable under concurrent inserts. A row inserted between two requests appears at its correct keyset position; no row disappears, no row duplicates. Page-mode ?page=2 shifts every row by one when a new row is inserted ahead of the page boundary.

Accepted cursor-key shapes

The #[field(cursor_key)] marker names the column the framework orders by. The accepted types are ferra::Id / Uuid, i64, and (0.11.0) ferra::DateTime, ferra::Date and ferra::Time; a cursor_key field of any other type fails to compile with FRG-351. A date key pages in time order, newest first with sort=-<key>; it need not be unique (the primary key breaks ties, below), and the cursor brings the key back to the microsecond the database keeps. The model’s ferra::Id key, which the server generates as a UUID v7, still sorts by creation time.

Keys need not be unique: on a model with a single-column primary key, the cursor carries the boundary row’s key and primary key, and rows with equal keys are ordered by primary key — no row is skipped or repeated between pages.

Cursor token opacity

The token is a URL-safe base64 string. Consumers MUST treat it as a single opaque value — pass it through unmodified, don’t parse it, don’t reconstruct it. The framework reserves the right to change the internal encoding in a future minor release while continuing to accept previously-issued tokens for one release window. Since 0.11.0 a token also carries the direction of the walk; a token issued by 0.10.0 is read as an ascending one, so a walk in flight when a server is upgraded goes on. The token is not signed, so a caller can build one by hand. A token of the right shape is read, and all it does is choose the row after which the page starts. It cannot widen what the caller may see: the caller’s authorization scope and the request’s filters are applied to every row returned, whatever the token says.

A malformed cursor produces HTTP 400 with the dedicated URI:

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/invalid_cursor",
  "title": "Invalid Cursor",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "the supplied cursor token is invalid; drop the `cursor` query parameter and restart pagination"
}

A cursor that decodes but does not fit the collection — a key of the wrong type, or a token issued before 0.9.0 — is refused the same way, before any query runs.

The framework never echoes the bad cursor bytes back to the consumer — the detail is a fixed recovery hint regardless of which decode step failed (base64 decode, JSON parse, shape mismatch, or unknown version byte). The recovery is always the same: drop the cursor parameter and restart pagination from the first page.

Cursor + filter trade-off

Cursor and filter compose in a single SQL statement:

GET /films?filter[director]=Alice&cursor=<token>&per_page=20

emits

SELECT ... FROM films
 WHERE deleted_at IS NULL       -- inherited from #[behavior(soft_delete)]
   AND (created_id > $1 OR (created_id = $2 AND id > $3))  -- cursor predicate: [key, primary key]
   AND director = $4            -- filter predicate
 ORDER BY created_id ASC, id ASC
 LIMIT $5

On a descending walk (?sort=-created_id) the two comparisons of the cursor predicate are < and the order is created_id DESC, id DESC.

The trade-off: cursor stability is per-request, not cross-request. A cursor issued on a request with ?filter[director]=Alice addresses “the next row after the boundary, filtered to Alice’s films”. If a follow-up request changes the filter to ?filter[director]=Bob, the same cursor is still meaningful — it addresses the next row after the (created_id, id) boundary — but the resulting page is filtered to Bob’s films, which may overlap, undershoot, or overshoot the originally-intended traversal. Consumers traversing a filtered cursor stream should keep the filter constant for the duration of the traversal.

Cursor + sort restriction

A cursor-paginated read walks the collection in the order of its cursor key: ascending by default, descending with a leading -. Whenever the cursor path serves the request (a cursor-mode model, or a both-mode model called with ?cursor=…) the sort parameter, if present, must name the cursor key:

RequestAnswer
?cursor=<token>200, ascending by the cursor key
?cursor=<token>&sort=created_id200, same order
?cursor=<token>&sort=-created_id200, descending, if the token was issued for a descending walk
?cursor=<ascending token>&sort=-created_id400 invalid_cursor: the token is for the other direction
?cursor=<token>&sort=title400 — title is not the cursor key

A descending walk starts without a cursor: ?sort=-created_id. The next link of a page carries sort and the request’s filter[...], so following it continues the walk. When you build the next request yourself from next_cursor (the flat representation has no links), repeat sort and the filters: a token keeps the direction it was issued for, and a request that sorts the other way is refused with the same invalid_cursor as a malformed token.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "sort field `title` does not match the cursor key `created_id`; cursor pagination requires `sort` to target the cursor key when present"
}

The request is refused rather than answered in another order than the one it asked for. The OpenAPI document of a cursor-mode model lists the cursor key and its - form as the only sort values.

Cursor + soft-delete composition

A model enrolled in #[behavior(soft_delete)] automatically excludes soft-deleted rows from every framework-generated SELECT — the same predicate composition that protects find_by_id and the page-mode find_collection applies to the cursor path by construction:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(pagination = "cursor")]
#[behavior(soft_delete)]               // ← inherited filter
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(cursor_key)]
    pub created_id: i64,
    pub title: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The cursor-mode SQL emits WHERE deleted_at IS NULL AND created_id > $1 automatically — soft-deleted rows are invisible to the cursor traversal. Restoring a soft-deleted row inserts it back into the cursor stream at its created_id position; subsequent cursor walks include it.

Cursor compile-time diagnostics

The cursor surface is compile-checked end-to-end. Four diagnostics surface at cargo check:

  • FRG-351 — cursor-key type not in the accepted set. Fires when #[field(cursor_key)] is applied to a String, a custom struct, or any type outside the closed list above (Id, Uuid, i64, DateTime, Date, Time). The diagnostic names the accepted shapes.

  • FRG-352 — cursor-key field is Option<T> (or a tuple with an Option<T> component).
