  • One version for the whole workspace, one git tag per release: v0.9.0, v0.9.1, v0.10.0. Nothing is published on crates.io.

  • An application depends on a tag, and on the facade only:

    ferra = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.17.0" }

  • A tag is never moved. CHANGELOG.md has one section per tag.

What the contract is

The contract is what the ferra crate exports, and nothing else:

  • the FerraModel derive and its attributes (#[ferra(...)], #[field(...)], #[authorize(...)], #[behavior(...)]), with the FRG- code of each refusal, and #[ferra(action(...))] with ActionBody, the derive and trait that type an action’s body;
  • Foundry, FoundryBuilder and their options;
  • JwtConfig and its types; the FerraIdentity trait; testing::bearer;
  • Id, DateTime, Date, Time;
  • the error types, and the problem+json documents they render — status, type URI, title;
  • ferra::hooks: FerraHooks, Saving, Saved, Committed, HookTx (with HookTx::system), TxResource, SystemAccess, and HookError, what an application’s hook or action handler returns to refuse a write;
  • for a route of your own: Resource, ResourceHandle, CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, Page, CursorPage, FerraPath, FerraJson, FerraAuthLayer, the two middlewares, CurrentUser;
  • the description of a model, to read: meta, model. Operation is a #[non_exhaustive] enum with the variant Action(name) since 0.14.0, so an authority matches it explicitly (see below); ModelMeta::actions lists a model’s actions, and OperationMeta and ModelMeta::operations are removed (only the derive used them);
  • the Cargo features observability and test-support;
  • the HTTP behavior of the generated routes: paths, methods, statuses, the shape of bodies and of the OpenAPI document.

The exact list, name by name, is api/ferra.txt; the signatures are in the other files of api/.

Not in the contract, whatever its visibility:

  • the implementation crates taken directly (ferra-core, ferra-db, ferra-forge, ferra-http, ferra-openapi): depend on ferra;
  • everything #[doc(hidden)] — the __private modules, the constructors of the meta types, ferra::ferra_core, ferra::ferra_http, FerraDraft, NoHooks, Hooked, ComputedFields, NoActions, Actioned, FerraActions, ApplyDraft, FerraHooksDeclared, FerraSystemOnly, FerraNotBlameable, FerraSystemGrant, HookRunner and ActionRunner, the write transaction WriteTx of ferra-db and its entry points (begin, commit, lock_row, lock_rows, insert_row, update_row, delete_row, soft_delete_row, restore_row, row_at, lock_parent_shared). It exists for the derive’s generated code and for Ferra’s own crates, and changes without notice;
  • the code the derive generates: read it with cargo expand, do not call it;
  • the text of a log event, of a detail member, of a compiler diagnostic beyond its FRG- code;
  • the inside of a cursor: it is an opaque string, hand it back as it came.

The repository is not in the contract

Since 0.10.0 the repository (PgRepository, FerraRepository, DatabaseTransaction, FerraDbError) and FerraState are not exported: a route of your own reaches a model’s rows through Resource<M>, which applies the model’s rules. See migrating-to-0.10.md.

What a version number means

Ferra is 0.x: it follows Semantic Versioning as Cargo reads it for 0.x.

From → toMay it break the contract?What you do
v0.9.0 → v0.9.1 (patch)No. Fixes and additions only.Change the tag.
v0.9.x → v0.10.0 (minor)Yes, each break listed in CHANGELOG.md under “Changed — breaking”, with what to do.Read the changelog, change the tag, follow the compiler.
v0.x → v1.0.0Yes, for the last time without a major bump.Same.

Two exceptions, both written in the changelog when they happen:

  • A security fix may change behavior in a patch release — a request that was wrongly served is refused. Refusing more is never held back for a minor.
  • Becoming more permissive is not a break. A 400 that becomes a 200 (a filter on a date field, a descending cursor walk), a new optional attribute, a new variant of a #[non_exhaustive] enum (Operation::Action: an authority whose can ends in _ => true allows it, so end the match with _ => false and name Action(_), see migrating-to-0.14.md), a new method on Resource, a new field on a meta type, a new member in a response object: all are additions (a client ignores members it does not know).

A removed attribute keeps a migration diagnostic for at least one minor version: the compiler says what to write instead (as FRG-105, FRG-106 and FRG-335 do for what 0.9.0 removed).

Metrics and spans

With the observability feature, Ferra records five metrics. With or without it, each request has a request span and its phase spans (the names and labels are in observability.md). The compatibility rule: from 0.18.0, a metric’s name, unit and label set are frozen (a new label is a new metric); a new value of a closed label is an addition; span attributes are add-only; Ferra’s names are the dotted OpenTelemetry names and translating them is the exporter’s job, with both Prometheus spellings shown: http_server_request_duration_seconds with OpenTelemetry exporters by default and with metrics-exporter-prometheus under with_recommended_naming(true), http_server_request_duration otherwise; and the metrics major is in the table of third-party crates in the contract, below.

Third-party crates in the contract

Types of other crates appear in Ferra’s signatures, and two crates are re-exported whole. A major version change of one of them is a break of Ferra, made in a minor release and listed in the changelog.

CrateWhere you meet itVersion
axumFoundry::build() returns an axum::Router; extractors, middlewares0.8
Sea-ORMferra::sea_orm, whole; the entity derives; DatabaseConnection2.x
gardeferra::garde, whole; ValidationErrors::from_garde_report0.23
metricswith observability, Ferra records through its facade: the recorder you install (metrics-exporter-prometheus, observability.md) must be built on the same copy0.24
tower-httpFerraLayerBuilder::cors, trace_layer0.7
secrecyJwtConfig::single_secret takes impl Into<SecretString>0.10
serdeevery model derives it1
uuidConditionType is implemented for uuid::Uuid: a Uuid column is a Field<M, Uuid> (ADR-0070)1

What ferra::sea_orm and ferra::garde contain is theirs, under their own version numbers: Ferra’s snapshots do not cover it, and no tool can see inside a re-export. Four things stand in for that:

  • Five of them are exact requirements. garde, utoipa-scalar, jiff, tower-http and base64 are declared =x.y.z in Ferra’s manifests. If your application also names one of them, it must name the same version (or a requirement that version satisfies): another patch fails to resolve. A patch of one of them, for an advisory for instance, reaches you in a Ferra patch release.
  • Sea-ORM is a public dependency of Ferra. A new major version of Sea-ORM (or a new minor of garde, a 0.x crate) is a breaking change of Ferra: it ships in a minor release, and the changelog says so.
  • Your sea-orm follows Ferra’s major. The documented way to use Sea-ORM is to declare sea-orm yourself, at the major version the release you use was built with. Each release’s changelog names it and gives the line to change in your Cargo.toml. A different major is two copies of the crate; #[derive(FerraModel)] refuses it with FRG-400, and cargo tree -d -i sea-orm shows it. Declaring no sea-orm and writing ferra::sea_orm::… is supported as well.
  • A gate pins it. reexport_pin fails CI when the lockfile holds two copies of sea-orm, garde or metrics, or another version than the one documented here; changing the pin is a decision made in one change with this page and the changelog. A new metrics minor (0.x) is a breaking change of Ferra too: a recorder built on another copy would receive none of Ferra’s metrics.

Sea-ORM in Ferra’s signatures

Ferra’s own signatures name a Sea-ORM type in four places only:

  1. the ferra::sea_orm re-export and the prelude’s glob of its entity prelude;
  2. the constructors that take the application’s connection, Foundry::new(DatabaseConnection) and api_key::PgApiKeyStore::new(DatabaseConnection), and the DatabaseConnection re-export;
  3. the trait bounds that make a model a Sea-ORM entity (Mountable’s, the builder’s, Resource’s, HookTx::resource’s and SystemAccess’s where clauses: ModelTrait, EntityTrait, ActiveModelTrait, ActiveModelBehavior, FromQueryResult, IntoActiveModel, IntoValueTuple, PrimaryKeyTrait), and PkValue<M>, the key type the entity declares;
  4. the trait impls that make a Ferra value type (Id, Date, DateTime, Time) a Sea-ORM column (feature sea-orm of ferra-core).

The rule for later lots: no other Ferra-owned signature names a Sea-ORM type. That covers hooks, authority, actions, computed fields, the request context and resource access: they take and return Ferra’s types (FerraError, Resource<M>). Your own code reaches Sea-ORM through your own DatabaseConnection, outside Ferra’s contract.

The gate sea_orm_surface reads api/*.txt and fails on any other line that names sea_orm::. The internal items of ferra-db (PgRepository, FerraRepository, FerraDbError, WriteGuard) are not in the facade; the gate lists them apart.

Rust version

  • The minimum supported Rust version is 1.94, checked in CI. Raising it is allowed in a minor release, never in a patch, and is listed in the changelog.
  • The repository pins the toolchain it is developed with (rust-toolchain.toml); an application is free to use a newer one.
  • Ferra builds and tests natively on Linux, macOS and Windows. What is proven: a real trial on Windows 11 on 2026-09-30, before lot L4, built the workspace, ran both test suites and check_compile_error_spans there. The checklist L4.28 runs it again on the final state of the lot, with a default clone; until it has passed, the claim rests on that first trial.

What is planned, and will not break you

Each of these is an addition under the rules above: an external authenticator next to .with_auth (RS256/JWKS, sessions); a response envelope for custom routes.

How the contract is kept

Four gates block CI (CONTRIBUTING.md has the commands):

  • public_api_snapshot — the public API of each crate is a text file under api/. Any difference fails until the snapshot is regenerated and committed with the change, which makes every change of the contract visible in review.
  • semver_checks — cargo-semver-checks compares each crate with the previous tag: a break without the minor version bump that allows it fails.
  • sea_orm_surface — fails when a line of api/ names sea_orm:: outside the places listed in “Sea-ORM in Ferra’s signatures”.
  • reexport_pin — ferra::sea_orm and ferra::garde are the crates themselves, and neither of the two gates above can see inside a re-export: this one fails when Cargo.lock holds two copies of either, or a version other than the documented one (Sea-ORM 2.x, garde 0.23.x). It pins metrics (0.24.x) the same way, the facade Ferra records its metrics through.

And one test names the contract item by item (crates/ferra/tests/contract_surface.rs), so that removing one breaks the build on the stable toolchain too.

Migrating from 0.16 to 0.17

0.17.0 (Soaking) makes a service under load answer what it can, and says so when it cannot. Each entry below is a change you may notice. This page grows with the release: read the entries, then update the application’s git dependency to v0.17.0. CHANGELOG.md lists every change.

A pool that gives no connection answers 503, not 500

Before. A request that waited for a database connection longer than the pool’s acquire_timeout answered 500 internal, the same as any database failure.

After. It answers 503 service_unavailable, with the fixed detail “the service could not handle the request in time; this operation was not applied”, and no Retry-After. The answer comes before the operation: nothing was applied and no hook ran, so the client may retry (an earlier write of a route of your own stands). A database that is down or starting gives the same 503 once the acquire_timeout elapses, because the pool retries a refused connection until then. A connection the database refuses at once (a wrong password, an unknown database) stays a 500 internal. One warn line, target ferra_db::pool, holds the resource and a fixed text. The OpenAPI document now declares the 503 (the one ServiceUnavailable response) on every operation, a read as well as a write. After a commit, if the pool gives no connection for the parents of the row just written, the answer is still a 500 with one error line, because the write stands.

Who is affected. A client, a gateway or an alert that treats 500 as “the service is broken” and 503 as “retry later”, or that matches the 500 of a saturated pool. A client generated from the OpenAPI document, which now sees a 503 on every operation, must be regenerated.

Migration. Treat 503 service_unavailable as transient: retry it with a backoff and full jitter, since no Retry-After is sent. Move any alert on a pool 500 to the 503 and to the ferra_db::pool line. Set the pool’s acquire_timeout under the request budget, so that the pool answers and not the budget’s timeout. See service_unavailable.

A failed COMMIT writes one ferra_db::commit line

A COMMIT the database fails no longer writes the generic “a database error answered 500” line (target ferra_http::error); it writes one ferra_db::commit error line with resource, outcome and db.response.status_code, and the answer is still the 500. An alert on the old line goes quiet for a failed COMMIT: move it to the new target.

Resource and TxResource create and update return Option<Read>

Before. Resource::create, Resource::update, TxResource::create and TxResource::update returned Result<Read, FerraError>: the row the call had written, whether or not the caller could read it. A route that echoed it sent a row the generated route would have kept back.

After. They return Result<Option<Read>, FerraError>. None means the row is written and the caller may not read it under the generated route’s rule: the get rule on the row, then the authority’s can(Get), mounted or not. An authority that panics or fails on the written row counts as “may not read” (one error line on ferra_http::policy; panic = "abort" defeats the catch). When it is None nothing derived from the row leaves the call: no computed field is called. The generated route answers that caller 201 or 204 with no body, no Location and no id in any header; your route should too. None comes only after a successful write: a refusal, a validation error and a row the caller cannot reach for update (the absent row’s 404) stay an Err, as before. SystemAccess::insert and SystemAccess::latest are unchanged: they return the whole row, read-checked by nothing, and it never belongs in a response.

Who is affected. Code that uses the value of one of the four calls: a route of your own, and a hook that reads what tx.resource::<N>().create(..) or .update(..) returns. A call whose value you drop (.await?;) compiles unchanged.

Migration. Replace let row = films.update(id, patch).await?; by let Some(row) = films.update(id, patch).await? else { return Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT.into_response()) }; (a create answers StatusCode::CREATED there, with no Location). A handler that answers Json(films.create(v).await?) now sends null for None: answer a status with no body instead. See Custom handlers.

A handler panic answers 500 internal, not a closed connection

Before. A panic in a generated route, in a route of your own added with .route before build(), in an extractor or in a layer of the stack ended the connection: the client saw no response, and the operator’s error rate, the request metric and the request span omitted the request.

After. The panic answers 500 internal with the constant body, Cache-Control: no-store and Vary. The request is observed once, with error.type 500 and ferra.error.type internal (with the observability feature), and one error line, target ferra_http::observe, “a handler panicked”, is written. The panic’s message is client-influenced text: it is in no body, label, span field or tracing line. The process’s panic hook (stderr by default) still prints it. The answer is made outside the per-model CORS layer, so it carries no Access-Control-Allow-Origin: a browser on another origin sees a CORS failure, not the 500. A row committed before the panic stands. panic = "abort" in your profile defeats the catch: the process ends. A route merged into the router after build() is outside the stack and is not caught.

Who is affected. A client or a gateway that treated a closed connection as the signal of a handler bug, and an alert that counted such closures: the panic is now a 500 in the metrics and the span.

Migration. Alert on 500 and on the ferra_http::observe line. Do not rely on a panic to cancel a write: a panic after a commit leaves the row written. See Custom handlers and internal.

Every response writes one ferra_http::request line

Before. The only line a request wrote was the one tower_http wrote in a model’s own stack, so a 401, a 404 for an unknown route and the 503 of .request_budget(..) wrote none, and an operator who set tower_http to a quiet level silenced what there was.

After. From 0.17.0 each response writes one tracing event, target ferra_http::request, inside the request span. Its fields are http.request.method, http.route, http.response.status_code, ferra.error.type and latency_ms, and nothing else: no path, query, header, token, claim, body or cookie value. http.route is absent when no route matched, and ferra.error.type when the answer is not a Ferra problem. The level follows the status: error for 500, warn for 503, info for everything else, so a 502 or 504 your own handler answers is info (alert on error.type on the histogram or the span). The refusal events and the lines of 0.17.0’s pool and COMMIT work (ferra_http::credential, ferra_http::auth, ferra_http::rate_limit, ferra_db::pool, ferra_db::commit, ferra_http::error) are unchanged and are written beside it.

Who is affected.

  • An operator who filtered tower_http to keep the logs short: that filter no longer silences the request line, which has its own target, and the default trace layer no longer writes its tower_http line. Every request writes one, GETs included, so set ferra_http::request to the level you want (RUST_LOG=ferra_http::request=warn keeps the 503 and the 500).
  • A test or an alert that counts the error lines of a 500: the request line is one more, at error. Select by target (ferra_http::request or not) rather than by level alone.

Migration. Add ferra_http::request to the log filter, and move an alert on a tower_http access line to it. The line, its levels and the other targets are in observability.md.

The request span has one name per attribute, and api_key.prefix is gone

Before. Each model’s own stack opened a span named request with the fields method, path, credential and, for an accepted API key, api_key.prefix. A 401, a 404 for an unknown route and a hand-written route had none, and a 500 also wrote the ERROR event “response failed” from tower_http.

After. From 0.17.0 one span per request is opened by the layer build() puts outside everything, so it exists for every response, and the per-model span and its INFO line are gone. Its attributes are a closed set, in the names of OpenTelemetry’s HTTP semantic conventions:

BeforeAfter
methodhttp.request.method (_OTHER for an extension method)
pathurl.path (the path as received, percent-encoded, no query)
credentialcredential, unchanged (token, cookie or api_key); recorded only for a credential Ferra verified
api_key.prefixdropped from the span; the prefix is on the warn of a refused key (ferra_http::credential)
(none)otel.name, otel.kind, http.route, network.protocol.version, http.response.status_code, ferra.error.type, and on a 5xx error.type and otel.status_code

A write also has four child spans: ferra.authorize, ferra.hook (with hook), ferra.db.write (one per attempt, so the number of them shows the retries) and ferra.after_commit. Each carries resource and operation and no outcome, id, SQLSTATE or error text. The ERROR event “response failed” is gone: a 500 is the request line at error.

Who is affected.

  • A subscriber or a collector that masks, drops or indexes the field path: it must now name url.path, or the path is no longer masked (SEC-047). The same goes for method → http.request.method.
  • A dashboard or an alert on api_key.prefix of an accepted request: no span carries it any more. A refused key still writes its prefix on the warn.
  • A layer you pass to FerraLayer::trace_layer still runs, beside the request span and its line; the default one, which wrote the old span and the old line, is gone.

Migration. Rename path and method in the masking and indexing rules, move an alert on the old line to ferra_http::request, and read the credential kind from credential on the request span. The span and its phase spans are in observability.md.

Migrating from 0.15 to 0.16

0.16.0 (Brazing) serves a model’s relations under each side’s own rules. Each entry below is a change you may notice. This page grows with the release: read the entries, then update the application’s git dependency to v0.16.0. CHANGELOG.md lists every change.

New routes appear: a parent and its child

Before. A HasMany or a HasOne was a declaration Ferra did not serve. A child was reached on its own path only.

After. An application that mounts a parent and its child gets new routes; here is how to remove them. When both sides of a HasMany or HasOne are mounted on the same Foundry, it serves GET and POST {parent}/{id}/{relation} (GET /films/{id}/reviews, POST /films/{id}/reviews), with no change in your code. They allow nothing the child’s own path does not, plus the parent’s refusals (it must be readable, and updatable for a POST); they appear in the OpenAPI document, and they go through the child’s layers. Sub-collections states the rules.

Who is affected. An application that mounts a parent and its child, both derived in the dense form. The routes are extra: a client that does not call them sees no change. If you do not want them exposed, for example because a gateway lists the allowed paths or a test pins the set of routes, remove them.

Migration. There is nothing to do to keep them. To remove them, either write the parent in the split form (a model with no relation field has no sub-collection, and none of the other features of its relations), or do not mount the child. There is no per-relation opt-out yet.

A relation named like a row action or restore of its own model would take the path of that route, so build() (and try_build()) refuses it with BuildError::RelationNameCollision, naming the model and both names. Rename the relation or the action.

Every write opens at READ COMMITTED

Before. A write ran at the server’s default_transaction_isolation, except the write of a model with a system grant, which already opened at READ COMMITTED.

After. Every write Ferra opens (the generated routes, Resource<M>, and the transaction a hook borrows) runs at READ COMMITTED, whatever the server’s default says. The protocol that keeps a parent’s check valid against a concurrent child write needs it. PostgreSQL’s own default is READ COMMITTED, so an application on that default changes nothing.

Who is affected. An application whose connection defaults to REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE loses the detection of lost updates in its hooks: a hook that reads a row through tx.resource and writes it back computed from that read no longer gets 40001. Under a SERIALIZABLE default, read-write anomalies across rows are likewise no longer detected. A write of the row’s own model is not affected, because before_* hooks receive the locked row.

Migration. Compute the new value in the target row’s own hook or action, where the row is locked. HTTP clients keep If-Match; tx.resource evaluates none. See Transactions.

The owner(from) foreign key is immutable

Before. A PUT or a PATCH that named the foreign key of a model with owner(from = ..) moved the row under another parent of the same owner (a 200), and an action could return the row with another key.

After. The key is set when the row is created and never changes. A PUT or a PATCH naming it is the 422 unknown_field that any key outside the write set gets, whatever value it names, with nothing written. A PUT that leaves it out keeps the row under its parent. A row action whose handler changes it is a 500 internal, and the same refusal applies to Resource::update and tx.resource().update. The OpenAPI document no longer lists the key in the PUT and PATCH request schemas of such a model; it stays in the POST one.

Who is affected. A client that sends the whole record back on a PUT, key included (the usual read-modify-write), now gets the 422. A client generated from the OpenAPI document must be regenerated.

Migration. Stop sending the key on PUT and PATCH. To move a child, delete it and create it again; the new row has a new identity (see Relations).

A child’s hook cannot write the parent it holds

Before. A hook of a model with owner(from = ..) could update or delete, through tx.resource, the parent its write holds FOR SHARE. The UPDATE asked for FOR UPDATE on a row the transaction only shared, and deadlocked against the parent’s other children in flight (40P01, retried, then the 503 retry_exhausted).

After. The call is refused before any statement: FerraError::Internal, the write answered 500 internal, one error! that names the child’s resource, the parent’s resource, the operation and the fix, and no key value. The refusal poisons the write, so a hook that swallows it still commits nothing. A read of the parent, a sibling create and a write of a row the write does not hold are unchanged, and so is a parent’s own action writing its children.

Who is affected. A hook that keeps a counter or a status on the parent (tx.resource::<Film>().update(..) from a review’s after_save, for instance).

Migration. Write the parent from its own action, or compute the value on read. See Relations.

A PUT of an owner(from) model reads the row first

A PUT of a model with owner(from = ..) now reads the row before it judges the body, so a bad body (a wrong type, an unknown key) on an absent row is the 404, no longer the 400 or 422. Nothing to migrate unless a client relied on the body’s refusal for a row that does not exist.

An exhausted retry is FerraError::RetryExhausted

Before. A Resource<M> write that the database aborted on each of its three attempts returned a FerraError::Internal over a private cause, which answered 503 retry_exhausted wherever it was returned. The public enum had no variant for it.

After. It returns the unit variant FerraError::RetryExhausted (wire type retry_exhausted, 503, Retry-After: 1; the status, title and detail do not change). A hook’s tx.resource write that gave up reaches the caller as the same variant, through the outer write. FerraError is #[non_exhaustive], so a match with a wildcard arm still compiles.

Who is affected. A route of your own that matches FerraError::Internal(_) to tell an exhausted retry from a 500: it no longer sees it, and the request falls to your other arms.

Migration. Add an arm for FerraError::RetryExhausted and answer it as a transient 503. Never replay the write in a loop of your own: the three attempts already ran. See Transient conflicts are retried.

A #[sea_orm(ignore)] field needs #[ferra(computed)]

Before. A field with #[sea_orm(ignore)] and no #[ferra(computed)] compiled. It has no column, so Sea-ORM built it with Default on every read, and Ferra served that value as the row’s.

After. The derive refuses it: FRG-364, spanned on the ignore (the code).

Who is affected. A model that keeps an in-memory field in its Model struct without computing it.

Migration. Add #[ferra(computed)] and the impl FerraComputed for Model that fills the field (an empty impl serves its Default, as before, but says so). Or move the field out of the model, into a type of your own or a Resource<M> route.

A composite foreign key is refused

Before. A relation with from = "(studio_id, studio_region)" compiled. The foreign-key gate reads one column, so it saw none: the key was served, and a write naming an unreadable parent was accepted.

After. The derive refuses it: FRG-365, spanned on the string (the code).

Who is affected. A model with a relation keyed by several columns.

Migration. Give the relation one foreign-key column, or keep the composite key out of the model’s relations.

The relations are typed, and the back key is checked at build()

Before. Foundry did not read the relation fields of a model. A HasMany whose target had no BelongsTo back, or two, built without complaint.

After. The derive emits one typed marker per relation, Mountable carries a hidden bound that reads them, and build() (and try_build()) refuses a HasMany or HasOne whose target is mounted on the same Foundry and has none, or more than one, BelongsTo back to the model: BuildError::RelationBackKey, naming both models, the relations and the fix. A pair with a single side mounted is not checked.

Who is affected. An application that mounts both sides of a HasMany or HasOne whose target has two BelongsTo back (two keys to the same parent), or none. A model written by hand against Mountable, without the derive.

Migration. Derived models: none, unless build() refuses a pair. Then keep exactly one BelongsTo back, or mount only one of the two models. A hand-written model also implements the hidden, derive-only FerraRelations for its entity (type Relations = (); when it declares no relation); it is outside the contract and may change. See Declaring relations.

Projections that embed each other are refused at build()

Before. A projection could not embed a relation.

After. A read list may name a BelongsTo (Embedding), and build() (and try_build()) refuses a loop of embeds: BuildError::EmbedCycle, with the path as resource names (the table name unless resource = says otherwise), from the first node the walk meets again (Embedding cycle: `films.summary → studios.summary → films.summary`; remove one embed from a `read` list.).

Who is affected. An application that adds embeds to the projections of two mounted models that point at each other.

Migration. Remove one embed from a read list; the relation stays a link.

The foreign key of a BelongsTo follows the readability of its parent

Before. A row served its foreign key (film_id) to everyone who could read the row, whatever they could read of the parent. FerraViews::Read held it as a plain value.

After. A caller who may not read the parent gets no key and no film link in _links: the member is absent, never null (a key that is NULL stays null, with no link). It holds on every response that serializes the row: item, list, /me, the write responses, each projection prefix, Resource<M> and a hook’s tx.resource. “May read the parent” is the get of GET {parent item}: its rule, its authority, its owner condition and soft delete. Ferra decides it with one extra SELECT ... WHERE key IN (...) per BelongsTo per page. A parent that is not mounted on the Foundry is read by nobody, so its key and link are absent for everyone. In FerraViews::Read the key is an Option (Option<Option<T>> for a nullable key). A PUT does not need to carry a key the caller may not read: the stored value is kept. The OpenAPI read schema no longer lists the key in required, and says it is absent when the caller may not read it.

Who is affected. A client that reads the foreign key of a model whose parent some callers cannot read. A hand-written route that reads read.film_id from Resource::get, Resource::list or tx.resource(). A client generated from the OpenAPI document (the key is optional now).

Migration. Treat the key as optional on the client. In a route of yours, if let Some(id) = read.film_id, or read.film_id.flatten() for a nullable key. An app that counted the statements of a read sees one more per BelongsTo. See Links and foreign keys.

A write naming a foreign key reads its target

Before. A create, PUT or PATCH that set the key of a plain BelongsTo (no owner(from)) wrote it whatever the caller could read of the target: a row the caller could not read was accepted (201 or 200), and a row that does not exist was a 500 internal (SQLSTATE 23503).

After. The target is read under the caller’s read scope in the write’s transaction, without a lock. A target that is absent, soft-deleted, unreadable by the caller or not mounted on the Foundry is the 422 reference_not_found on the key, byte for byte the same in each case, and nothing is written. It holds through Resource<M> and a hook’s tx.resource. null and a write that does not name the key read nothing.

Who is affected. A client that wrote a key to a row it cannot read (it now gets the 422), or that handled the 500 of an absent one. A model whose BelongsTo target is not mounted on the same Foundry: its key can only be null through the API now, unless a before_save hook sets it from another value of the body. An app that counted the statements of a write sees one more per key named.

Migration. Handle the 422 reference_not_found as “that reference does not exist for you”. Mount the target model if callers must be able to point at it. See Writing a foreign key.

A create of an owner(from) model needs its parent mounted

Before. Since 0.13.0 a create of a model with owner(from = ..) accepted a key whose parent the caller cannot GET: a parent that the get rule refuses (GET {parent} answers 403), a parent that the default projection’s rule refuses (404), or a parent that is not mounted on the Foundry. The caller wrote a row (201) under a parent it cannot read.

After. The key is judged as GET {parent} judges the parent, for the caller. A parent that is refused by the get rule or by the default projection’s rule, or that is not mounted (an unmounted parent is read by nobody, whatever the value), is the one 422 reference_not_found on the key, the bytes of an absent parent, with nothing written. It holds for the route, Resource::create and a hook’s tx.resource. See Writing a foreign key.

Who is affected. An application whose owner(from) child is created by a caller that cannot GET the parent (a role that may create reviews but whose get on films is refused, say), or whose parent model is not mounted on the same Foundry as the child.

Migration. Mount the parent model, and give each caller that creates children a get on it (and a default projection that admits them). Handle the 422 reference_not_found as “that parent does not exist for you”.

A hand-written FerraModel derives its column table

Before. Ferra parsed a field’s name into its Sea-ORM column, which failed for a field such as film_1.

After. The derive emits the table from each field to its column, and no code parses a name. A FerraModel written by hand gets None from the hidden column_of_field: every request that needs a column (a write of a field, a sort, a filter) is a 500 or a refusal.

Who is affected. A model that implements FerraModel by hand. A derived model: nobody.

Migration. Derive FerraModel.

A delete a foreign key refuses is a 409

Before. A DELETE that a foreign-key constraint refused (a film that still has reviews under ON DELETE RESTRICT) was a 500 internal, and so was a write the database refused for a foreign key after Ferra’s read (the target removed in between).

After. The delete is the 409 conflict with its fixed detail: nothing is deleted, the statement is run once, and the OpenAPI document declares the 409 on the DELETE of every model that a BelongsTo targets. The write is the 422 reference_not_found on the key the constraint names, the bytes of an absent target. The log holds the constraint’s name, never a key value. ferra_db::FerraDbError gains the variant ForeignKey { constraint } (it is #[non_exhaustive]: a match on it already has a wildcard arm).

Who is affected. A client or a monitor that treated that 500 as a server fault. A generated client that now sees a 409 on a DELETE. An application that matches FerraDbError exhaustively with a wildcard that assumed a database failure.

Migration. Handle the 409 on a DELETE as “this row is still referenced”. See Deleting a parent.

Migrating from 0.14 to 0.15

0.15.0 (Alloying) describes a model without invalid states. Each entry below is a break. This page grows with the release: read the entries, then update the application’s git dependency to v0.15.0. CHANGELOG.md lists every change.

FieldMeta loses its six flags and is_id: read mode

Before. ferra_core::meta::FieldMeta carried seven independent booleans, readable, writable, skip_api, read_only, write_only, computed and is_id. Any combination compiled, including the ones that mean nothing (a field that is readable and skip_api).

After. A field has one mode: FieldMode, and four const fn methods answer the questions the flags answered. FieldMode is #[non_exhaustive]: Key { read_only }, ReadWrite, ReadOnly, WriteOnly, Computed and Hidden (#[ferra(skip)]). See FieldMeta for what each variant answers.

FieldMeta::new and FieldMeta::new_with_collection_meta take a FieldMode in place of the seven flag parameters. Both are #[doc(hidden)]: the derive is the way to build a description.

Migration. Code that reads a FieldMeta (a loop over meta().fields) changes like this:

You readRead instead
f.readablef.readable()
f.writablef.writable(), which is false on a computed field
f.is_idf.is_id()
f.read_onlyf.is_read_only(), or matches!(f.mode, FieldMode::ReadOnly)
f.computedmatches!(f.mode, FieldMode::Computed)
f.write_onlymatches!(f.mode, FieldMode::WriteOnly)
f.skip_apimatches!(f.mode, FieldMode::Hidden)

A skip field that also carried read_only had f.read_only == true; f.is_read_only() answers false for it, because the field is Hidden and never appears in a document. No output changes.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::meta::{FieldMeta, FieldMode};

fn is_served(field: &FieldMeta) -> bool {
    field.readable() && !matches!(field.mode, FieldMode::Hidden)
}
}

skip with write_only or computed, or on a primary key, is refused (FRG-359)

Before. #[ferra(skip, write_only)] compiled. The field was absent from the description, the OpenAPI document and PATCH, yet POST and PUT on the bare path still wrote it. skip with computed, and skip or computed on a primary key, compiled and did nothing useful.

After. Each of the four is a compile error, FRG-359, spanned on the skip (on the computed when there is no skip).

Migration. Remove skip to keep a field the API accepts and never returns (write_only), or remove the other attribute to keep a field the API never touches (skip). On a primary key, keep neither.

A computed field has no column: add #[sea_orm(ignore)] (FRG-360, FRG-361)

Before. A #[ferra(computed)] field was a column the framework never wrote: the table held it (NULL), SELECT read it, and filterable, sortable or cursor_key on it compiled, although the value the server computes is not what the column holds.

After. A computed field is #[sea_orm(ignore)]: Sea-ORM leaves it out of every SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE, and builds it with Default (the type must implement it). Without the attribute the model is refused with FRG-360, spanned on the computed. filterable, sortable and cursor_key on a computed field are refused with FRG-361, spanned on the key.

Migration. Three steps, in this order:

  1. Add #[sea_orm(ignore)] above each #[ferra(computed)] field, and remove filterable, sortable and cursor_key from it.
  2. Add a migration that drops the column (ALTER TABLE invoices DROP COLUMN total;). Do not edit the migration that created it.
  3. Rewrite the impl FerraComputed per field (next entry). A response still carries the computed value, and a write body that names the field is still a 422 unknown_field.
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "invoices")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub subtotal: f64,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)] // new in 0.15: the field has no column
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub total: Option<f64>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
impl ferra::compute::FerraComputed for Model {}
}

A computed field needs an impl FerraComputed, even unmounted (FRG-362)

Before. A model with a #[ferra(computed)] field and no impl FerraComputed compiled as long as it was never mounted; the error came only at Foundry::mount (rustc’s E0277 on Mountable).

After. It does not compile: FRG-362, on the computed field, names the impl to write. Write impl FerraComputed for Model {} (the default hooks compute nothing) or the per-field hooks.

FerraComputed computes one field at a time: match on ModelComputed

Before. FerraComputed had three methods, compute(&mut self), compute_async(&mut self, ctx) and compute_async_batch(rows, ctx), none told which field it computed. A model with two computed fields filled both in the same body.

After. The trait has two, compute_field(&mut self, field, ctx) and compute_field_batch(rows, field, ctx), and Ferra calls compute_field_batch once for each computed field, with that field’s rows. field is a variant of ModelComputed, an enum the derive writes next to the model, one variant per computed field in PascalCase (total is ModelComputed::Total). A model with no computed field is unchanged: the derive still writes the empty impl FerraComputed.

Migration. Write the impl FerraComputed as a match on the field. A synchronous computation goes in the async body; compute_async takes the same body, and compute_async_batch takes the new field parameter.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use ferra::compute::{FerraComputeError, FerraComputed};
use ferra::request_context::RequestContext;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "invoices")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub subtotal: f64,
    pub tax: f64,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub total: Option<f64>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}

// 0.14: fn compute(&mut self) { self.total = Some(self.subtotal + self.tax); }
impl FerraComputed for Model {
    async fn compute_field(
        &mut self,
        field: ModelComputed,
        _ctx: &RequestContext,
    ) -> Result<(), FerraComputeError> {
        match field {
            ModelComputed::Total => self.total = Some(self.subtotal + self.tax),
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
}

A hand-written FerraModel that also implements FerraComputed now needs the #[doc(hidden)] trait ComputedFields as well; it is outside the derive’s guarantees, as a hand-built ModelMeta is. Computed fields is the page of the feature.

A write_only owner column is no longer in the write body

Before. On a model whose #[field(owner)] column was also #[ferra(write_only)], the bare-path write body named the owner, while the description, the OpenAPI document and PATCH left it out. POST without owner_id answered 400 invalid_json (missing field owner_id); POST with it answered 201, the value replaced by the caller’s identity; PUT with it answered 200, the value dropped. A plain owner column answered 422 unknown_field to both.

After. The owner is not in the write body, whatever its other attributes. POST without owner_id answers 201 and the owner is the identity; POST or PUT with owner_id answers 422 unknown_field.

Migration. Remove owner_id from the bodies your clients send to such a model. Nothing in the OpenAPI document changes.

PaginationMode carries the cursor key: read pagination_mode.cursor_key()

Before. ModelMeta held the mode and, beside it, cursor_key_field_name: Option<&'static str> and cursor_key_field_type: Option<FieldType>. A cursor model with None in either compiled.

After. PaginationMode is #[non_exhaustive]: Page, Cursor { key, ty } and Both { key, ty }, so a cursor mode cannot exist without its key. The two ModelMeta members are gone, and PaginationMode::cursor_key() answers Some((key, ty)) for Cursor and Both, None for Page. A page-mode model no longer reports a #[field(cursor_key)] field. The hidden constructors ModelMeta::new_with_pagination and ModelMeta::new_with_auth lose the two key parameters.

Migration.

You readRead instead
meta.cursor_key_field_namemeta.pagination_mode.cursor_key().map(|(key, _)| key)
meta.cursor_key_field_typemeta.pagination_mode.cursor_key().map(|(_, ty)| ty)
meta.pagination_mode == PaginationMode::Cursormatches!(meta.pagination_mode, PaginationMode::Cursor { .. })
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::meta::{FieldType, PaginationMode};

fn cursor_key(mode: PaginationMode) -> Option<(&'static str, FieldType)> {
    match mode {
        PaginationMode::Cursor { key, ty } | PaginationMode::Both { key, ty } => Some((key, ty)),
        _ => None,
    }
}
}

FieldMeta::validation_rules is typed: match ValidationRule

Before. validation_rules was a &'static [&'static str]: each #[field(...)] rule encoded as a short string ("min_length=1", "min=0", "pattern=^a$", "email", "required"), which the OpenAPI emitter parsed again and silently dropped when it did not know it.

After. validation_rules is a &'static [ValidationRule]. ValidationRule is #[non_exhaustive]: MinLength(u64), MaxLength(u64), Min(Bound), Max(Bound), Pattern(&'static str), Email, Url and Required, with Bound::{Int(i64), Float(f64)}. The derive emits them from the parse that also produces the request validator, and ValidationRule::schema_keyword() gives the JSON Schema keyword the document carries. The hidden FieldMeta::new, FieldMeta::new_with_collection_meta and FieldMetaInit take the typed slice. The emitted OpenAPI document does not change.

Migration.

You read or writeUse instead
"min_length=3", "max_length=3"ValidationRule::MinLength(3), ValidationRule::MaxLength(3)
"min=0", "max=1.5"ValidationRule::Min(Bound::Int(0)), ValidationRule::Max(Bound::Float(1.5))
"pattern=^a$"ValidationRule::Pattern("^a$")
"email", "url", "required"ValidationRule::Email, ValidationRule::Url, ValidationRule::Required
rules.contains(&"required")rules.contains(&ValidationRule::Required)
parsing the string to a JSON Schema keywordrule.schema_keyword()
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::meta::{FieldMeta, ValidationRule};

fn is_required(field: &FieldMeta) -> bool {
    field.validation_rules.contains(&ValidationRule::Required)
}
}

A write body is decoded once: send each key once

Before. A key sent twice in a POST, PUT or PATCH body was read differently by each step. On a model with hooks, POST and PUT answered 500 internal (the hooks’ draft refused the duplicate that the first decoding had taken). On a model with rename_all, or without hooks, POST, PUT and PATCH succeeded with the last value, and a repeated key inside a JSON field was stored with its last value. In a declared action’s body, an unknown key sent twice was a 422 unknown_field.

After. The body is parsed once, and a key repeated in any object, at any depth, a JSON field included, is a 400 validation, code invalid_json, field body, whose message is a key is repeated at line L column C (no value of the body). The same holds for an action’s body, known key or not: a repeated unknown key is now a 400 invalid_json instead of a 422 unknown_field.

The refusals of a write also come in one order: the row’s 404 (when something reads the row; otherwise a PUT or a PATCH with no precondition header judges the body first), then 415, 412, 413, 400, the 422 unknown_field, the 403, the 422 of the bounds and the rules, and last the 400 of a required key the body does not send, so that a hidden required key never answers differently from an absent one. The visible change is that a body with an unknown key and a wrong-typed value on a key the caller may read is now the 400, where it was the 422. The type of a key the caller may not read is never judged: it is still the 422 unknown_field of an unknown key.

Migration. Send each key once. A client that builds a body by merging objects should merge before it serializes. Nothing in the OpenAPI document changes.

Migrating from 0.13 to 0.14

0.14.0 (Riveting) removes declarations that read as a restriction and restricted nothing, and changes some behavior of the writes. Each entry below is a break. Most stop a 0.13 application from compiling; four change what it does with no compile error (the OpenAPI names, Resource::update, an authority that ends in _ => true, and a hook that writes its own row, the last entry). Read the entries, then update the application’s git dependency to v0.14.0. CHANGELOG.md lists every change.

groups is a compile error (FRG-137)

Before. #[ferra(groups = [...])] on a field, and groups = [...] inside projection(...), compiled. Ferra parsed the key and dropped it: the field was served on every read and accepted in the default write body, whatever the list, the empty list groups = [] included. A password hash declared with #[ferra(groups = [])] was served to every caller allowed to read the model.

After. The key is refused whatever its value, on a field, inside projection(...) and on the struct, with FRG-137, spanned on the groups key. FieldMeta::groups (ferra_core::meta::FieldMeta) is removed: it was always empty. FRG-306 (skip next to a non-empty groups) is retired with it.

Migration. Replace groups with what Ferra enforces:

You wrote groups to…Write instead
keep a field out of every response and write body#[ferra(skip)]
accept a field on write and never serve it (a password)#[ferra(write_only)]
choose the fields of a shaperead = [...] and write = [...] on a projection(...), see Projections and routing
serve or accept a field only to some callers#[field(read = …)] and #[field(write = …)], see Authentication and Authorization
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "users")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[ferra(write_only)]
    pub password_hash: String,
    #[ferra(skip)]
    pub internal_notes: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Code that reads FieldMeta::groups (a loop over meta().fields) no longer compiles: delete the loop. The slice was empty for every field, so the loop never ran.

A Ferra attribute where the derive does not read it is a compile error (FRG-138)

Before. The derive declares the helper attributes ferra, field, behavior, operation and authorize, so the compiler accepted each of them on the struct and on every field, and Ferra read each in one place only. A #[field(owner)] written on the struct marked no field as the owner; an #[authorize(...)] or #[behavior(...)] written on a field declared nothing. The model compiled, and the declaration did nothing.

After. Each of these is refused with FRG-138, spanned on the attribute path:

You wroteWhere it goes instead
#[field(...)] on the structon the field it describes
#[authorize(...)] on a fieldon the struct; a rule for one field is #[field(read = …, write = …)]
#[behavior(...)] on a fieldon the struct
#[operation(...)] on a fieldnowhere: add the route yourself with .route(...), see Custom handlers

Migration. Build, and move or remove each attribute the compiler points at. A model that carried a struct-level #[field(owner)] had no owner field: check that the rows are still protected as you meant, then put #[field(owner)] on the column that holds the owner.

#[ferra(hooks)] on a system_only model is a compile error (FRG-135)

Before. A #[ferra(system_only)] model is a table that only a system grant writes (see System grant). It could declare #[ferra(hooks)] and an impl FerraHooks. It compiled, and the hooks never ran: the model serves no write, and a grant inserts into it without running its hooks.

After. The hooks key on a system_only model is refused with FRG-135, spanned on hooks, as a write rule on it already was. The hooks of a grant are those of the model that declares the grant, never the target’s.

Migration. Delete hooks and the impl FerraHooks from the system_only model. That code never ran, so nothing is lost. If it was meant to write an entry into the model, move it to the impl FerraHooks of the model whose writes it records, and call tx.system().insert(..) there:

#[ferra(system_only)]                                   // the log model: no `hooks`, no `impl FerraHooks`
#[ferra(auth = "bearer", hooks(system = log::Model))]   // the hooked model: it owns the hooks and the grant

promotes_from off a default projection, or malformed, is a compile error (FRG-316)

Before. promotes_from compiled on a projection without default = true, where it was read and dropped, and with any string as its value, "v1" or the name of a projection that does not exist included. Only the presence of the key was checked, and only next to default = true.

After. FRG-316 refuses promotes_from on a projection without default = true, spanned on the key, and a value that is neither "auto-derived" nor "named:<name>" with <name> another projection declared in the same model (never the projection itself), spanned on the value. The value is still not checked against repository history: a former named default that you removed in the same change can no longer be named; write "auto-derived".

Migration. Remove promotes_from from a projection that is not the default. Write the value of a promoted projection as "auto-derived", or as "named:" followed by the name of a projection the model declares.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(projection(name = "v1", read = [id, title]))]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "v2",
    default = true,
    promotes_from = "v1",
    breaking_change_version = "0.2.0",
    read = [id, title],
))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(projection(name = "v1", read = [id, title]))]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "v2",
    default = true,
    promotes_from = "named:v1",
    breaking_change_version = "0.2.0",
    read = [id, title],

    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
}
